=== NOTES 4:0 | The Universe and the Solar System – Origin Theories, the Sun, Planets, Asteroids, Comets, Meteors
## SUB 0 | Planets – Superlatives, Moons and Planet Facts
[0:0:0] # Superlatives (asked most)
[0:0:1] TABLE head: Feature | Planet
  [0:0:1.0] Nearest to the Sun, smallest, shortest year (88 days), fastest orbit, least mass | Mercury
  [0:0:1.1] Closest to Earth on average (stays nearest longest) | Mercury (APPSC 2019)
  [0:0:1.2] Hottest (~464°C, CO₂ greenhouse), brightest planet, Morning/Evening Star, Earth's twin, nearest at closest approach (41.4 million km) | Venus
  [0:0:1.3] Densest (5.5 g/cm³) | Earth
  [0:0:1.4] Red Planet; day 24 h 37 min and axial tilt 25°12' almost identical to Earth's (23 h 56 min; 23°30') | Mars
  [0:0:1.5] Largest, heaviest (~318 Earth masses), fastest spin (~10 h) | Jupiter
  [0:0:1.6] Least dense (0.7 g/cm³, less than water); most famous rings; looks yellowish; second largest | Saturn
  [0:0:1.7] Rotates on its side; lowest single temperature (~–224°C); blue-green (methane) | Uranus
  [0:0:1.8] Farthest planet, coldest on average (~–200°C), longest year among planets (164.9 yr) | Neptune
  [0:0:1.9] Retrograde (east-to-west) rotation | Venus and Uranus
  [0:0:1.10] No natural satellite | Mercury and Venus (APPSC 2019: Venus)
[0:0:2] - **Earth's twin:** **Venus** – close to the Earth in **size, mass and density** (APPSC G1; asked 4 times).
[0:0:3] - **Hottest = Venus, not Mercury** (thick CO₂ atmosphere traps heat although Mercury is nearer the Sun); **Saturn is warmer than Neptune** (nearer the Sun).
[0:0:4] - **Nearest planet to Earth:** traditional key **Venus** (closest approach 41.4 million km), then **Mars** (78.4 million km) when Venus is not offered; on a time-averaged basis Mercury is closest.
[0:0:5] - **Brightness:** Venus is the brightest planet, but the **Moon** is brighter than Venus, so "Venus is the brightest object after the Sun" is **false** (CDS 2009 A-R: A false, R true).
[0:0:6] - **Rings:** **Saturn** (famous), but **Jupiter, Uranus and Neptune also have rings** – "Saturn is the only ringed planet" is false.
[0:0:7] - **Atmospheres:** Jupiter, Saturn = mostly **hydrogen and helium**; Uranus, Neptune = H, He + **methane** (blue-green tint; "ice giants"); **Mars = carbon dioxide** (95%), so "H, He and methane on Mars" is wrong.
[0:0:8] - **Mars water:** a **subsurface lake** of liquid water under the **south polar ice cap** was reported in *Science* on **25–26 July 2018** (MARSIS radar, Mars Express).
[0:0:9] - **Pluto** (dwarf planet since 2006) has the longest year of all (**247.9 years**); it was farther in than **Neptune** from **1979 to 1999**, when Neptune was the farthest.
[0:0:10] # Moons
[0:0:11] TABLE head: Moon | Planet | Fact
  [0:0:11.0] Ganymede | Jupiter | Largest moon of the solar system (5,268 km), bigger than Mercury
  [0:0:11.1] Titan | Saturn | Saturn's largest (Rhea 2nd); thick nitrogen atmosphere; methane lakes ~100 m deep (APPSC 2019)
  [0:0:11.2] Europa | Jupiter | Ocean under an icy crust
  [0:0:11.3] Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto | Jupiter | Galilean moons (Galileo, 1610)
  [0:0:11.4] Phobos, Deimos | Mars | Mars's two moons
  [0:0:11.5] Charon | Pluto | Largest of Pluto's 5 (Charon, Styx, Nix, Kerberos, Hydra)
  [0:0:11.6] The Moon | Earth | Earth's only natural satellite
[0:0:12] - **Most moons: Saturn** – 274 after 128 were confirmed (March 2025); **March 2026**: the Minor Planet Center added 15 (**11 Saturn, 4 Jupiter**) → **Saturn 285, Jupiter 101** (as of 2026).
[0:0:13] - **History of the "most moons" key:** **Jupiter led until 2019** (63 v. 61–62 in 2009; 79 v. 62 in 2018); **Saturn took the lead in October 2019** (82) – keys of 2009/2011 papers that said Jupiter are now outdated.
[0:0:14] > Statement angle (CGPSC 2020): "Mercury hottest" ✗ (Venus); "Ganymede satellite of Saturn" ✗ (Jupiter); "Neptune has methane / rings" ✓; "Phobos and Deimos – Mars" ✓ → "3 and 4".
[0:0:15] ~~ Sources: Rocket General Geography #1 p.2-4; NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 01 p.9-13; PMF Physical Geography 01 p.31-32; earthsky.org / space.com (moon counts, March 2026); app notes 4:0 sub 5-6
[0:0:16] - **Jupiter's rings:** faint rings of fine **dust (silicate/rocky particles)** knocked off its small inner moons – not gases.
[0:0:17] - **NGTS-4b** ('forbidden planet', 2019): a **Neptune-sized** exoplanet found in the **'Neptunian desert'** close to its star, where such planets were thought unable to survive.
## SUB 1 | Distance Units, Light Travel and the Universe
[0:1:0] # Units of astronomical distance
[0:1:1] TABLE head: Unit | Meaning | Value
  [0:1:1.0] Astronomical unit (AU) | Mean Earth–Sun distance | ~149.6 million km (149.598 × 10⁶ km)
  [0:1:1.1] Light year | Distance light travels in one year | 9.461 × 10¹² km (~9.46 trillion km)
  [0:1:1.2] Parsec | Largest of the three | 3.26 light years
[0:1:2] - **Light year = distance, not time** (asked 9 times); it is the unit for **distances of stars**. Sun–Earth = **1 AU**.
[0:1:3] - **Why light years:** the **speed of light is constant** (~3 × 10⁵ km/s) (UPSC 2021).
[0:1:4] - **"4.3 light years away"** (Alpha Centauri) = its light takes **4.3 years** to reach Earth.
[0:1:5] - **Sunlight reaches Earth in 8 min 19 s** (~**500 seconds**, "about 8 minutes").
[0:1:6] - **Order of size:** AU < light year < parsec. **Not** distance units: mile/fathom are not used for stars; "longsec" is not a unit at all.
[0:1:7] - **Cepheids** (stars that brighten and dim) are used to measure astronomical distances.
[0:1:8] # The universe
[0:1:9] - **Cosmology** = study of the origin, evolution and structure of the **universe**.
[0:1:10] - **Age of the universe: 13.8 billion years** (APPSC 2019). **Age of the Earth: ~4.54 billion years** (~4.6 billion for the solar system).
[0:1:11] - **Most abundant element** in the universe and in the Sun: **hydrogen**, then **helium** (Sun ~74% H, ~24% He).
[0:1:12] - **Milky Way** = **barred spiral galaxy**; the Sun lies in the **Orion Arm**, ~26,000 light years from the centre, and takes **~225–250 million years (~25 crore years)** to go once round the galactic centre (a "galactic year").
[0:1:13] - **Constellations:** **88** recognised by the **IAU** (founded 1919, Paris).
[0:1:14] - News terms **event horizon, singularity, string theory, Standard Model** belong to the observation and understanding of the **universe** (UPSC 2017).
[0:1:15] ~~ Sources: Rocket General Geography #1 p.5-6; PMF Physical Geography 01 p.8, p.19; NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 01 p.7; app notes 4:0 sub 0
[0:1:16] - **Cosmic dust:** tiny solid particles of matter spread throughout space (interplanetary and interstellar dust).
[0:1:17] - **Moonlight reaches Earth in ~1.3 seconds** (384,400 km ÷ 3 × 10⁵ km/s).
## SUB 2 | Planets – Order, Distance, Size and Classification
[0:2:0] # Order and data
[0:2:1] TABLE head: Planet | Distance from Sun (million km) | Diameter (km) | Revolution | Density (g/cm³)
  [0:2:1.0] Mercury | 57.9 | 4,879 | 88 days | 5.4
  [0:2:1.1] Venus | 108.2 | 12,104 | 224.7 days | 5.2
  [0:2:1.2] Earth | 149.6 | 12,756 | 365.25 days | 5.5
  [0:2:1.3] Mars | 228 | 6,792 | 687 days | 3.9
  [0:2:1.4] Jupiter | 778.5 | 142,984 | 11.86 years | 1.3
  [0:2:1.5] Saturn | 1,432 | 120,536 | 29.4 years | 0.7
  [0:2:1.6] Uranus | 2,867 | 51,118 | 84.07 years | 1.3
  [0:2:1.7] Neptune | 4,515 | 49,528 | 164.9 years | 1.6
[0:2:2] - **Order from the Sun:** Mercury → Venus → **Earth** → Mars → **Jupiter → Saturn** → Uranus → Neptune (Pluto, dwarf, beyond).
[0:2:3]   - Between Mars and Uranus: **Jupiter and Saturn** (UPSC 2008); Earth lies between **Venus and Mars**; between the Sun and Earth: **Mercury and Venus**.
[0:2:4] - **Size (decreasing):** **Jupiter > Saturn > Uranus > Neptune > Earth > Venus > Mars > Mercury**; Venus is the only listed planet just **smaller than Earth**.
[0:2:5] - **Number of planets:** **8** since the IAU decision of **August 2006** (Pluto dropped); **9** before 2006.
[0:2:6] - **Period rises with distance:** a smaller orbit gives a **shorter year** (if the Sun–Earth distance fell by a quarter, the year would be shorter). Tropical year: **365 d 6 h 9 min 9.51 s**.
[0:2:7] # Classification
[0:2:8] - **Inner / terrestrial planets:** **Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars** – rocky, dense, solid surface; lie **between the Sun and the asteroid belt**.
[0:2:9] - **Outer / Jovian planets:** **Jupiter, Saturn** (**gas giants**), **Uranus, Neptune** (**ice giants**) – beyond the asteroid belt, thick H-He atmospheres.
[0:2:10] - **Planets are non-luminous** – they **shine by reflected sunlight**; stars twinkle, planets do not. The Sun's gravity gives the **centripetal force** that keeps planets in orbit.
[0:2:11] ~~ Sources: Rocket General Geography #1 p.2-4; NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 01 p.8-9; app notes 4:0 sub 0, 5
## SUB 3 | Stars – Nearest Star, Colour, Brightness, Twinkling and Constellations
[0:3:0] # Nearest stars
[0:3:1] - **Nearest star to Earth: the Sun**; next: **Proxima Centauri** (4.2 ly), part of the **Alpha Centauri** system (4.37 ly).
[0:3:2] - **Sirius** (Dog Star, in Canis Major) = **brightest star** of the night sky; found by following the line of **Orion's belt** – as the Pole Star is found with Ursa Major.
[0:3:3] # Colour, brightness, twinkling
[0:3:4] - **Colour of a star = its surface temperature** (asked 3 times): **blue** (hottest, 50,000–28,000 K) → white → **yellow** (Sun, 6,000–4,900 K) → orange → **red** (coolest).
[0:3:5]   - Decreasing temperature: **Blue, White, Yellow, Orange, Red**.
[0:3:6] - **Apparent brightness** depends on a star's **size, temperature and distance from the Earth**.
[0:3:7] - **Magnitude:** lower number = brighter (logarithmic); **absolute magnitude** = brightness at **10 parsecs**.
[0:3:8] - **Twinkling:** starlight passing through the atmosphere is refracted by air of **fluctuating density / temperature** (changing **refractive index**); stars twinkle because they are **very distant** point sources; planets do not.
[0:3:9] - **In space** (no atmosphere): the **sky is black** and **stars do not twinkle**.
[0:3:10] - Hubble's first direct image of the surface of another star: **Betelgeuse** (red supergiant in Orion).
[0:3:11] # Constellations and the Pole Star
[0:3:12] - **Constellation** = a pattern of stars in the sky; its stars are **not equidistant** from Earth – they only look grouped.
[0:3:13] - **Saptarishi** (Big Dipper, part of **Ursa Major**) points to the **Pole Star** and so gives the direction of the pole.
[0:3:14] - **Polaris** (**Ursa Minor**) lies within 1° of the north celestial pole → always shows **north**; walking **east**, keep the Pole Star on your **left**. **Vega** will be pole star in ~**12,000 years**.
[0:3:15] - **Nebulae** (gas and dust clouds where stars form) are **not members of the solar system**; asteroids, comets and planets are.
[0:3:16] ~~ Sources: PMF Physical Geography 01 p.8, p.18, p.37; NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 01 p.7-8; app notes 4:0 sub 3
## SUB 4 | Stars – Life Cycle, Black Holes and the Chandrasekhar Limit
[0:4:0] # Life cycle
[0:4:1] - **Nebula** → **protostar** → **main sequence**; then low/medium mass (Sun): **red giant** → planetary nebula → **white dwarf**; massive: **supergiant** → **supernova** → **neutron star** or **black hole**.
[0:4:2] - **Supernova** = the explosive death of a star (**a dying star**).
[0:4:3] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [0:4:3.0] Nebulae | Giant clouds of dust and gas
  [0:4:3.1] Cepheids | Stars that brighten and dim periodically
  [0:4:3.2] Pulsars | Spinning neutron stars formed when massive stars run out of fuel and collapse
  [0:4:3.3] Black hole | Remains of a collapsed massive star; no light escapes
[0:4:4] - UPSC 2023 pairs: Cepheids–"clouds of dust" ✗, Nebulae–"brighten and dim" ✗, Pulsars ✓ → **only one** correct.
[0:4:5] # Black holes
[0:4:6] - **Black hole:** gravity so strong (very **high density**) that **not even light escapes** → it **cannot be seen by a telescope** (A-R: both true, R explains A).
[0:4:7] - A black hole is a **collapsed star**, a celestial phenomenon of stars; Pulsar, Black Hole, Quasar are in space – **Brittle Star** is a sea animal (echinoderm).
[0:4:8] # Chandrasekhar
[0:4:9] - **S. Chandrasekhar** gave black-hole/white-dwarf theory (paper to the Royal Astronomical Society, London, **11 January 1935**; Nobel 1983).
[0:4:10] - **Chandrasekhar limit ≈ 1.44 solar masses**: stars below it end as **white dwarfs**; above it the core suffers **internal collapse** (neutron star or black hole).
[0:4:11] ~~ Sources: PMF Physical Geography 01 p.9-12; UPSC CSE 2023 pair question; app notes 4:0 sub 2-3
## SUB 5 | The Sun – Composition, Layers and Activity
[0:5:0] - **Chief body of the solar system** and the **primary source of energy for the Earth**; **99.8%** of the solar system's mass; diameter **109 × Earth's**.
[0:5:1] - **Composition:** mostly **hydrogen** (~74%), then helium; energy from **nuclear fusion** of H into He in the core (**~15 million °C**).
[0:5:2] - **State:** the interior is **plasma (gas)** – the centre is in the **gaseous state only**, not liquid or solid.
[0:5:3] - **Light of the Sun is white** (all colours together); it looks yellow from Earth because of scattering.
[0:5:4] # Layers (centre outward)
[0:5:5] TABLE head: Layer | Key fact
  [0:5:5.0] Core | Fusion H → He; ~15 million °C
  [0:5:5.1] Photosphere | Bright visible outer surface emitting most radiation; ~5,500–6,000°C (5,778 K)
  [0:5:5.2] Chromosphere | Reddish lower atmosphere (~4,300°C), seen at eclipses
  [0:5:5.3] Corona | Outermost; visible only during a total solar eclipse; over 1 million °C
[0:5:6] # Solar activity
[0:5:7] TABLE head: Phenomenon | Fact
  [0:5:7.0] Sunspots | Cooler dark magnetic patches on the photosphere; the interval between two maxima (~11 years) = cycle of solar activity (solar cycle)
  [0:5:7.1] Solar flares | Bursts from magnetic reconnection; classes A, B, C, M, X (X strongest)
  [0:5:7.2] CMEs | Coronal plasma (not rock), 250–3,000 km/s, reach Earth in 1–3 days
  [0:5:7.3] Aurora | Borealis (north), Australis (south)
[0:5:8] ~~ Sources: Rocket General Geography #1 p.6; PMF Physical Geography 01 p.22-23; app notes 4:0 sub 4
## SUB 6 | Origin of the Universe and the Solar System – Theories
[0:6:0] TABLE head: Theory | Proponent | Year
  [0:6:0.0] Geocentric (Earth at the centre) | Ptolemy | 2nd c. AD
  [0:6:0.1] Heliocentric | Copernicus | 1543
  [0:6:0.2] Nebular hypothesis | Immanuel Kant; revised by Laplace | 1755; 1796
  [0:6:0.3] Planetesimal hypothesis | Chamberlin and Moulton | 1904
  [0:6:0.4] Tidal hypothesis | James Jeans and Harold Jeffreys | –
  [0:6:0.5] Nova hypothesis | Hoyle and Lyttleton | –
  [0:6:0.6] Interstellar dust (gas and dust) | Otto Schmidt | 1943
  [0:6:0.7] Big Bang (expanding universe) | Georges Lemaitre | 1927
  [0:6:0.8] Steady State | Hoyle, Bondi and Gold | 1948
[0:6:1] - **Earth from gases and dust particles = O. Schmidt** (asked 4 times: APPSC G2 2008, IAS 1999); not Jeans (tidal) or Hoyle (nova).
[0:6:2] - **Big Bang** explains the **origin of the universe** (not continental drift, the Himalayas or volcanoes).
[0:6:3] - **Evidence for Big Bang / expansion:** **red-shift** of galaxies (**Hubble, 1929**) = **expansion of the universe**, and the **cosmic microwave background** → UPSC 2012 answer "**1 and 2**" (asteroids and supernovae are not evidence).
[0:6:4] - Lemaitre proposed the Big Bang (1927); Hubble only showed expansion (1929). Steady State = **Gold and Bondi** (with Hoyle).
[0:6:5] - **Present view:** planets formed from the same spinning disc; the hot inner disc kept only metals and rocky minerals, ices stayed in the cool outer disc (giant planets).
[0:6:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Physical Geography 01 p.18-20; Rocket General Geography #1 p.10; app notes 4:0 sub 1
## SUB 7 | Astronomers and Discoveries
[0:7:0] TABLE head: Person | Contribution
  [0:7:0.0] Nicolaus Copernicus (16th-c. astronomer) | First to state that the Earth and planets revolve round the Sun (heliocentric model, 1543)
  [0:7:0.1] Johannes Kepler | Planets move in ellipses (first law); equal areas in equal times (second law)
  [0:7:0.2] Galileo | Discovered the four Galilean moons of Jupiter (Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto), 1610
  [0:7:0.3] Newton | Laws of gravitation
  [0:7:0.4] William Herschel | Discovered Uranus, 1781
  [0:7:0.5] Johann Galle | First saw Neptune, 1846
  [0:7:0.6] Clyde Tombaugh | Discovered Pluto, 1930
  [0:7:0.7] Aryabhata (476–550 CE) | Earth rotates on its axis; explained eclipses; India's first satellite named after him
[0:7:1] - **⚠ Trap:** Copernicus = heliocentrism (not the spherical Earth: that was Pythagoras/Aristotle); circular orbits were replaced by ellipses only with **Kepler**.
[0:7:2] ~~ Sources: Rocket General Geography #1 p.10; PMF Physical Geography 01 p.20; NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 01 p.12; app notes 4:0 sub 2
## SUB 8 | Dwarf Planets, Asteroids, Comets and Meteors
[0:8:0] TABLE head: Basis | Asteroids | Comets
  [0:8:0.0] Made of | Rock and metal | Ice, frozen gases, dust, rock
  [0:8:0.1] Where | Mars–Jupiter belt; largest Ceres (~1,000 km) | Kuiper Belt, Oort Cloud
  [0:8:0.2] Orbit | Less eccentric | Highly elliptical
  [0:8:0.3] Tail | Usually none | Coma and tail, points away from the Sun (radiation pressure + solar wind)
[0:8:1] - **Kuiper Belt** (30–50 AU, beyond Neptune) → **short-period** comets; **Oort Cloud** → **long-period** comets.
[0:8:2] TABLE head: Comet | Fact
  [0:8:2.0] Halley's | Short-period, ~76 yr; last 1986, next 2061
  [0:8:2.1] Hale-Bopp | Long-period, ~2,534 yr
  [0:8:2.2] Shoemaker-Levy 9 | Hit Jupiter, 16–22 July 1994
  [0:8:2.3] 3I/ATLAS | Third interstellar object; JWST found methane (a first)
[0:8:3] - **Meteoroid** = body in space; **meteor** = **shooting star**; **meteorite** = reaches the ground; **bolide** = explodes in the air.
[0:8:4] - **Leonids:** debris of **Comet Tempel-Tuttle**; appear to come from **Leo**; peak ~17–18 November.
[0:8:5] - Match (UPPCS 1992): Planet – **Uranus**; Satellite – **Moon**; Comet – **Halley**; Spacecraft – **Mariner**.
[0:8:6] # Dwarf planets
[0:8:7] - **IAU General Assembly (August 2006, Prague):** a planet must orbit the Sun, be nearly round and **clear its orbit**; Pluto fails → dwarf planet; trigger **Eris**.
[0:8:8] - Dwarf planets: **Ceres** (asteroid belt); **Pluto, Haumea, Makemake, Eris** (Kuiper belt). Pluto: Indian name **Yama**; Eris is not a moon of Jupiter.
[0:8:9] ~~ Sources: Rocket General Geography #1 p.9-10; NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 01 p.11-13; app notes 4:0 sub 8
## SUB 9 | Earth, Moon and Eclipses
[0:9:0] # Earth's unique features
[0:9:1] - **Goldilocks (habitable) zone:** "just right" for liquid water; Earth lies in it (APPSC 2019). Earth-like **K2-18b**: possible biomarker molecule.
[0:9:2] TABLE head: Sphere | Evolution
  [0:9:2.0] Lithosphere | Differentiation: heavy iron sank to the core, light material formed the crust
  [0:9:2.1] Atmosphere | H-He lost to the solar wind → degassing (water vapour, N₂, CO₂) → photosynthesis added oxygen
  [0:9:2.2] Hydrosphere | Degassed vapour condensed → rain → oceans
  [0:9:2.3] Magnetic field | Geodynamo of the liquid-iron outer core; 2026 study: some reversals lasted ~70,000 years
[0:9:3] # Earth's orbit
[0:9:4] TABLE head: Basis | Perihelion | Aphelion
  [0:9:4.0] Date | ~3 January | ~4 July
  [0:9:4.1] Distance | ~147 million km | ~152 million km
  [0:9:4.2] Speed | Fastest | Slowest
  [0:9:4.3] N. Hemisphere | Winter | Summer
[0:9:5] - **Kepler's Second Law** (equal areas in equal times) explains the speed change. Seasons come from **revolution + axial tilt**, not distance.
[0:9:6] # The Moon
[0:9:7] - Mean distance **384,400 km**; gravity **1/6** of Earth's; rotation = revolution = **27 d 7 h 43 min** (same face); synodic (lunar) month **29.5 days**.
[0:9:8] - **Supermoon:** full moon when the Moon is **nearest the Earth (perigee)**, with Sun, Earth and Moon in line → bigger, brighter, higher tides. **Micromoon:** full moon at **apogee**, 6–7% smaller.
[0:9:9] - **Blue moon:** 2nd full moon in a calendar month; **blue micromoon** in 2026. Half moon: angle **90°**.
[0:9:10] TABLE head: Basis | Solar eclipse | Lunar eclipse
  [0:9:10.0] Position | Moon between Sun and Earth | Earth between Sun and Moon (Earth's shadow on the Moon)
  [0:9:10.1] Phase | New moon (Amavasya) | Full moon
  [0:9:10.2] Feature | Corona, diamond ring | Reddish "blood moon"
[0:9:11] - Longest total solar eclipse of the 21st century: **22 July 2009**; longest annular eclipse of the millennium: **15 January 2010**.
[0:9:12] - **Apollo 11** (20 July 1969): Armstrong and Aldrin walked, **Collins** orbited. **Blue Marble** photo: Apollo 17.
[0:9:13] ~~ Sources: Rocket General Geography #1 p.5-9; NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 01 p.2-3; app notes 4:0 sub 7
[0:9:14] - **Sea of Tranquility** (Mare Tranquillitatis): a dark lava plain (mare) on the **Moon**; Apollo 11 landed there (1969).
[0:9:15] - **Diamond ring:** beads of sunlight shining through valleys on the Moon's rugged edge just **before and after totality**; UPSC 1996 key (PMF): seen **only along the peripheral regions of the totality trail**.
[0:9:16] - **Last man on the Moon:** **Eugene Cernan**, Apollo 17 (December 1972); 12 men in all walked on it (Artemis II, 2026, was a flyby, no landing).
[0:9:17] - **Escape velocity:** Earth **11.2 km/s** (Moon ~2.4 km/s); orbital velocity near Earth ~7.9 km/s.
[0:9:18] - **Totality only in a narrow path:** the **Moon's shadow (umbra) on the Earth is small**, so a total solar eclipse is seen only along a narrow **path of totality**.
[0:9:19] - **No air on the Moon:** there is **no atmosphere / no oxygen**, so nothing can burn there, sound does not travel and the sky is black.
## SUB 10 | Space Missions and Lagrange Points
[0:10:0] TABLE head: Mission | Target / achievement
  [0:10:0.0] Chang'e 4 (China) | First soft landing on the far side of the Moon (3 January 2019)
  [0:10:0.1] Chandrayaan-3 (2023) | India first near the Moon's south pole
  [0:10:0.2] OSIRIS-REx (NASA) | Bennu samples (24 Sep 2023); renamed OSIRIS-APEX for Apophis (2029)
  [0:10:0.3] DART | Kinetic impact on Dimorphos (planetary defence)
  [0:10:0.4] Hera (ESA) | Surveys Didymos-Dimorphos after DART
  [0:10:0.5] Hayabusa2 (Japan) | Ryugu samples (not Bennu)
  [0:10:0.6] Phoenix Mars Lander | Landed 25 May 2008 near Mars's north pole; found ice
  [0:10:0.7] SMILE (ESA-China) | Solar wind hitting Earth's magnetic shield, in X-ray and UV
[0:10:1] - **Aditya-L1:** first Indian solar observatory; **PSLV-C57** (2023) from **SDSC-SHAR, Sriharikota (AP)**; halo orbit at Sun–Earth **L1** (~**1.5 million km**); **VELC** made the first **visible-light** spectroscopy of CMEs.

=== NOTES 4:1 | Earth – Shape, Size, Geoid; Latitudes and Longitudes, the Graticule
## SUB 0 | Key Parallels, Meridians and the Countries They Cross
[1:0:0] # The five key lines (asked most: 25 PYQs)
[1:0:1] TABLE head: Line | Value | Passes through | Does NOT pass through (traps)
  [1:0:1.0] Equator | 0° | 13 countries: Ecuador, Colombia, Brazil, São Tomé and Príncipe, Gabon, Rep. of Congo, DR Congo, Uganda, Kenya, Somalia, Maldives (waters), Indonesia, Kiribati | Rwanda, Equatorial Guinea (UPPSC 2020), Mexico, Venezuela, Zambia, Sudan, Ethiopia, Malaysia, Cameroon, Costa Rica
  [1:0:1.1] Tropic of Cancer | 23½°N | Mexico, Bahamas, Western Sahara, Mauritania, Mali, Algeria, Niger, Libya, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Oman, India, Bangladesh, Myanmar, China, Taiwan | Iran (UPPSC 2005)
  [1:0:1.2] Tropic of Capricorn | 23½°S | Chile, Argentina, Paraguay, Brazil, Namibia, Botswana, South Africa, Mozambique, Madagascar, Australia | Bolivia (asked 3 times)
  [1:0:1.3] Arctic Circle | 66½°N | Norway, Sweden, Finland, Russia, USA (Alaska), Canada, Greenland | Iceland – mainland lies just south of it (only tiny Grímsey island is touched)
  [1:0:1.4] Prime Meridian | 0° | UK (Greenwich), France, Spain, Algeria, Mali, Burkina Faso, Togo, Ghana | Niger (on the Tropic of Cancer instead), Nigeria, Portugal
[1:0:2] - **Equator groups (UPSC 2006, asked twice):** **Colombia, Kenya and Indonesia** ✓; Brazil–Zambia–Malaysia ✗, Brazil–Sudan–Malaysia ✗, Venezuela–Ethiopia–Indonesia ✗.
[1:0:3] - **Continents:** **Africa** is the only continent crossed by the **Equator and both Tropics**; South America has the Equator and Capricorn; Asia the Equator and Cancer.
[1:0:4] - **0° latitude, 0° longitude** = **Gulf of Guinea, Atlantic Ocean** (south of Ghana) – not Ghana, not Greenwich (asked 3 times).
[1:0:5] - **49th Parallel** = long stretch of the **USA–Canada** boundary.
[1:0:6] - **Torrid zone** = between the two Tropics; temperate zones 23½°–66½°; frigid zones beyond the polar circles (**Antarctic Circle 66½°S**). The **International Date Line** follows roughly **180°**, not 0° (SSC 2012: II and III wrong).
[1:0:7] - **Arctic** region lies around the **North Pole**, **Antarctica** around the **South Pole**.
[1:0:8] - **Tropics are 47° apart**; on the **December solstice** the noon Sun at the Tropic of Cancer stands at **90° − 47° = 43°** (UPPSC 1997).
[1:0:9] - **Midnight sun:** seen beyond the polar circles up to the **poles** (North Pole ✓, Equator ✗).
[1:0:10] - **Longest north–south (latitudinal) extent:** **Chile** (~39° of latitude, ~4,300 km; CIA World Factbook), then Brazil (~38–39°); **not China** (~35° on the mainland).
[1:0:11] > NOT-angle: the trap countries in the last column are the answers to "does not pass through".
[1:0:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket General Geography #2 p.16; PMF Physical Geography 01; CIA World Factbook (Chile); app notes 4:1 sub 3
## SUB 1 | Shape and Size of the Earth – Geoid, Gravity, Dimensions
[1:1:0] # Shape
[1:1:1] - **Geoid** = "earth-shaped"; the Earth is an **oblate spheroid** – **flattened at the poles, bulging at the Equator**.
[1:1:2] - **Cause:** **centrifugal force of rotation**, maximum at the Equator (the faster-moving equatorial belt) – not the Sun's pull or stronger sunlight (CDS 2010: "only I").
[1:1:3] - **Equatorial bulge:** equatorial radius exceeds polar radius by **~21 km** (diameters by ~43 km) (CDS 2008, NDA 2016).
[1:1:4] - **Gravity and weight:** **g is greater at the poles** than at the Equator; **weight is least at the Equator, greatest at the poles** (poles are ~21 km nearer the centre + no centrifugal force). Moving to **higher latitude, weight increases** (IAS 2003 A-R: A false, R true).
[1:1:5] - Surface point nearest the Earth's centre: the **poles** (Arctic Ocean floor near the North Pole).
[1:1:6] - **Proofs of sphericity:** circular shadow of the Earth on the Moon in a **lunar eclipse**; ship's mast seen first; circumnavigation; satellite images.
[1:1:7] - **First to say the Earth is spherical:** **Pythagoras** (c. 6th century BC) proposed it; **Aristotle** (4th century BC, *On the Heavens*) gave the first proofs – Indian books and keys say **Aristotle** when Pythagoras is not offered (IAS 2001). Not Copernicus (heliocentric model), Ptolemy, Newton (polar flattening) or Columbus.
[1:1:8] - **Stars rise perpendicular to the horizon** for an observer on the **Equator** (celestial poles lie on the horizon there); at the poles stars circle parallel to the horizon (UPSC 2001, asked twice).
[1:1:9] # Dimensions
[1:1:10] TABLE head: Measure | Value
  [1:1:10.0] Equatorial diameter | 12,756 km (~12,800 km)
  [1:1:10.1] Polar diameter | 12,714 km (~43 km less)
  [1:1:10.2] Mean radius | 6,371 km
  [1:1:10.3] Equatorial circumference (length of the Equator) | ~40,075 km (~40,000 km)
  [1:1:10.4] Water : land | 71 : 29 – about two-thirds of the surface is water
[1:1:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket General Geography #1 p.4, p.7; PMF Physical Geography 01; Wikipedia "Equatorial bulge" (WGS-84: radii differ by 21.38 km); app notes 4:1 sub 0-1
## SUB 2 | The Graticule – Latitude, Longitude, Great Circles
[1:2:0] # Latitude and longitude
[1:2:1] - **Latitude** = angular distance of a point **north or south of the Equator**, measured **from the centre of the Earth** (NDA 2011); 0°–90°.
[1:2:2] - **Parallels of latitude run east–west** (APPSC G1); **meridians run north–south**, pole to pole; longitude 0°–180° E or W.
[1:2:3] - Parallels at 1°: **179** (89 N + 89 S + Equator; the poles are points). Meridians: **360**.
[1:2:4] - 1° of latitude ≈ **111 km** everywhere; 1° of longitude: 111 km at the Equator → **55.5 km at 60°** → 0 at the poles.
[1:2:5] - **Antipode** of (x°N, y°E) = (x°S, (180 − y)°W): 20°N 80°E → **20°S 100°W**.
[1:2:6] # Great circles
[1:2:7] - A **great circle** divides the globe into **two equal halves** (its plane passes through the centre): the **Equator** (the only great-circle parallel) and every meridian with its opposite – **0° + 180°** form one (UPPSC 2000).
[1:2:8] - **60°N latitude is NOT a great circle** (all parallels except the Equator are small circles); 60°E longitude is half of a great circle.
[1:2:9] - NDA 2009 A-R: Equator is a great circle ✓; R (its plane divides the Earth into two equal halves) ✓ and explains A.
[1:2:10] # What varies with latitude (CDS 2017: all three true)
[1:2:11] - **Rainfall, temperature and vegetation** vary with latitude; the **difference between longest and shortest day increases with latitude**.
[1:2:12] - **Longitude does not affect insolation** (latitude, atmospheric transparency, distance from sea do).
[1:2:13] # Places by longitude / latitude
[1:2:14] - **West to east:** **Lisbon (9°W) → London (0°) → Frankfurt (8.7°E) → Beirut (35.5°E)** (MPPSC 2008).
[1:2:15] - **Nearest the Equator:** **Singapore (1°17'N)** < Jakarta (6°12'S) < Colombo (6°56'N) < Manila (14°35'N) (IAS 2008).
[1:2:16] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket General Geography #2; PMF Physical Geography 01; NCERT Class 6 "The Earth: Our Habitat" Ch. 2; app notes 4:1 sub 2
## SUB 3 | India and Andhra Pradesh on the Graticule
[1:3:0] # India
[1:3:1] TABLE head: Extreme | Point
  [1:3:1.0] North | Indira Col, Karakoram (Ladakh)
  [1:3:1.1] South (mainland) | Kanyakumari (Cape Comorin), 8°4'N
  [1:3:1.2] South (overall) | Indira Point (6°45'N), Great Nicobar – nearest the Equator
  [1:3:1.3] East | Kibithu, Arunachal Pradesh (97°25'E)
  [1:3:1.4] West | Guhar Moti, Kutch, Gujarat (68°7'E)
[1:3:2] - India: **8°4'N – 37°6'N**, **68°7'E – 97°25'E**; area **32,87,263 sq km**; **3,214 km** N–S, **2,933 km** E–W.
[1:3:3] - **Tropic of Cancer** crosses **8 states:** Gujarat, Rajasthan, MP, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura, Mizoram (**not Odisha**).
[1:3:4] - **24°N** crosses the most states (CAPF 2019; ~9: Gujarat, Rajasthan, MP, UP, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, WB, Tripura, Mizoram/Manipur) – more than 20°, 22° or 26°N.
[1:3:5] - **Longitude nearest Delhi (77.2°E):** **Bengaluru (77.6°E)**; Hyderabad 78.5°, Nagpur 79.1°, Pune 73.9°E.
[1:3:6] - **70°E** passes through **Jaisalmer** district (western Rajasthan); Jodhpur, Nagaur, Dholpur lie east of it.
[1:3:7] - North to south: Srinagar > Bhopal > Visakhapatnam > Hyderabad > Chennai > Kanyakumari.
[1:3:8] # Andhra Pradesh
[1:3:9] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [1:3:9.0] Latitude | 12°41'N – 19°07'N (wholly between the Equator and the Tropic of Cancer; tropical Aw)
  [1:3:9.1] Longitude | 77°E – 84°40'E (older/undivided figures: 76°45'E – 84°46'E)
  [1:3:9.2] Area | 1,62,970 sq km = 4.96% of India; 7th largest state (NextGen: 8th – counted J&K before 2019)
  [1:3:9.3] Coastline | 974 km, 2nd longest (traditional) → 1,053.07 km, 3rd after Gujarat and Tamil Nadu (re-measurement, MoPSW circular 29 Apr 2025)
  [1:3:9.4] Districts | 13 (2014) → 26 (April 2022) → 28 (as of 2026)
[1:3:10] - AP's northern limit is **19°07'N, not 22°N**. Neighbours: Odisha, Chhattisgarh (north), Telangana (west), Karnataka (south-west), Tamil Nadu (south).
[1:3:11] - **IST meridian 82½°E** passes through **Kakinada** district.

## SUB 4 | Pioneers, Maps and Projections
[1:4:0] TABLE head: Who / what | Fact
  [1:4:0.0] Eratosthenes | Father of Geography; coined "Geography"; first correct estimate of the Earth's circumference
  [1:4:0.1] Hipparchus | First to divide the circle into 360°
  [1:4:0.2] Anaximander | First Greek world map
  [1:4:0.3] Ptolemy | First used latitude and longitude (*Geographia*)
  [1:4:0.4] Amundsen | First at the South Pole, 1911
  [1:4:0.5] International Meridian Conference, 1884 | Fixed the Prime Meridian at Greenwich
  [1:4:0.6] Mercator, 1569 | Right-angled graticule, straight rhumb lines, polar areas greatly enlarged
[1:4:1] - **Survey of India** (1767, Dehradun) prepares **topographical maps**; Geological Survey of India – geological maps; NATMO – thematic maps.
[1:4:2] - **"Correct the Map":** UNGA non-binding resolution of **4 September 2026** (164–1, **US against**), led by Togo and the **African Union**, promotes the **Equal Earth** projection (2018) over Mercator.
[1:4:3] - **EOS-05**: ISRO Earth-imaging satellite meant for **geosynchronous orbit (~36,000 km)**.
[1:4:4] - **Earth Day: 22 April** (first observed 1970).
[1:4:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket General Geography #1 p.7; surveyofindia.gov.in; un.org/osaa "Correct the Map" (Sep 2026); app notes 4:1 sub 4

=== NOTES 4:2 | Motions of the Earth – Rotation and Revolution; Effects (day and Night, Coriolis Force, Tides)
## SUB 0 | Rotation – Axis, Speed and Effects
[2:0:0] # Rotation basics
[2:0:1] - **Rotation** = the Earth spinning on its **axis** (line through both poles); **revolution** = moving round the Sun.
[2:0:2] - Direction **west to east** – **counter-clockwise** seen from above the North Pole; only **Venus and Uranus** spin the other way.
[2:0:3] - **Axis tilted 23½° (23°30') from the perpendicular to the orbital plane** ("from the ecliptic axis"; 66½° with the orbital plane) – so it is **not at 90°** to the orbit (NDA 2009: both statements ✓).
[2:0:4] - Angular speed **15° per hour** (1° in 4 min). Linear speed **~1,670 km/h at the Equator – the maximum velocity of rotation** – falling to **zero at the poles**.
[2:0:5] TABLE head: Day | Measured against | Length
  [2:0:5.0] Sidereal (one true rotation) | A distant star | 23 h 56 min 4.09 s
  [2:0:5.1] Solar | The Sun | 24 h (~4 min longer, as the Earth also moves along its orbit)
[2:0:6] - Not felt: motion is uniform and the atmosphere moves along with the Earth.
[2:0:7] - **Pole Star** seems fixed because it lies almost **in line with the Earth's axis of rotation**.
[2:0:8] # Effects of rotation (Strahler; NDA 2019: all three)
[2:0:9] - **Day and night** – the diurnal rhythm of daylight and air temperature.
[2:0:10] - **Coriolis deflection** – flow paths of air and water turned sideways.
[2:0:11] - **Movement of the tides** – a place is carried through the tidal bulges twice a day.
[2:0:12] - Also: time difference between longitudes, centrifugal bulge.
[2:0:13] - **Seasons are NOT caused by rotation** (they come from revolution + tilt); day and night are **not** caused by revolution (Jharkhand 2021: both statements false).
[2:0:14] - **No rotation** → no sunrise/sunset and no day-night cycle, but seasons would remain (CDS 2015: I and II).
[2:0:15] - **Faster rotation** → stronger centrifugal effect → **g decreases at the Equator, unchanged at the poles** (NDA 2018).
[2:0:16] # Evidence and pioneers
[2:0:17] - **Aryabhata** (5th century) first explained that the **rotation of the Earth** causes the daily rising and setting of the Sun (*Aryabhatiya*; also his *Aryasiddhanta*).
[2:0:18] - **Foucault pendulum**, Paris **1851**: the plane of swing slowly turns. Other proofs: Coriolis deflection, equatorial bulge, apparent east-to-west motion of the sky.
[2:0:19] # The axis is shifting (UPSC 2025)
[2:0:20] - Studies (ETH Zurich, *Nature Geoscience*/*PNAS* 2024) show the rotation axis drifting and the day lengthening; cause = **mass redistribution**: as **polar ice melts, water moves towards the Equator** (also groundwater loss) – day longer by **~1.33 ms per century** (2000–2020).
[2:0:21] - **Solar flares and CMEs** do bombard the upper atmosphere with energy (true) but **do not shift the axis** → "both II and III correct, only one (III) explains I".
[2:0:22] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket General Geography #2 p.11-13, p.18; NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 01 p.8-9; Strahler, Physical Geography (effects of rotation); app notes 4:2 sub 0-1
## SUB 1 | Coriolis and Centrifugal Effects
[2:1:0] - **Coriolis force** = an **apparent force** caused by the **Earth's rotation** (not revolution, tilt, pressure, temperature or magnetism); it shapes winds, ocean currents, cyclones and **large-scale weather patterns**.
[2:1:1] - **Ferrel's law:** moving air and water are deflected to the **right in the Northern Hemisphere** and to the **left in the Southern Hemisphere** – "left in NH" is the trap (APPSC 2022: I and III only).
[2:1:2] - Force = **2Ωv sin(latitude)**: **zero at the Equator**, **maximum at the poles**; grows with **latitude and wind speed**; linked to the **decreasing rotational velocity with increasing latitude** (CDS 2012: all three).
[2:1:3] - Cyclones rarely form within **5° of the Equator**; NH cyclones spin **anticlockwise**, SH clockwise.
[2:1:4] - AP angle: **Cyclone Montha (Oct 2025)** was steered north-northwest to the **Kakinada** coast.
[2:1:5] - **Centrifugal force** of rotation: maximum at the Equator, zero at the poles → **equatorial bulge, polar flattening (oblate spheroid)**; **weight of a body is maximum at the poles**, least at the Equator.
[2:1:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket General Geography #2 p.12-13; NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 03 p.12; app notes 4:2 sub 3
## SUB 2 | Tides
[2:2:0] - **Causes (UPSC 2015: a, b and c):** gravitational pull of the **Moon** (main) and the **Sun**, and the **centrifugal force** of the Earth–Moon system (bulge on the far side). Tide-generating force = gravitational attraction − centrifugal force.
[2:2:1] - Semi-diurnal tide: **two high and two low tides a day**; successive high tides **~12 h 25 min apart** (≈ **12 h 26 min**, NDA 2010).
[2:2:2] - The **lunar day is ~24 h 52 min**, so high tide comes **~52 min later each day**: **8:00 am → 8:52 am** (APPSC G1 2002, asked 3 times).
[2:2:3] TABLE head: Tide | Position | When
  [2:2:3.0] Spring (highest) | Sun, Earth, Moon in a straight line | New moon and full moon – twice a month
  [2:2:3.1] Neap (lowest range) | Sun and Moon at right angles | First and third quarter, ~7 days after spring tides – twice a month
[2:2:4] - Highest spring tides: full/new moon at an **equinox**; tides are larger when the Moon is at **perigee**. Ebb = falling tide, flow/flood = rising tide.
[2:2:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 01 p.3-4, 03 p.9-11; app notes 4:2 sub 4
## SUB 3 | Day and Night, Day Length, Midnight Sun
[2:3:0] - **Day and night** are caused by the **rotation of the Earth on its axis** – not revolution, not tilt alone, not the Moon.
[2:3:1] - **Circle of illumination** = terminator = "**grey line**" (APPSC 2019); passes through both poles **only at the equinoxes**.
[2:3:2] - **Unequal day and night:** tilt + revolution. The difference is **least near the Equator** (~12 h day all year) and **increases away from it** to the poles (CDS 2014).
[2:3:3] - **Poles:** ~6 months of day + 6 months of night (**revolution with axial tilt**). **Midnight Sun** in the **Arctic and Antarctic regions** (beyond the polar circles) near the summer solstice; **Norway** = "Land of the Midnight Sun".
[2:3:4] - **Twilight** is shortest at the Equator (Sun rises almost vertically) and longest at high latitudes.
[2:3:5] - Equatorial seasons are marked by **wet and dry periods**, not by day length.
[2:3:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket General Geography #2 p.11-12, p.15; app notes 4:2 sub 2
## SUB 4 | Revolution, Seasons and Leap Year
[2:4:0] - Orbit slightly **elliptical**, Sun at one focus; period **~365¼ days** (365.25; sidereal year 365 d 6 h 9 min 9.5 s); mean speed **29.78 km/s**; the **Sun's gravity** is the centripetal force.
[2:4:1] - **Perihelion** early January (~147 million km; **3 Jan in 2026**), **aphelion** early July (~152 million km; **6 July in 2026**) – Earth moves faster at perihelion; the Earth–Sun distance is **not constant**.
[2:4:2] - **Seasons = revolution + 23½° tilt + parallelism of the axis**; Sun overhead at the Equator on **21 March and 23 September**, at Cancer on 21 June, at Capricorn on 22 December.
[2:4:3] - **Circular orbit instead of elliptical** → the varying distance would vanish, so the **difference between seasons would be reduced** (CDS 2011 key); the effect is small because tilt is the main cause.
[2:4:4] - Extra ¼ day a year → **leap year** of 366 days (29 February); a century year only if divisible by **400** (**2000 yes, 1900 no**).
[2:4:5] - Rotation gives day and night, time zones and Coriolis; **revolution** gives the year, seasons, solstices, equinoxes and perihelion/aphelion.
[2:4:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket General Geography #2 p.13-17, #3 p.19; app notes 4:2 sub 5

=== NOTES 4:4 | Seasons – Inclination of the Axis, Solstices and Equinoxes, Distribution of Insolation
## SUB 0 | Solstices, Equinoxes and Day Length
[4:0:0] # The four positions (asked most: 29 PYQs)
[4:0:1] TABLE head: Date | Event (NH) | Sun overhead at | NH | SH
  [4:0:1.0] 21 March (20/21) | Vernal (spring) equinox | Equator | Spring; day = night | Autumn begins
  [4:0:1.1] 21 June (20/21) | Summer solstice | Tropic of Cancer | Longest day | Shortest day
  [4:0:1.2] 23 September (22/23) | Autumnal equinox | Equator | Autumn; day = night | Spring begins
  [4:0:1.3] 22 December (21/22) | Winter solstice | Tropic of Capricorn | Shortest day | Longest day
[4:0:2] - Matches asked: winter solstice **22 Dec**, summer solstice **21 June**, vernal equinox **21 March**, autumnal equinox **23 Sept** (APPSC G1 2018, CDS 2014, WBCS 2020: all correct).
[4:0:3] - Order in a year: March equinox → June solstice → September equinox → December solstice.
[4:0:4] - **Equinox** = "equal night": Sun **overhead at the Equator**, **day = night everywhere** on Earth (SSC 2020); never at the Arctic Circle (NDA 2008 wrong pair). The tilt itself does not change – statement "day length changes because the tilt changes" is false (NDA 2009: I and II only).
[4:0:5] - "Vernal equinox": **20/21 March** in the NH; in the **Southern Hemisphere** the spring (vernal) equinox is **22/23 September** – so the APPSC flashcard key is "**both a and b**".
[4:0:6] - **Longest NH day:** **second half of June** (UPSC 2022, asked twice); **SH longest day: 22 December** (second half of December); **SH shortest day: 21 June**; NH shortest **22 December**.
[4:0:7] - On the shortest day in India (22 Dec) it is the **longest day in Australia** (also New Zealand) – Southern Hemisphere.
[4:0:8] - **Uttarayana** = the Sun's apparent **northward** movement, **22/23 Dec → 21 June**; Dakshinayana the reverse.
[4:0:9] - **21 June** = **International Day of Yoga** (UN, since 2015; 2026 theme "**Yoga for Healthy Ageing**").
[4:0:10] # Day length by latitude
[4:0:11] TABLE head: Latitude | 21 June | Equinoxes | 22 Dec
  [4:0:11.0] Equator | 12 h | 12 h | 12 h
  [4:0:11.1] Tropic of Cancer | ~13½ h | 12 h | ~10½ h
  [4:0:11.2] Arctic Circle | 24 h day – the Sun does not set | 12 h | 24 h night
  [4:0:11.3] North Pole | Continuous day | Sunrise / sunset | Continuous night
[4:0:12] - **Equator: day = night all year** (12 h on every date, incl. the September equinox) – at the June solstice the 12-h day is at the Equator.
[4:0:13] - **North Pole lit from 21 March to 23 September** (about **six months** of day, then six of night); when the North Pole has continuous daylight the South Pole has continuous darkness.
[4:0:14] - 23 Sept → 21 Dec: NH days **become progressively shorter**.
[4:0:15] - **June day length grows northward**: **Srinagar > Delhi > Hyderabad > Chennai > Kanyakumari/Thiruvananthapuram** – Srinagar has the longest summer sunlight, Delhi the longest June day of Delhi/Bhopal/Hyderabad/Chennai, Thiruvananthapuram the shortest.
[4:0:16] - **Midnight sun** = Sun above the horizon at midnight, beyond the polar circles in summer.
[4:0:17] > Date-match angle: memorise 21 Mar – 21 Jun – 23 Sep – 22 Dec and what is overhead on each.
[4:0:18] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket General Geography #1 p.5-6, #3 p.14-22; Britannica "equinox" (SH vernal equinox 22/23 Sept); app notes 4:3 sub 8, 4:4 sub 2-3
## SUB 1 | Why Seasons Occur – Tilt, Revolution, Perihelion
[4:1:0] - **Seasons = revolution of the Earth + inclination (tilt) of its axis** (Jharkhand 2013, NDA 2014); **day-length variation** from season to season = **revolution on a tilted axis** (UPSC 2013, APPSC 2018) – not rotation, not the elliptical orbit, not oceans/mountains/altitude.
[4:1:1] - Axis tilted **23½° (23.5°) from the perpendicular** = **66½° to the orbital plane**.
[4:1:2] - **Parallelism**: the axis keeps pointing the same way (towards the **Pole Star**) through the year – because of **angular momentum** – so hemispheres tilt alternately towards (summer) and away (winter) → **opposite seasons**.
[4:1:3] - Full set: **axial inclination + parallelism + revolution + spherical shape** → changing **angle of insolation** and **day length**.
[4:1:4] - Tilt gives seasons, unequal days, the tropics and polar circles – **not day and night** (that is rotation, with the **circle of illumination** dividing day from night; rotation also gives the **Coriolis** deflection, to the **right in the NH**).
[4:1:5] - **What-if:** tilt raised from 23.5° to **30°** → **more intense seasonal contrasts**; axis **perpendicular** to the orbit → no seasons, equal day and night all year, Sun always over the Equator – but the North Pole would **not** lie always in darkness (NDA 2011).
[4:1:6] TABLE head: Point | Date | Distance | NH season
  [4:1:6.0] Perihelion (nearest the Sun) | ~3/4 January | ~147 million km | Winter
  [4:1:6.1] Aphelion (farthest) | ~4 July | ~152 million km | Summer
[4:1:7] - Earth is **nearest the Sun in northern winter**, so distance does not cause seasons (NDA 2014 trap).
[4:1:8] - Long term: **precession** (axial wobble) – **Vega** was pole star ~14,000 years ago and will be again in ~12,000 years; **Milankovitch cycles** drive long-term climate change. Melting ice moving mass away from the axis **slows rotation**.
[4:1:9] > Cause angle: "revolution on an inclined axis" is the answer; rotation and distance are the traps.
[4:1:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket General Geography #1 p.5, #2 p.16-18, #3 p.19; NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 01 p.10; app notes 4:4 sub 0-1, 4:3 sub 7
## SUB 2 | Overhead Sun, Shadows and Insolation
[4:2:0] # Vertical rays and shadows
[4:2:1] - Noon Sun overhead only **between the Tropics**, **twice a year** (**zero-shadow days**); places north of 23½°N – **Delhi, Srinagar** – **never** get vertical rays; **Hyderabad, Mumbai, Kolkata** (south of the Tropic) do (APPSC G1 2002).
[4:2:2] - **Andhra Pradesh** (12°41'N–19°07'N) gets the overhead noon Sun **twice a year**.
[4:2:3] - **21 June:** Sun overhead at the **Tropic of Cancer** – no noon shadow there; in north India the noon **shadow is smallest on 21 June** (UPPCS 2006), longest in December. On 21 June the Sun **does not set at the Arctic Circle** (UPSC 2019).
[4:2:4] - At the **Equator** there is no noon shadow in **March and September**.
[4:2:5] - **Delhi is hotter at noon in summer** because in winter the Sun's rays fall **more slanting (oblique)** – not because the Earth is nearer the Sun (IAS 1993).
[4:2:6] TABLE head: Basis | Summer | Winter
  [4:2:6.0] Hemisphere | Tilted towards the Sun | Tilted away
  [4:2:6.1] Rays | More direct | More oblique – same energy spread over a larger area
  [4:2:6.2] Days | Longer | Shorter
  [4:2:6.3] Sun altitude / shadow | Higher / shorter | Lower / longer
[4:2:7] # Insolation and latitude zones
[4:2:8] - Factors: **angle of incidence**, **duration of day**, **transparency of the atmosphere**, land configuration – **not** the direction of ocean tides.
[4:2:9] - Insolation generally **falls from the tropics to the poles**; maximum over **cloudless subtropical deserts**, not the Equator.
[4:2:10] TABLE head: Zone | Seasonal feature
  [4:2:10.0] Low latitudes | Small temperature contrast; wet and dry seasons
  [4:2:10.1] Mid-latitudes | Four distinct seasons
  [4:2:10.2] High latitudes | Greatest seasonal differences – day length, insolation and annual temperature range all largest
[4:2:11] - **Seasonal variation increases with latitude** → "seasonal differences are maximum in **high latitudes**" (APPSC G1).
[4:2:12] - **Southern Hemisphere**: hottest summer month **January**; **Christmas in Australia falls in summer** (UKPSC 2010).
[4:2:13] # Related one-liners
[4:2:14] - **Albedo** = share of the Sun's radiation reflected by the Earth's surface; **weather changes occur in the troposphere**, not the stratosphere – the **stratosphere** holds the ozone layer (**Ozonosphere**).
[4:2:15] - India: hot season March–May, ~**50°C at Ganganagar (1935)**; **IMD's four seasons** – winter, pre-monsoon, **South-West monsoon**, **post-monsoon**; traditional calendar: **six ritus**.
[4:2:16] - AP: SW monsoon (June–September) brings about **two-thirds** of the rain; winter October–February; coldest place **Lambasingi** (~2°C).
[4:2:17] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket General Geography #3 p.20-24, p.53; PMF Physical Geography 03 p.46; app notes 4:4 sub 4-7

  x: Seasons come mainly from axial tilt affecting solar angle and day length; Earth is in fact nearest the Sun during northern winter.

=== NOTES 4:5 | Interior of the Earth – Crust, Mantle, Core; Discontinuities and Seismic Evidence
## SUB 0 | Layers of the Earth and Their Composition
[5:0:0] # Crust, mantle, core (asked 11 times)
[5:0:1] TABLE head: Layer | Depth | State | Density (g/cm³) | Made of
  [5:0:1.0] Crust – outermost layer | Oceanic ~5 km, continental ~30 km (~70 km under mountains) | Solid | 2.8–3.0 | Continental: granite (Si, Al); oceanic: basalt (Fe, Mg)
  [5:0:1.1] Mantle – largest layer | Moho → 2,900 km | Solid, flows plastically (convection) | ~4.6 | Silicate minerals of iron and magnesium (upper mantle mostly silicates)
  [5:0:1.2] Outer core | 2,900–5,150 km (~2,260 km thick) | Liquid iron–nickel | ~10–12 | Fe + Ni
  [5:0:1.3] Inner core | 5,150–6,371 km (radius ~1,220 km) | Solid – immense pressure; P-waves at 11.23 km/s | 13.3–13.6 | Mostly iron
[5:0:2] - **Mantle = 83% of volume, 68% of mass** → the **largest** layer; **core = 16% of volume, 32% of mass**.
[5:0:3] - **Core is mainly iron** (with nickel) – not aluminium, chromium or silicon (UPSC 2009, asked twice). Its **lighter elements: silicon, sulphur, oxygen** – the APPSC G2 answer is **silicon**; not aluminium, magnesium, calcium or cobalt.
[5:0:4] - **Mantle = "mixed metals and silicates"** (iron–magnesium silicates) (SSC 2013); Sial is only silica + aluminium, Nife only metal.
[5:0:5] - **Lithosphere = crust + uppermost solid mantle** (~100 km) (NDA 2019).
[5:0:6] - Continental crust: thicker, older, granitic, lighter; oceanic crust: thinner, younger, **basaltic**, denser.
[5:0:7] - **Compositional layering:** crust, mantle, core. **Mechanical:** lithosphere, asthenosphere, mesosphere, outer core, inner core.
[5:0:8] # Suess's chemical layers
[5:0:9] TABLE head: Suess term | Elements | Feature
  [5:0:9.0] SIAL | Silica + Aluminium | Granite; forms the continents; density ~2.9
  [5:0:9.1] SIMA | Silica + Magnesium | Basalt; source of magma and lava
  [5:0:9.2] NIFE | Nickel + Ferrum (iron) | Core; very dense (~11); explains Earth's magnetism (SSC 2018; State PSC "Nickel and ferrum")
[5:0:10] - **Eduard Suess** coined SIAL, SIMA and NIFE.
[5:0:11] - **Whole Earth by mass:** **iron 32.1%** > oxygen 30.1% > **silicon 15.1%** > magnesium 13.9% > sulphur 2.9% > nickel 1.8% (RRB 2005: after iron and oxygen comes **silicon**).
[5:0:12] > Trap: crust question → oxygen/aluminium; whole-Earth question → iron.
[5:0:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 02 p.2-5 (pp.16-19); NextGen Rocket General Geography p.28-29, p.31; app notes 4:5 sub 2, 5
## SUB 1 | Seismic Waves, Shadow Zone and the Seismograph
[5:1:0] # Seismic waves (asked 7 times)
[5:1:1] TABLE head: Basis | P (primary) | S (secondary) | Surface (L)
  [5:1:1.0] Type | Longitudinal, push–pull, compressional; vibration parallel | Transverse, shear; vibration perpendicular | Along the surface (Love, Rayleigh)
  [5:1:1.1] Speed | Fastest, arrive first | Slower | Slowest
  [5:1:1.2] Medium | Solid, liquid, gas | Solids only | –
  [5:1:1.3] Damage | Lower | – | Highest
[5:1:2] - An earthquake generates **P, S and L (surface) waves** – "P.S.L" (CGPSC 2013). P and S are **body waves**.
[5:1:3] - **P-waves are sound (acoustic) waves:** compressional like sound, and they become audible sound when they reach the air – so of P, S and L, **P-waves** are the sound waves.
[5:1:4] - Wave speed changes with density → **reflection and refraction** at boundaries reveal the layers. The **S-wave** behaviour (vanishing in the outer core) gave the key evidence of a **liquid outer core** – the CDS 2012 answer "secondary waves".
[5:1:5] - **Shadow zone:** P-waves strongly refracted at the mantle–core boundary → no direct P **~105°–145°** (Rocket: 103°–142°); **S-waves absent everywhere beyond ~105°**. The belt **105°–145°** gets **neither P nor S** (APSLPRB 2023).
[5:1:6] - Each earthquake has its **own** shadow zone, set by its epicentre (CGPSC 2020).
[5:1:7] # Recording
[5:1:8] - **Seismograph** records seismic waves (FBO). NCERT Class 8: the seismograph is a **vibrating rod** or pendulum that starts vibrating with the tremors.
[5:1:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket General Geography p.29-30; NextGen Indian Geography 02 p.1 (p.15); PMF Physical Geography 01 (P-waves "take the form of sound waves" in air); NCERT Class 8 Science ch.12 (seismograph); app notes 4:5 sub 1
## SUB 2 | Earth's Magnetism, Heat and Pressure
[5:2:0] # Magnetic field (asked 4 times)
[5:2:1] - **Cause:** electric **currents in the liquid outer core** – convection of molten iron = **geodynamo** (UPPCS 2011) – not a giant magnet at the centre. It shields life from **solar wind and cosmic radiation**; flow changes are linked to **reversals**.
[5:2:2] - **Magnetic axis ~11.5°** to the geographic axis (not 23½°).
[5:2:3] - **Magnetic equator:** field lines **horizontal**, dip = 0 (NDA 2017); it passes near **Thumba** (Kerala) – hence TERLS. At the magnetic poles the field is vertical.
[5:2:4] - **North magnetic pole:** first located (1831) on the **Boothia Peninsula, northern Canada** – UPSC 2005 key; it has since drifted into the Arctic Ocean towards Siberia (~86°N as of 2025, World Magnetic Model 2025).
[5:2:5] - **Direction of the field** at a place = **declination** (angle from true north) **and inclination/dip** (angle from horizontal) (CDS 2018).
[5:2:6] - ESA **Swarm** mission: outer-core flow under the Pacific switched from westward to eastward.
[5:2:7] # Heat, pressure, density
[5:2:8] - Temperature, pressure and density **all rise with depth**; ~**1°C per 32 m** in the upper crust. Earth's mean density **5.5 g/cm³** (densest planet).
[5:2:9] - Geothermal sites: **Puga Valley (Ladakh)**, Manikaran (Himachal), Tattapani (Chhattisgarh), Cambay (Gujarat), **Bakreshwar (West Bengal)**.
[5:2:10] - Diamonds rise from the mantle via **kimberlite pipes**; **Madhya Pradesh** ~90% of India's reserves.
[5:2:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket General Geography p.31; NextGen Indian Geography 02 p.4 (p.18); NOAA/BGS World Magnetic Model 2025 (north magnetic pole position); app notes 4:5 sub 6
## SUB 3 | Discontinuities, Lithosphere and Asthenosphere
[5:3:0] TABLE head: Discontinuity | Separates | Note
  [5:3:0.0] Conrad | Upper and lower crust (SIAL–SIMA) | 1st from the surface
  [5:3:0.1] Mohorovicic (Moho) | Crust and mantle (APPSC G1) | P 6.9 → 8.1 km/s; 1909, Andrija Mohorovicic (Croatian)
  [5:3:0.2] Repetti | Upper and lower mantle | ~700–1,000 km
  [5:3:0.3] Gutenberg (Weichert–Gutenberg) | Mantle and outer core | ~2,900 km; S-waves vanish
  [5:3:0.4] Lehmann | Outer and inner core | ~5,150 km
[5:3:1] - 410 km and 660 km: mantle mineral **phase changes**. IUGG mantle zones: Moho–200, 200–700, 700–2,900 km.
[5:3:2] TABLE head: Basis | Lithosphere | Asthenosphere
  [5:3:2.0] Nature | Rigid; crust + uppermost mantle (~100 km) | Weak, plastic, partly molten (~100–200 km), in the upper mantle
  [5:3:2.1] Role | Broken into plates | Plates glide over it; main source of magma
[5:3:3] - Sequence: lithosphere → asthenosphere → mesosphere → **barysphere** (core).
[5:3:4] - Indian plate under Tibet: dense lower layer **delaminating** into the mantle at ~**100 km** (94 seismic stations).
[5:3:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 02 p.2-3 (pp.16-17); NextGen Rocket General Geography p.29-30; app notes 4:5 sub 3-4
## SUB 4 | Sources of Information about the Interior
[5:4:0] TABLE head: Direct | Indirect
  [5:4:0.0] Surface rocks from mining areas and deep drilling (APPSC G1) | Seismic waves – most important
  [5:4:0.1] Volcanic material (magma, lava) | Gravity anomalies, magnetic surveys
  [5:4:0.2] Kola Peninsula (USSR, 1970s): ~12 km, deepest hole | Meteorites
  [5:4:0.3] Mponeng, TauTona (South Africa): ~3.9 km, deepest mines | Rise of temperature and pressure with depth
[5:4:1] > Trap: seismic, gravity and magnetic data are **indirect**; meteorites are indirect evidence.
[5:4:2] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 02 p.5-6 (pp.19-20); app notes 4:5 sub 0

  x: S-waves are absent beyond 105°, so the S-wave shadow zone is larger than the P-wave shadow zone.

=== NOTES 4:6 | Rocks and Minerals – Igneous, Sedimentary, Metamorphic; the Rock Cycle
## SUB 0 | Composition of the Crust and Minerals
[6:0:0] # Elements of the crust (asked 8 times)
[6:0:1] TABLE head: Rank | Element | % by weight of crust
  [6:0:1.0] 1 | Oxygen | 46.6 – most abundant element (in oxides and silicates)
  [6:0:1.1] 2 | Silicon | 27.7 – second; not a metal; bulk of rocks and minerals as silica/silicates
  [6:0:1.2] 3 | Aluminium | 8.1 – most abundant metal
  [6:0:1.3] 4 | Iron | 5.0 – second-most abundant metal
  [6:0:1.4] 5–8 | Calcium, sodium, potassium, magnesium | 3.6, 2.8, 2.6, 2.1
[6:0:2] - Highest and lowest among O, Si, Ca, Na, Mg: **oxygen and magnesium** (CDS 2015).
[6:0:3] - "Element present in large amounts in rocks and minerals" = **silicon** (APPSC G1 2012).
[6:0:4] # Minerals (asked 7 times)
[6:0:5] - **Feldspar:** Si and O common to all feldspars; Na, K, Ca, Al in specific varieties; feldspar makes up about **one-half** of the crust (NCERT) – "one-fourth" is **wrong** (APPSC G1 2024 → **Statement I only**).
[6:0:6] - **Quartz** = SiO₂ (silicon dioxide); hard, resists weathering; Mohs 7; major part of granite and sandstone.
[6:0:7] TABLE head: Silicate class | Example
  [6:0:7.0] Inosilicate – single chain | Augite (pyroxene)
  [6:0:7.1] Inosilicate – double chain | Hornblende (amphibole)
  [6:0:7.2] Phyllosilicate (sheet) | Muscovite, biotite (mica) (APPSC FRO)
  [6:0:7.3] Tectosilicate (framework) | Albite, orthoclase (feldspar), quartz
[6:0:8] - **Bowen's reaction series** = order in which minerals crystallise from magma (APPSC FRO): **olivine first** → pyroxene → amphibole → biotite → K-feldspar → muscovite → **quartz last** (most stable).
[6:0:9] - **Mohs scale** measures **hardness of minerals** (APPSC G1 2002, repeated): talc 1, gypsum 2, calcite 3, fluorite 4, apatite 5, orthoclase 6, quartz 7, **topaz 8**, corundum 9, diamond 10. (Mercalli/Rossi-Forel = earthquake intensity; Beaufort = wind.)
[6:0:10] - **Calcium carbonate (CaCO₃):** limestone, **chalk and marble** (NDA 2020); **granite is not** a form of CaCO₃ (APPSC ASO 2017).
[6:0:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 02 p.5 (p.19); NCERT Class 11 Fundamentals of Physical Geography ch.5 (feldspar one-half); PMF Physical Geography 01 (felsic, feldspar); app notes 4:6 sub 0, 6
## SUB 1 | Igneous Rocks
[6:1:0] - **Formed by cooling and solidification of magma or lava** (State PSC); called **primary rocks**; **no layers, no fossils**; both **crystalline and non-crystalline** (State PSC: the true statement).
[6:1:1] TABLE head: Type | Formation | Examples
  [6:1:1.0] Intrusive (plutonic) | Cools slowly at depth → large grains / crystals | Granite (APPSC G2 2024), gabbro, diorite, pegmatite
  [6:1:1.1] Extrusive (volcanic) | Lava cools fast at the surface → fine grains | Basalt (APPSC FBO), rhyolite, andesite
[6:1:2] - **By silica:** rhyolite = felsic extrusive; granite = felsic intrusive; **diorite = intermediate intrusive**; basalt = mafic extrusive.
[6:1:3] - **Felsic:** silica-rich, light-coloured. **Mafic (basic):** rich in Fe, Mg, Ca; dark, dense.
[6:1:4] - **Not igneous:** **quartzite** (metamorphic, APSLPRB 2023), **dolomite** (sedimentary carbonate, NDA 2017). Granite and basalt = igneous (NDA 2007).
[6:1:5] - **Granite has no fossils** – formed from magma (JPSC 2013).
[6:1:6] # Deccan Trap basalt
[6:1:7] - The **Deccan Plateau / Deccan Traps** are made mainly of **basalt** – igneous lava flows (asked 4 times by APPSC).
[6:1:8] - Fissure eruptions at the end of the Cretaceous, **~65–66 million years ago** (APPSC Tech. Asst: nearest 65), as India passed over the Réunion hotspot.
[6:1:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 02 p.6 (p.20); NextGen Rocket General Geography p.32; NextGen AP Geography 02 p.4 (Deccan Trap: Cretaceous fissure lava, basalt); app notes 4:6 sub 2, 9
## SUB 2 | Sedimentary Rocks, Fossils and Geological Time
[6:2:0] - Formed at the Earth's surface by the **hydrological system**, from **weathering of pre-existing rocks**; sediments are transported, deposited, compacted and **lithified** in **layers** (strata) → "stratified rocks"; they **contain fossils** – all four UPSC 2001 statements are correct.
[6:2:1] - Cover about **75% of the Earth's surface**; hold most fossils and **coal, petroleum, natural gas**.
[6:2:2] TABLE head: Mode | Examples
  [6:2:2.0] Mechanically (clastic) | Sandstone, conglomerate, shale, loess
  [6:2:2.1] Chemically | Rock salt, gypsum, halite, chert, limestone
  [6:2:2.2] Organically | Coal (Uttarakhand 2006), chalk, coral limestone
[6:2:3] - **Sandstone** forms **under water** (MPPSC 1993); the **Red Fort and Agra Fort** are built of red **sandstone** – sedimentary.
[6:2:4] - **Himalayan rocks** are mainly **sedimentary** (folded Tethys sediments) (AP surveyor 2017; Sachivalayam 2020).
[6:2:5] - **Limestone** occurs white as well as black; igneous rocks have no layers; fossils are **not** found in igneous rocks.
[6:2:6] # Porosity vs permeability (UPSC 2025)
[6:2:7] TABLE head: Term | Rocks
  [6:2:7.0] Porous and permeable | Chalk (very permeable, aquifers), sandstone
  [6:2:7.1] Porous but impermeable | Clay – very fine pores, poorly connected
  [6:2:7.2] Neither | Granite
[6:2:8] - UPSC 2025: Statement II (chalk porous) correct and explains I; Statement III ("clay not at all porous") **wrong** → "Only one of II and III is correct and that explains I".
[6:2:9] # Fossils and time
[6:2:10] - **Fossils** = preserved remains, impressions or traces of ancient organisms (SSC 2018).
[6:2:11] - **Dinosaurs: Mesozoic era** (Triassic, Jurassic, Cretaceous); died out ~66 million years ago.
[6:2:12] - **Age of the Earth:** **uranium (radiometric) dating**; carbon dating only for young organic remains.
[6:2:13] - Giovanni Arduino (1760) made the first geological time scale.
[6:2:14] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 02 p.6 (p.20); PMF Physical Geography 02 (porosity); app notes 4:6 sub 3-4, 8
## SUB 3 | Metamorphic Rocks
[6:3:0] - Igneous **or** sedimentary rocks recrystallise under **heat and pressure** ("change of form") – they come from **both** (JPSC 2011).
[6:3:1] TABLE head: Parent rock | Metamorphic rock
  [6:3:1.0] Limestone (and chalk, dolomite) | Marble (UPPCS 1991; APPSC Panchayat Secretary)
  [6:3:1.1] Shale / clay | Slate (then schist)
  [6:3:1.2] Sandstone | Quartzite (UPSC 2001, asked twice) – not limestone, obsidian or shale
  [6:3:1.3] Granite | Gneiss
  [6:3:1.4] Basalt | Amphibolite, schist
  [6:3:1.5] Coal | Graphite (via anthracite)
[6:3:2] - Typical metamorphic minerals: **garnet** (UP 2010), kyanite, sillimanite, staurolite; **halite is not**.
[6:3:3] - Odd one out: **gneiss** (metamorphic) among sandstone, limestone, shale (sedimentary); **granite** (igneous) among marble, quartzite, slate (metamorphic); limestone among marble, slate, quartzite.
[6:3:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 02 p.6 (p.20); app notes 4:6 sub 5
## SUB 4 | Petrology and the Rock Cycle
[6:4:0] - **Petrology** = science (study) of rocks, a branch of geology (APPSC G2 2019). Rocks: igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic.
[6:4:1] - **Rock cycle:** magma → (cooling) igneous → (weathering, erosion, deposition, **lithification**) sedimentary → (heat, pressure) metamorphic → (melting) magma; **any rock type can become another**; exposed metamorphic rock weathers into sediment.
[6:4:2] - Rainwater with dissolved **CO₂** forms **carbonic acid**, which weathers rocks.
[6:4:3] - **Enhanced rock weathering:** crushed **basalt** spread on farmland locks CO₂ as bicarbonate.
[6:4:4] - **Lithology** = physical character of a rock unit – texture, grain size, composition.
[6:4:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 02 p.1 (p.15); app notes 4:6 sub 1, 7-8

  x: Albite and orthoclase (feldspars) and quartz are framework silicates, called tectosilicates.
[n1872c002539] sub1
  Which of the following is a coarse-grained intrusive igneous rock?
  Basalt | Rhyolite | *Gabbro | Obsidian
  x: Intrusive rocks cool slowly at depth, forming coarse grains, as in granite and gabbro.
[n47d893cb606] sub1
  Which of the following is a felsic extrusive igneous rock?
  *Rhyolite | Diorite | Granite | Basalt
  x: Rhyolite is felsic extrusive; granite is felsic intrusive, diorite intermediate intrusive and basalt mafic extrusive.
[n4b3fe0fa94e] sub1
  Consider the following statements:
1. Felsic igneous rocks are generally light-coloured and silica-rich.
2. Mafic rocks are always less dense than felsic rocks.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
  *1 only | 2 only | Both 1 and 2 | Neither 1 nor 2
  x: Felsic rocks are silica-rich, light-coloured and relatively low in density; mafic rocks, rich in iron, magnesium and calcium, are dark and dense, so statement 2 is wrong.
[fc222e439d12a] sub1
  What are dark, dense igneous rocks rich in iron, magnesium and calcium called?
  Felsic | Intermediate | *Mafic | Siliceous
  x: Mafic (basic) rocks are rich in Fe, Mg and Ca; felsic rocks are silica-rich and light-coloured.
[fbdf338010a37] sub1
  Which type of rock is diorite?
  Felsic extrusive rock | Mafic extrusive rock | Felsic intrusive rock | *Intermediate intrusive rock
  x: Diorite is intermediate intrusive; rhyolite is felsic extrusive, granite felsic intrusive and basalt mafic extrusive.
[ngeneral-geography-4-41] sub1
  Which of the following is NOT correct about rocks?
  Igneous rocks form by cooling of magma or lava | *Granite is extrusive igneous and basalt is intrusive igneous | Metamorphic rocks are existing rocks altered by heat or pressure | Sedimentary rocks form through surface deposition
  x: It is the reverse: granite is intrusive igneous and basalt is extrusive igneous.
[nfd23d6b10ad] sub2
  Which one of the following groups consists entirely of sedimentary rocks?
  *Sandstone, limestone, shale and conglomerate | Granite, basalt, gabbro and dolerite | Marble, slate, quartzite and gneiss | Granite, sandstone, marble and basalt
  x: Sandstone, limestone, shale and conglomerate are sedimentary rocks. The other groups contain igneous or metamorphic rocks.
[nea35322a33a] sub2
  Sedimentary rocks are called ‘stratified rocks’ because they are generally formed as:
  *Successive layers of deposited, compacted and cemented sediments | Single layers of volcanic ash only | Metamorphosed rocks melted beneath the crust | Unlayered masses of crystallised magma
  x: Sediments are transported, deposited, compacted and cemented into successive layers called strata.
[nafccc6f15d8] sub2

[n4aa79e42deb] sub2

  x: Clay has pore spaces, but its very fine particles prevent easy passage of water, so it is porous but impermeable.

  x: Sedimentary rocks cover about 75% of the Earth's surface and hold most fossils and mineral oil.

  x: Coal is metamorphosed into graphite via anthracite; slate comes from shale.

=== NOTES 4:8 | Folding, Faulting, Mountain Building; Isostasy
## SUB 0 | Types of Mountains – Fold, Block, Volcanic, Residual, Dome
[8:0:0] # Five types (asked 15 times)
[8:0:1] TABLE head: Type | How formed | Features | Examples
  [8:0:1.0] Young fold | Tertiary (Alpine) compression of geosyncline sediments | Very high, rugged, sharp conical peaks; world's highest peaks | Himalaya, Alps, Andes, Rockies, Atlas
  [8:0:1.1] Old fold | Caledonian/Hercynian or Precambrian folding + long denudation | Low, rounded, highly eroded | Aravallis (Precambrian), Appalachians, Urals, Pennines
  [8:0:1.2] Block | Faulting – uplifted block (horst) beside a sunken block (graben) | Steep fault scarps; linked with rift valleys | Sierra Nevada, Vosges (France), Black Forest (Germany), Salt Range
  [8:0:1.3] Volcanic | Accumulation of lava and ash around a vent | Conical, with a crater | Kilimanjaro, Fujiyama, Etna (Sicily), Mount St. Helens, Cotopaxi
  [8:0:1.4] Residual | Erosion leaves the resistant core of an old range | Remnants of older surfaces | Aravallis, Nilgiris, Vindhyas, Appalachians, Pennines
  [8:0:1.5] Dome | Magma pushes the crust up without erupting | Dome-shaped uplift | Black Hills, Bighorns (USA)
[8:0:2] - **Mountain:** most geologists take a landform rising at least **300 m (1,000 ft)** above its surroundings as a mountain (APPSC FSO).
[8:0:3] - **World's highest peaks** (Everest) lie in **young fold** mountains; Everest and Mont Blanc are fold, **not volcanic**.
[8:0:4] - **Young vs old:** **Alps** is the only young fold range among Appalachians, Aravallis, Alps, Urals (APPSC G2); the **Andes** are young, not old (UKPSC 2016); the **Appalachians** are not Tertiary (UPPSC 2014 – Kunlun, Alps, Andes are). Pennines, Appalachians, Aravallis = **old mountains** (State PSC).
[8:0:5] - **Block:** **Sierra Nevada** is a block mountain, not young fold (MPPSC 2021); **Black Forest = Germany** (Feldberg 1,493 m), Vosges = France, across the Rhine graben.
[8:0:6] - **Residual mountain of India = Aravallis** (UPPSC 2005; APPSC Asst Director). Match (UP UDA 2013): **Alps – folded, Vosges – block, Vindhya – residual, Fujiyama – volcanic**.
[8:0:7] - **Volcanic mountain:** **Mount Etna** (APPSC G1); Kilimanjaro, Fuji.
[8:0:8] - **Highest of Cotopaxi, Kilimanjaro, Pinatubo, Taal:** **Cotopaxi** (~5,897 m, Ecuador) just above Kilimanjaro (5,895 m) (UPPSC 2015). Highest volcano overall: Ojos del Salado (6,893 m).
[8:0:9] - **Andes** (~7,000 km) = longest range; Himalayas = highest.
[8:0:10] - **"Island of precipitation":** **dome** mountains like the Black Hills rise abruptly from dry plains and get about twice the plains' rainfall (APPSC G2 2011, printed as "Down mountains").
[8:0:11] > Trap: Aravallis are both old fold and residual; when "old mountains" and "fold mountains" are both offered, the books' key is "old mountains".
[8:0:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket General Geography p.33-34; NextGen Indian Geography 02 p.7-8 (pp.21-22); PMF Physical Geography 02 p.46-48 (pp.133-135); NPS/NWS Black Hills climate; app notes 4:8 sub 1
[8:0:13] - **Appalachians** = old fold mountains of the **Caledonian** orogeny (Palaeozoic).
## SUB 1 | The Aravalli – India's Oldest Fold (Residual) Range
[8:1:0] - **Oldest mountain range of India** (asked 6 times: vs Himalaya, Shiwalik, Vindhya, Satpura, Nilgiri, Western Ghats); Precambrian, from Dharwar sediments; age about **570 million years** (IAS 2001).
[8:1:1] - **Old fold mountain** (APPSC FSO flashcard: "fold mountain") and a **residual** mountain – "continuously denuded, typical residual hills" 400–600 m.
[8:1:2] - Runs ~800 km from **Delhi** through **Haryana** and **Rajasthan** to northern **Gujarat** – mainly **Rajasthan** (UPRO 2014).
[8:1:3] TABLE head: Peak | Height | Note
  [8:1:3.0] Guru Shikhar | 1,722 m | Highest; Mount Abu, Sirohi district, Rajasthan (UPSC 2007, asked twice)
  [8:1:3.1] Kumbhalgarh | ~1,224 m | Highest when Guru Shikhar is not offered (RAS 2012)
  [8:1:3.2] Sajjangarh, Lilagarh, Taragarh | ~938, 874, 873 m | Lower
[8:1:4] - Guru Shikhar is also the **highest peak of the Central Highlands** of the Peninsular Plateau (APPSC Degree Lecturers 2020); Parasnath and Dalma are Chotanagpur, Kamet is Himalaya.
[8:1:5] - **Supreme Court (Nov 2025):** an Aravalli **hill** = landform rising at least **100 m** above local relief (not 500 m); an Aravalli **range** = hills lying within **500 m** of each other; new mining leases paused. MoEF&CC banned new leases on **24 Dec 2025**; the SC later stayed its own directions (Dec 2025).
[8:1:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Indian Geography p.43; NextGen Indian Geography 05 p.10; PMF Physical Geography 02 p.48 (p.135); app notes 4:8 sub 2 (SC 2025 items, as of 2026)
## SUB 2 | Faults, Block Mountains and Rift Valleys
[8:2:0] # Faults
[8:2:1] TABLE head: Fault | Force | Movement
  [8:2:1.0] Normal | Tension | Hanging wall down
  [8:2:1.1] Reverse | Compression | Hanging wall up
  [8:2:1.2] Thrust | Compression | Low-angle reverse
  [8:2:1.3] Strike-slip | Shear | Horizontal
[8:2:2] - **Horst** = uplifted fault block → **block mountain** (APPSC AEE 2023); **graben** = down-faulted block → **rift valley**.
[8:2:3] - **Rift valley:** tension → faulting → central block subsides → elongated depression. Examples: **Rhine** (between Vosges and Black Forest), **Great Rift Valley** (East Africa), **Death Valley** (California – UPPSC 2012), **Narmada, Tapi**. Sierra Nevada = horst.
[8:2:4] # UPSC 2024 (asked twice): mountain – region – type
[8:2:5] TABLE head: Row | Correct?
  [8:2:5.0] Central Asia – Vosges – fold | Wrong – Vosges is a block mountain in Europe
  [8:2:5.1] Europe – Alps – block | Wrong – Alps are fold
  [8:2:5.2] North America – Appalachians – fold | Correct
  [8:2:5.3] South America – Andes – fold | Correct
[8:2:6] - Answer: **only two** rows correct.
[8:2:7] # Rift valleys of India (asked 6 times)
[8:2:8] - **Narmada** flows **west** through a **rift valley (fault trough)** between the **Vindhyas (north)** and **Satpuras (south)** → valley of **structural** origin (CDS 2010); forms an **estuary, no delta** (A false, R true – UPPSC 2005).
[8:2:9] - Why the Narmada flows west: **only because it occupies a rift valley** (UPSC 2015: "Only I"); lying between Vindhya and Satpura is just its location.
[8:2:10] - **Damodar** = east-flowing river in a **rift valley due to down-warping** (IAS 1998). Tapi also flows in a rift.
[8:2:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket General Geography p.36; NextGen Indian Geography 02 p.8 (p.22); NextGen Indian Geography 05 (Narmada rift); NCERT Class 11 India Physical Environment ch.3; app notes 4:8 sub 4
## SUB 3 | Young Fold Mountains – Evidence from the Himalaya
[8:3:0] - **Youngest/most recent range:** the **Himalayas** (CGPSC 2018); within them the **Shiwaliks** are the youngest chain (UPPSC 2010).
[8:3:1] - **Evidence of youth** (UPSC 2012, asked twice → **all four**): **deep gorges**, **U-turn river courses**, **parallel mountain ranges**, **steep gradients causing landslides**.
[8:3:2] - Formed by the **northward movement of the Indian Plate** squeezing the **Tethys** sediments; main uplift Eocene–Pliocene.
[8:3:3] - **Tertiary (Alpine) orogeny:** Himalaya, Alps, Andes, Rockies, Atlas, Kunlun. **Caledonian:** Appalachians (old).
[8:3:4] ~~ Sources: NCERT Class 11 India Physical Environment ch.2; PMF Physical Geography 02 p.48 (p.135); NextGen Rocket General Geography p.33; app notes 4:8 sub 1
## SUB 4 | Diastrophism – Endogenic and Exogenic Forces
[8:4:0] - **Endogenic** (internal heat → mantle dynamics → plate movement): **diastrophism and volcanism**; **earthquakes are endogenic** (APPSC Inspector of Factories). **Exogenic:** weathering, erosion, deposition.
[8:4:1] - **Diastrophism** = all processes that move, raise or build up the crust: orogeny, epeirogeny, **earthquakes**, **plate tectonics**; **"heterogenic" is NOT** one (MPPSC 2023).
[8:4:2] TABLE head: Orogenic | Epeirogenic
  [8:4:2.0] Mountain building; severe folding in narrow belts | Continent building; uplift or warping of large areas
  [8:4:2.1] Horizontal (tangential) forces → folding (State PSC) | Vertical (radial) forces (UKPSC 2024)
[8:4:3] - **APPSC G1 – incorrect statement:** "Orogeny is the continental building process" – orogeny is **mountain** building; epeirogeny is continental building.
[8:4:4] ~~ Sources: NCERT Class 11 Fundamentals of Physical Geography ch.5; NextGen Rocket General Geography p.31; app notes 4:8 sub 0
[8:4:5] - **Epeirogenic example:** vertical movements of the **Peninsular Block** (marine transgression and regression).
## SUB 5 | Folds
[8:5:0] - **Anticline** = **upfold** (arch; oldest strata in the core) (NDA 2015); **syncline** = downfold (trough).
[8:5:1] - Rising pressure: symmetrical → asymmetrical → overturned → **recumbent** (axial plane horizontal; **both limbs horizontal and parallel** – NDA 2019) → **nappe** (recumbent fold broken and thrust far forward).
[8:5:2] - **Isoclinal** fold = limbs parallel to each other (and to the axial plane).
[8:5:3] - Shiwaliks: simple anticline–syncline folds (Jura type). Cuddapah sediments lie in **synclinal troughs**.
[8:5:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Physical Geography 02 p.47-49 (pp.134-136); app notes 4:8 sub 3
## SUB 6 | Isostasy and Geosynclines
[8:6:0] - **Isostasy:** crustal blocks float in balance on denser material below.
[8:6:1] TABLE head: Airy | Pratt
  [8:6:1.0] Uniform density, varying thickness | Varying density, same depth of compensation
  [8:6:1.1] Mountains have deep roots | Higher blocks are lighter
[8:6:2] - **Kober's geosynclinal theory:** long shallow sediment-filled troughs (geosynclines) between rigid forelands (**kratogens**) are squeezed into mountains; Tethys → Himalaya. Stages: **lithogenesis** (sedimentation) → **orogenesis** → **gliptogenesis**.
[8:6:3] ~~ Sources: app notes 4:8 sub 5; PMF Physical Geography 02 p.47 (geosyncline)

  x: The Aravalli, India's oldest range, is about 570 million years old; the Himalayan uplift began about 70 million years ago.
[g25456cd54451] sub1

  x: Guru Shikhar (1,722 m) is on Mount Abu in Sirohi district of Rajasthan.
[gf1c36ff84c71] sub1

  x: In November 2025 the Supreme Court defined an Aravalli hill as 100 m above local relief, and a range as hills within 500 m of each other.
[ngeneral-geography-5-15] sub2

  Gorge | U-shaped valley | *Rift valley | Hanging valley
  x: A rift valley forms when the central block sinks between faults after divergence, producing a long depression.
[n8c5bc9999ea] sub2

  x: Sierra Nevada is a block mountain (horst), not a graben; the Great Rift Valley, Death Valley and Rhine Rift Valley are grabens.

  x: The Narmada flows west through a rift valley situated between the Vindhyas in the north and the Satpuras in the south.

  What is an uplifted fault block associated with block mountains called?

[fe6844070af5c] sub2

  *Tension – hanging wall down | Compression – hanging wall up | Shear – horizontal movement | Compression – hanging wall down
  x: A normal fault forms under tension with the hanging wall moving down; a reverse fault forms under compression with it moving up.
[fdda81553e932] sub2
  A strike-slip fault results from which force?
  Tension | Compression | *Shear | Gravity
  x: Strike-slip faults form by shear and involve horizontal movement.

  x: The Rhine graben lies between the Vosges and the Black Forest block mountains.

[n95620fa7193] sub3
