=== NOTES 4:14 | Atmosphere – Structure (layers) and Composition
## SUB 0 | Ozone Layer – Location, Formation and UV Shield
[14:0:0] # Where the ozone layer lies (asked 17 times)
[14:0:1] - **Ozone (O₃) = three oxygen atoms** (APPSC BC Welfare). It lies mainly in the **stratosphere** – the standard answer to "ozone layer is located in / found mainly in / maximum concentration in / rich in ozone" (UPPCS ×8, CGPSC, SSC, CDS 2009, APPSC AEE, APPSC AMVI) – not the troposphere, mesosphere, ionosphere or exosphere.
[14:0:2] - **Lower stratosphere:** main layer **~15–30 km**, densest **~15–35 km** (NCERT/Rocket); exam heights "**15–20 km above the surface**" (State PSC) are the accepted option – never "below the surface", never 40–50 or 70–80 km.
[14:0:3] - About **90%** of all ozone is **stratospheric**, ~10% tropospheric.
[14:0:4] - Formation (**Chapman cycle**): **UV + O₂ → O + O; O + O₂ → O₃**; O₃ absorbs UV and splits again.
[14:0:5] - Column ozone is measured in **Dobson Units (DU)**; 1 DU = 0.01 mm of pure ozone at 0°C, 1 atm.
[14:0:6] # What it does (asked 13 times)
[14:0:7] - **Absorbs harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation** of the Sun and acts as **Earth's shield** (APPSC FBO, APPSC ASO; MPPSC 1994 ×2; UKPSC 2002, 2006; UPPCS 2006, 2013; CGPSC 2013) – it does **not** supply oxygen, control Earth's temperature, trap heat, reflect sunlight, cause rain or stop earthquakes/monsoon failure.
[14:0:8] - It does **not** absorb cosmic rays, infrared, visible light or microwaves – only **UV**.
[14:0:9] TABLE head: UV band | Wavelength | Ozone layer
  [14:0:9.0] UV-A | 315–400 nm | Mostly reaches the surface
  [14:0:9.1] UV-B | 280–315 nm | Mostly absorbed, part reaches the ground
  [14:0:9.2] UV-C | 100–280 nm (shortest, most harmful) | Completely absorbed (APPSC FSO 2025)
[14:0:10] - Excess UV → **skin (dermal) cancer** (UPPSC 2014), **cataract**, weaker immunity, lower crop yield → ozone is **essential for biotic life** because it screens high-energy radiation (UPPSC Mains 2010: A and R true, R explains A).
[14:0:11] - Stratosphere **warms with height** because ozone turns absorbed UV into heat.
[14:0:12] TABLE head: Ozone | Role
  [14:0:12.0] Stratospheric | Protective shield – good
  [14:0:12.1] Ground-level (tropospheric) | Secondary pollutant from NOx + VOCs in sunlight (photochemical smog); heatwaves raise it (north-west India, Indo-Gangetic Plain) – bad
[14:0:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Environment #27 p.47-49; NextGen Rocket General Geography #6 p.45; NextGen Indian Geography 03 p.4, 6 (pp.32, 34); app notes 4:14 sub 8
## SUB 1 | Ozone Depletion, the Ozone Hole and Treaties
[14:1:0] # Cause (asked 13 times)
[14:1:1] - Depletion happens in the **stratosphere** (APPSC AEE; APPSC Degree Lecturers).
[14:1:2] - **Main cause: halocarbons** – **CFCs** (most damaging), HCFCs, halons – that release **chlorine and bromine** (APPSC 2023 Lecturers ×2; APPSC 2025 Welfare Organiser and Sainik Welfare Officer: **CFCs**, not UV rays, heavy metals or reactive oxygen species).
[14:1:3] - **Carbon dioxide has no direct role** in ozone depletion (APPSC Sainik Welfare) – nor do CO, nitrogen, acetylene, ethylene, SO₂ or O₂.
[14:1:4] TABLE head: ODS | Use
  [14:1:4.0] CFCs | Refrigeration, ACs, aerosols, foam
  [14:1:4.1] HCFCs | CFC substitute – also deplete ozone
  [14:1:4.2] Halons | Fire extinguishers
  [14:1:4.3] Methyl bromide | Fumigant
  [14:1:4.4] Carbon tetrachloride, methyl chloroform | Solvents
[14:1:5] - CFCs, halons **and** carbon tetrachloride are all ozone-depleting (UPPSC 2012 → I, II and III).
[14:1:6] - **HFCs** spare ozone but have high global-warming potential; CFCs destroy ozone **and** are strong GHGs.
[14:1:7] # The Antarctic ozone hole (asked 8 times)
[14:1:8] - Maximum over **Antarctica** – the **poles**, not the equator or tropics (MPPSC 2008; CDS 2012); forms in the southern spring **Aug–Nov**.
[14:1:9] - Reason (UPSC 2011): **a prominent polar front (polar vortex) and polar stratospheric clouds (PSCs), plus the inflow of CFCs** – PSCs (12–22 km, nitric acid ice) turn inactive chlorine into reactive forms that destroy ozone when sunlight returns.
[14:1:10] - First reported in **1985** by a **British team** (British Antarctic Survey: **Farman, Gardiner, Shanklin**) (RAS 2012; UPPSC Mains 2013).
[14:1:11] - 2025 hole peaked at just over **21 million sq km** and closed early (record ~29 million sq km, 2006).
[14:1:12] TABLE head: Treaty | Year | Point
  [14:1:12.0] Vienna Convention | 1985 | Framework: research, monitoring
  [14:1:12.1] Montreal Protocol | 1987 | Legally binding; phases out ~100 ODS; universally ratified (first UN treaties ratified by all, with Vienna)
  [14:1:12.2] Kigali Amendment | 2016 (Kigali, Rwanda) | HFC phase-down 80–85%; in force 1 Jan 2019
[14:1:13] - **World Ozone Day: 16 September** (Montreal Protocol signing).
[14:1:14] - India: **first developing country** to phase out **HCFC-141b** in rigid foam; HCFCs cut **44%** vs 35% target by Jan 2020.
[14:1:15] - AP: **Mission SANA** (Red Balloon Aerospace) – India's first home-made **stratospheric super-pressure balloon**, launched from **Vijayawada** (May 2026).
[14:1:16] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Environment #27 p.48-49; PMF Environment 04 p.26-28 (PSCs, polar vortex); app notes 4:14 sub 9
## SUB 2 | Composition – Gases of the Atmosphere
[14:2:0] # Gases of dry air (asked 10 times)
[14:2:1] TABLE head: Gas | Share by volume | Type
  [14:2:1.0] Nitrogen | 78.08% (~78%) – most abundant | Permanent
  [14:2:1.1] Oxygen | 20.95% (~21%, rounded "20%" – APPSC G1 2012) | Permanent
  [14:2:1.2] Argon | 0.93% – third, inert | Permanent
  [14:2:1.3] Carbon dioxide | ~0.04% (0.036% in NCERT) | Variable
  [14:2:1.4] Water vapour | 0–4% | Variable
  [14:2:1.5] Neon, helium, krypton, xenon, hydrogen, ozone | Traces | —
[14:2:2] - **N₂ > O₂ > Ar > CO₂** (APPSC G1 2023). **Nitrogen + oxygen = 99%** – the air near the surface is "mainly nitrogen and oxygen" (RAS 1997).
[14:2:3] - **Permanent gases** keep a constant proportion: nitrogen, oxygen, argon (and the noble gases); **variable:** CO₂, water vapour, ozone → UPPCS Mains 2017 answer **nitrogen**.
[14:2:4] - **Chlorine** is **not** a normal constituent of air (APPSC G2 2008); neon, helium and CO₂ are.
[14:2:5] - **Xenon = "Stranger Gas"** (Greek *xenos*), found by **Ramsay and Travers, 1898** (UPSC 2008).
[14:2:6] - Weather balloons are filled with **helium** (light, inert) (RAS 1997).
[14:2:7] - **0.03% CO₂** = the optimum for natural balance (UPPCS 2017); today it is ~0.04% (**423.9 ppm in 2024**, WMO Greenhouse Gas Bulletin, Oct 2025).
[14:2:8] - Air is held to the Earth by **gravity** (SSC 2011).
[14:2:9] # Change with height and with time
[14:2:10] - **99% of the mass lies within 32 km.** Moving up, **CO₂ and water vapour vanish first (~90 km)**, then **oxygen (negligible by ~120 km)**, while nitrogen continues → order of disappearance **CO₂ → O₂ → N₂** (NDA 2009).
[14:2:11] - Light gases rise highest: the **exosphere** is mostly **hydrogen** (with helium) (NDA 2015).
[14:2:12] - **Early atmosphere:** **reducing** – methane, ammonia, hydrocarbons, little free oxygen; methane and hydrocarbons were oxidised and replaced by **carbon dioxide** (BPSC 1995); photosynthesis later made it oxygen-rich.
[14:2:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 03 p.3 (p.31); NextGen Rocket General Geography #6 p.42-43, 48; PMF Physical Geography 04 p.21 (oxygen negligible at 120 km, CO₂ to 90 km); app notes 4:14 sub 0
## SUB 3 | Layers – Basis, Sequence and Temperature Trend
[14:3:0] # Sequence (asked 10 times)
[14:3:1] - Layers are divided on the **vertical profile of air temperature** (APPSC G1) – not wind, humidity or pressure.
[14:3:2] TABLE head: Order | Layer | Height | Temperature | Identity
  [14:3:2.0] 1 | Troposphere – lowest (SSC CGL 2019; UKPSC 2016) | 0 to 8 km (poles) / 18 km (equator); avg 13 km | Falls | Weather
  [14:3:2.1] 2 | Stratosphere – second layer (APPSC AMVI) | to 50 km | Rises | Ozone
  [14:3:2.2] 3 | Mesosphere | 50–80 km | Falls to −100°C – coldest (Astt. Comm. 2018) | Meteors burn
  [14:3:2.3] 4 | Thermosphere (ionosphere 80–400/640 km) | from 80 km | Rises sharply | Ions, radio waves, aurora
  [14:3:2.4] 5 | Exosphere | outermost | Rarefied | Merges into space
[14:3:3] - Upward order **Troposphere → Stratosphere → Mesosphere → Thermosphere/Ionosphere** (UPSC 1998, CDS 2015, UPPCS 2005, UPPCS 2015).
[14:3:4] - The troposphere is the layer of **smallest height** (SSC 2011).
[14:3:5] - The **atmosphere** = the thin layer of gases around the Earth (APPSC Jr Asst); it has **no definite upper limit** and **thins gradually** until imperceptible (CDS 2015).
[14:3:6] - Temperature trend upward: **falls, rises, falls, rises**; reversal layers: **stratosphere and thermosphere**.
[14:3:7] TABLE head: Boundary | Height
  [14:3:7.0] Tropopause | 8–18 km
  [14:3:7.1] Stratopause | ~50 km
  [14:3:7.2] Mesopause | ~80 km
[14:3:8] # Matching (UPPCS Mains 2002)
[14:3:9] - Troposphere – weather; stratosphere – ozone; ionosphere – radio waves reflected to Earth → correct. **Mesosphere – aurorae is wrong** (aurora = ionosphere/thermosphere) → **1, 2 and 3**.
[14:3:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 03 p.6-7 (pp.34-35); NextGen Rocket General Geography #6 p.43, 47-49; app notes 4:14 sub 2-3
[14:3:11] - **Thermosphere** warms with height because its thin gases absorb **high-energy solar radiation** (X-rays, extreme UV); the stratosphere warms because **ozone absorbs UV**.
## SUB 4 | Troposphere and Tropopause
[14:4:0] # Troposphere (asked 12 times)
[14:4:1] - **Average height 13 km**; ~8 km at the poles, ~**18 km at the equator** (State PSC: "average height 13 km" is the true statement; it is not the top layer and its temperature falls with height).
[14:4:2] - **Thickest at the equator** because **high insolation and strong convection** carry heat to great heights → UPSC 2004 (A and R true, R explains A; "thickness of the atmosphere" in the stem means the troposphere) and UPSC 2024 (I and II correct, II explains I).
[14:4:3] - **Almost all weather** – clouds, rain, fog, hail, storms – happens here (RAS 1999; MPPSC 2023); the **cloud mass of a cyclone** rises only within the troposphere (APPSC AE 2017).
[14:4:4] - Contains nearly all **water vapour and dust**; most important for **biological activity**.
[14:4:5] - **Normal lapse rate ~6.5°C per km** (≈ **1°C per 165 m**) – temperature **decreases** with height (NDA 2018 option "6.4°C per km" = the approximate normal rate).
[14:4:6] - **Agra and Darjeeling** lie on about the same latitude; Darjeeling is much colder in January because temperature falls with **height** (UPPCS 2022: A and R true, R explains A).
[14:4:7] # Tropopause
[14:4:8] - **Transition zone between troposphere and stratosphere**, lying **below the stratosphere**; its height **varies with season** (higher in summer) and **latitude** (higher at the equator) → APPSC G1 2018: **i, ii and iii all correct**.
[14:4:9] - It is a **zone of mixing** (NDA 2012) – not formed by meteoric dust, not 5–10 km thick, and it is ~18 km (not 8 km) over the equator.
[14:4:10] - Temperature at the tropopause: about **−80°C over the equator**, **−45°C over the poles**.
[14:4:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 03 p.6 (p.34); NextGen Rocket General Geography #6 p.43-44; app notes 4:14 sub 4
## SUB 5 | Stratosphere, Mesosphere, Ionosphere and Exosphere
[14:5:0] # Phenomenon → layer (asked 9 times)
[14:5:1] TABLE head: Phenomenon | Layer
  [14:5:1.0] Jet aircraft fly in the lower stratosphere | No clouds or weather, dry, stable (JPSC 2010)
  [14:5:1.1] Meteors burn up | Mesosphere (APPSC G2) – not thermosphere/exosphere
  [14:5:1.2] Radio waves deflected / reflected; wireless communication; telecommunication | Ionosphere (UPSC 1996, UPPCS 2005, 2013, JPSC 2013)
  [14:5:1.3] Aurora Borealis (north) / Australis (south) | Ionosphere (the ionised part of the thermosphere) (UPPCS 2010)
  [14:5:1.4] Communication satellites (geostationary ~36,000 km) | Exosphere (UKPSC 2005)
[14:5:2] - Ionosphere: **80–400 km** (NextGen; 80–640 km in older books); **electrically charged ions** reflect radio waves back to Earth; expands by day, contracts at night.
[14:5:3] - Aurora: solar charged particles excite upper-air atoms near the magnetic poles.
[14:5:4] - **MST (Mesosphere–Stratosphere–Troposphere) radar** at the **National Atmospheric Research Laboratory (NARL), Gadanki, near Tirupati** (APPSC Hostel Welfare Officer).
[14:5:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 03 p.6 (p.34); NextGen Rocket General Geography #6 p.45-47; NextGen Rocket AP Geography p.39 (NARL Gadanki, Tirupati); app notes 4:14 sub 6
## SUB 6 | Carbon Dioxide, Water Vapour, Dust and the Greenhouse Property
[14:6:0] # CO₂ as a greenhouse gas (asked 5 times)
[14:6:1] - CO₂ is **transparent to incoming solar (short-wave) radiation** but **opaque to outgoing terrestrial (long-wave, infrared) radiation** – it **absorbs infrared** and re-radiates heat (UPSC 2012; CDS 2012; RAS 1992) – not UV, not all radiation, not water vapour.
[14:6:2] - **Greenhouse effect** = heating of the atmosphere by absorption of infrared by CO₂ and other gases; **CO₂** is the gas that contributes most (APPSC FBO) and whose rise enhances it (UPPSC 2015) – not CO, O₂, N₂ or argon.
[14:6:3] - Other GHGs: **methane, nitrous oxide, water vapour (most abundant GHG), CFCs**; not hydrogen, krypton, neon, helium or argon.
[14:6:4] # Water vapour and dust
[14:6:5] - **Water vapour:** up to **4%** in warm wet tropics, **under 1%** in deserts and polar air; decreases with height and from equator to poles; absorbs insolation and Earth's heat (**blanket**); decides air stability.
[14:6:6] - **Dust:** sea salt, fine soil, smoke-soot, ash, pollen, meteor dust; mostly in lower layers; **more in subtropical and temperate regions because of dry winds** than in equatorial and polar regions → UPSC 2025: **Statement I correct, Statement II ("less dry winds") wrong**.
[14:6:7] - Dust and salt act as **hygroscopic nuclei** for condensation → clouds.
[14:6:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 03 p.3-6 (pp.31-34); PMF Physical Geography 04 p.21-22; app notes 4:14 sub 0-1
## SUB 7 | Homosphere, Heterosphere and Ionospheric Layers
[14:7:0] TABLE head: Region | Height | Layers | Composition
  [14:7:0.0] Homosphere | 0 to ~90 km | Three: troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere (APPSC Degree Lecturers) | Gases evenly mixed
  [14:7:0.1] Heterosphere | Above ~90 km | Thermosphere (ionosphere), exosphere | Layered by molecular weight: N₂ → atomic O → He → H
[14:7:1] - The **ionosphere is not in the homosphere** (UKPSC 2021).
[14:7:2] TABLE head: Ionospheric layer | Height | Role
  [14:7:2.0] D | 60–90 km | Absorbs medium/long waves; fades at night
  [14:7:2.1] E (Kennelly-Heaviside) | 90–150 km | Reflects medium-frequency waves
  [14:7:2.2] F (Appleton) | 150–400 km | Main reflector of short-wave radio
[14:7:3] - Solar flares and geomagnetic storms disturb the ionosphere and disrupt **GNSS** signals.
[14:7:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket General Geography #6 p.46; app notes 4:14 sub 5, 7

=== NOTES 4:15 | Insolation and Heat Budget; Distribution of Temperature, Inversion
## SUB 0 | Heating of the Atmosphere – Radiation, Conduction, Convection, Advection
[15:0:0] # How the air is heated (asked 8 times)
[15:0:1] TABLE head: Process | Mechanism
  [15:0:1.0] Insolation | Direct heating by incoming short-wave solar radiation
  [15:0:1.1] Conduction | Heats the lower layers of air in contact with the warm ground
  [15:0:1.2] Convection | Vertical transfer – warm air rises, cool air sinks (troposphere)
  [15:0:1.3] Advection | Horizontal transfer by wind (e.g. the Loo)
  [15:0:1.4] Terrestrial radiation | Long-wave infra-red from the Earth = main heater of the air
[15:0:2] - APPSC Group-II 2024 match: **Advection – horizontal; Convection – vertical; Insolation – direct; Conduction – lower layers** (a-I, b-II, c-III, d-IV).
[15:0:3] - The atmosphere is **heated from below**: the troposphere is warmest near the ground because it is **heated by the Earth's surface** (SSC 2011) – not because it is closest to the Sun or makes its own heat. It is **not** mainly heated by incoming sunlight (UPSC 2024: that statement is wrong).
[15:0:4] - Sun's radiation = **short-wave**: mostly **visible light + short-wave (near) infra-red** (NDA 2019); the Earth re-radiates **long-wave infra-red**, not ultraviolet (Asst. Comm. 2009: both "receives at infra-red end" and "re-radiates as UV" are wrong → **neither**).
[15:0:5] - Long-wave terrestrial radiation is absorbed mainly by **carbon dioxide and water vapour** (concentrated in the lower atmosphere) – UPSC 2023 correct statement; infra-red is **not** part of the visible spectrum and is **not** two-thirds of insolation (about half of insolation is infra-red).
[15:0:6] - **Conduction, convection and radiation** are tied to long-wave (terrestrial) heat transfer; **scattering** is a short-wave process (IAS 2018 odd one out).
[15:0:7] - **Radiation needs no medium** (UPRO 2017); conduction and convection need matter.
[15:0:8] - Wind on a hot summer day = **convection current** of air (CDS 2011); trade winds too arise from **convection** (Hadley cell).
[15:0:9] ~~ Sources: NCERT Fundamentals of Physical Geography ch.9 (via PMF Physical Geography 04 p.16, 29-31); NextGen Rocket General Geography #7 p.52; app notes 4:15 sub 0
## SUB 1 | Insolation – Meaning, Factors and Distribution
[15:1:0] # Meaning and factors (asked 7 times)
[15:1:1] - **Insolation = incoming solar radiation** (APPSC Group-1) – energy received by the Earth's surface as short waves.
[15:1:2] - Factors: **angle of the Sun's rays (set by latitude)**, **length of the day**, **transparency of the atmosphere** (clouds, dust, water vapour), Earth–Sun distance, land–sea distribution, slope and aspect.
[15:1:3] - Intensity depends mainly on **latitude** (NDA 2011) – not on **longitude** (APSLPRB SI 2023: longitude has no influence).
[15:1:4] - **Perihelion ~3 January, ~147 million km**; **aphelion ~4 July, ~152 million km** – distance matters little; tilt and angle matter more.
[15:1:5] # Distribution
[15:1:6] - Equator gets **direct** rays, poles **oblique** rays → insolation **decreases** from the Equator to the poles.
[15:1:7] - **Least seasonal variation: equatorial regions** (CDS 2013 – near-constant day length and high Sun); **greatest seasonal contrast: polar zones** (NDA 2013 – months of continuous day and night).
[15:1:8] - At the same latitude insolation is **higher over continents than oceans**; **maximum insolation and highest temperatures** over the **subtropical deserts** (clear skies, dry air), not the Equator.
[15:1:9] - Equator receives on the whole only about **2.5 times** (not 10 times) the annual insolation of the poles.
[15:1:10] - Heat **surplus in the tropics**, deficit at the poles; winds and ocean currents carry heat poleward.
[15:1:11] ~~ Sources: PMF Physical Geography 04 p.4, 16, 29-31; NextGen Rocket General Geography #7 p.53; app notes 4:15 sub 1
## SUB 2 | Albedo, Heat Budget and Greenhouse Effect
[15:2:0] # Albedo (asked 7 times)
[15:2:1] - **Albedo = reflecting power** of a surface – the share of incoming radiation it reflects (UPPCS 2019).
[15:2:2] - Highest albedo: **fresh snow** (APPSC Group-I 2019; APPSC Group-1; UPSC 2010 ×2) – reflects **75–95%**; then sand > grass > forest > **water (lowest)**.
[15:2:3] TABLE head: Surface | Albedo (approx.)
  [15:2:3.0] Fresh snow | 75–95%
  [15:2:3.1] Dry sand / desert | 20–40%
  [15:2:3.2] Grass | 20–25%
  [15:2:3.3] Crop land (paddy) | 15–25%
  [15:2:3.4] Water (sun high) | below 10%
[15:2:4] - **Low, thick clouds reflect** sunlight (cooling); **high, thin clouds trap heat** (warming).
[15:2:5] - **Ice-albedo feedback**: melting ice exposes darker ocean that absorbs more heat; the **Arctic warms 3–4 times** the global average (Apr 2025).
[15:2:6] # Heat budget – 100 units
[15:2:7] TABLE head: Of 100 units of insolation | Units
  [15:2:7.0] Reflected to space (clouds 27, scattering 6, snow/ice 2) = planetary albedo | 35
  [15:2:7.1] Absorbed by the atmosphere | 14
  [15:2:7.2] Absorbed by the surface | 51
[15:2:8] - About **30–35%** of insolation goes back to space without heating the Earth = **Earth's albedo** (CDS 2013).
[15:2:9] - Surface gives back all 51: **17 directly to space**, 34 to the atmosphere; atmosphere radiates **48** (14 + 34) to space → 35 + 17 + 48 = 100, so the Earth neither warms nor cools.
[15:2:10] # Greenhouse effect
[15:2:11] - Atmosphere is **transparent to short waves**, **opaque to long waves**; greenhouse gases send part of the long-wave heat back.
[15:2:12] - Without the greenhouse effect / atmosphere: **about −18°C** instead of **+15°C** (UPPSC 2020); day–night extremes would **increase** (CDS 2010).
[15:2:13] TABLE head: Gas | Share of effect
  [15:2:13.0] CO₂ | ~60%
  [15:2:13.1] Methane ("marsh gas") | ~20%
  [15:2:13.2] CFCs | ~15%
  [15:2:13.3] N₂O | ~5%
[15:2:14] - **Water vapour** = most abundant GHG, acts as a feedback. **GWP (100 yr)**: CO₂ 1; methane **28–36**; N₂O **265–298**.
[15:2:15] - Global **land** temperature up **1.59°C** since pre-industrial (UNEP Emissions Gap Report 2025).
[15:2:16] ~~ Sources: PMF Physical Geography 04 p.32-35 (albedo, heat budget); NCERT Fundamentals of Physical Geography ch.9; app notes 4:15 subs 2-4
## SUB 3 | Cloudy and Clear Nights; Range of Temperature
[15:3:0] # Cloudy vs clear nights (asked 5 times)
[15:3:1] - **Cloudy nights are warmer**: clouds **reflect / send back the heat given off by the Earth** (UPSC 2001) and **hinder terrestrial radiation** (NDA 2010) – a blanket.
[15:3:2] - **Clear nights are colder** because of free **(terrestrial) radiation** to space (State PSC; RRB 2016) – not conduction or condensation; clear skies give the greatest night cooling, dew and frost.
[15:3:3] # Range of temperature (asked 3 times)
[15:3:4] - **Interior / continental** = large daily and annual range; **coasts** = equable, small range.
[15:3:5] - **Highest daily range in India: desert areas of Rajasthan** (CGPSC 2011); highest winter diurnal range **NW India**.
[15:3:6] - **Chennai** (IAS 2002): annual mean **~26°C** and an annual range of only **~9°C** fit a tropical coastal station – Allahabad has a large range, Cherrapunji far more rain, Kolkata a cooler winter.
[15:3:7] - **Seasonal range maximum in high latitudes**; largest annual range in **continental interiors such as Siberia**; **minimum at the Equator**.
[15:3:8] - AP: **interior Rayalaseema** high daily range; coast (Visakhapatnam, Kakinada) small range – sea breezes.
[15:3:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket General Geography #7 p.52-53 (cloudy vs clear sky); PMF Physical Geography 04 p.37; app notes 4:15 sub 7
## SUB 4 | Distribution of Temperature – Isotherms, Lapse Rate, Inversion
[15:4:0] # Horizontal distribution (asked 4 times)
[15:4:1] - **Isotherms** join places of equal temperature (reduced to sea level); more regular in the **Southern Hemisphere** (mostly ocean).
[15:4:2] TABLE head: Month (NH) | Over land | Over oceans
  [15:4:2.0] January | Bend equatorward | Bend poleward (oceans warmer)
  [15:4:2.1] July | Bend poleward | Bend equatorward
[15:4:3] - UPSC 2025: in January isotherms bend equatorward over land and poleward over oceans **because air over the oceans is warmer than over land** → both statements true, II explains I.
[15:4:4] - **Highest temperatures** are recorded not at the Equator but around **20° N** (MPPCS 2010) – subtropical deserts.
[15:4:5] - **Thermal equator** (line of highest mean temperature) lies **north of the geographical equator** (CDS 2011) – more land in the NH; it moves with the Sun.
[15:4:6] - India: **January 18°C isotherm** divides India into tropical (south) and sub-tropical (north) (UPSC 1997); winter **20°C isotherm** runs from the Tapi mouth to the **Mahanadi delta**.
[15:4:7] - Controls: latitude, **altitude** (Himalayas cool), distance from sea, **ocean currents** (cold currents lower coastal temperature), relief, cloud cover.
[15:4:8] # Vertical distribution
[15:4:9] - **Normal lapse rate 6.5°C per km** – the ground heats air from below; higher air is thinner, with less water vapour and dust.
[15:4:10] # Temperature inversion
[15:4:11] - Temperature **rises with height** instead of falling. Favoured by **long winter nights, clear skies, calm dry air, snow cover** (not cloudy skies).
[15:4:12] TABLE head: Type | Feature
  [15:4:12.0] Surface (radiation) | Night cooling of the ground
  [15:4:12.1] Valley (air drainage) | Cold air drains downslope → frost pockets on valley floor; orchards on upper slopes
  [15:4:12.2] Frontal | Warm air over a cold-air wedge along a front
  [15:4:12.3] Permanent | Stratosphere = permanent inversion layer
[15:4:13] - Effects: **fog, frost, smog**; pollutants trapped in the planetary boundary layer (north Indian winter fog).
[15:4:14] ~~ Sources: PMF Physical Geography 04 p.24, 37; NextGen Indian Geography 07 p.3 (inversion and fog); NCERT India Physical Environment ch.4 (18°C isotherm); app notes 4:15 subs 5, 6, 8
## SUB 5 | Heat Waves and Temperature Extremes
[15:5:0] # IMD heat-wave criteria (asked 4 times)
[15:5:1] TABLE head: Region | Heat wave considered only when max reaches | Cold wave (min)
  [15:5:1.0] Plains | 40°C | 10°C or below
  [15:5:1.1] Coast | 37°C | —
  [15:5:1.2] Hills | 30°C (APPSC AMVI 2023 ×2) | 0°C or below
[15:5:2] - Departure from normal: heat wave **4.5–6.4°C**; **severe above 6.4°C**. Old IMD rule (for stations with normal max above 40°C): heat wave 4–5°C, **severe 6°C or more** – the APPSC ASO 2017 key.
[15:5:3] - Plains by actual maximum: **45°C = heat wave**, **47°C = severe**. Cold wave (plains, actual) 4°C or below; severe 2°C or below.
[15:5:4] - **NDMA** heat-wave guidelines first issued **2016** (revised 2017, 2019).
[15:5:5] # AP Heat Wave Action Plan
[15:5:6] - **AP Heat Wave Action Plan since 2016**; **APSDMA** district-wise alerts. Duties (APPSC ASO): **Rural Development – reschedule (MGNREGS) working hours; Animal Husbandry – posters and pamphlets; Labour – employers shift outdoor work or give shade and water; I&PR – wide circulation of alerts**.
[15:5:7] - Severe-heatwave districts (HAP 2026): Tirupati, Prakasam, SPSR Nellore, Markapuram, Guntur, Bapatla, **Palnadu**.
[15:5:8] - **2026 peak: 48.1°C at Piduguralla** (Palnadu), 21 May 2026.
[15:5:9] # Records
[15:5:10] TABLE head: Record | Place | Value
  [15:5:10.0] India's highest | Phalodi, Rajasthan (19 May 2016) | 51.0°C
  [15:5:10.1] World hottest | Death Valley | 56.7°C
  [15:5:10.2] World coldest | Vostok | −89.2°C
  [15:5:10.3] India coldest | Dras (Ladakh) | about −45°C (1908)
  [15:5:10.4] AP hottest | Rentachintala (Palnadu) | above 47°C
  [15:5:10.5] AP coldest | Lambasingi (ASR) – "Kashmir of AP" | ~2°C
[15:5:11] - **Urban heat island**: concrete and asphalt store heat. **Heat dome**: stalled high pressure under a slowed, winding jet stream.
[15:5:12] - **TRISHNA**: **ISRO–CNES** thermal-infrared satellite (land surface temperature).
[15:5:13] ~~ Sources: IMD heat-wave criteria (mausam.imd.gov.in); NDMA Heat Wave Guidelines 2016/2019; APSDMA Heat Wave Action Plan; IMD (Phalodi 51.0°C, 2016); app notes 4:15 sub 9

=== OWN MCQs of 4:15 (83)
[n03ae250431b] sub0
  Which one of the following correctly describes insolation?
  Vertical transfer of heat by rising air | Horizontal transfer of heat by moving air | Direct heating of the atmosphere by outgoing long-wave radiation | *Direct heating by incoming short-wave solar radiation

  What is the horizontal transfer of heat by wind called?
  Convection | *Advection | Conduction | Insolation
  x: Advection is the horizontal transfer of heat by wind; vertical transfer by rising warm air is convection.

  The Loo, a hot wind of northern India, is an example of which of the following processes?
  Radiation | *Advection | Conduction | Convection
  x: The Loo transfers heat horizontally through moving air and is therefore an example of advection.
[nd816845f1b0] sub0
  By which of the following is the atmosphere mainly heated?
  Direct absorption of incoming short-wave solar radiation | Heat from the Earth's interior | *Outgoing long-wave terrestrial radiation from below | Radiation reflected by clouds
  x: The atmosphere is largely transparent to incoming short-wave radiation but absorbs outgoing long-wave terrestrial radiation, so it is heated mainly from below.
[f4d3569b2f06f] sub0
  In what form is terrestrial radiation, the main heater of the atmosphere, emitted?
  Short-wave radiation | Ultraviolet radiation | Visible light | *Long-wave infra-red radiation
  x: The Earth re-emits heat as long-wave infra-red radiation, which heats the air from below.
[fea0d630a79af] sub0
  Which gases mainly absorb the long-wave radiation re-emitted by the Earth?
  *Carbon dioxide and water vapour | Nitrogen and oxygen | Argon and nitrogen | Oxygen and helium
  x: Carbon dioxide and water vapour absorb the Earth's long-wave infra-red radiation.
[f63ef00ebac0b] sub0
  Which of the following pairs of heating process and mechanism is correctly matched?
  Advection – Vertical transfer of heat | *Conduction – Heats the lower layers of air | Convection – Horizontal transfer of heat | Insolation – Long-wave heat from the Earth
  x: Conduction heats the lower air in contact with warm ground; advection is horizontal, convection vertical and insolation short-wave.
[n585a32d9a23] sub1
  Which of the following is NOT correct about insolation?
  The angle of the Sun's rays affects the insolation received at a place. | The length of the day affects the insolation received at a place. | *Atmospheric transparency has no effect on the insolation received. | The slope and aspect of the land affect the insolation received.
  x: Atmospheric transparency does influence insolation, along with the angle of the rays, duration of sunshine, and slope and aspect of land.
[n18587fd0a78] sub1
  Which one of the following correctly represents the Earth's aphelion?

  x: Aphelion occurs around 4 July, when the Earth is approximately 152 million kilometres from the Sun.
[ne80619ce523] sub1
  Why do the highest temperatures on Earth generally occur in the sub-tropical deserts rather than at the Equator?
  The maximum annual rainfall of the deserts | The permanent presence of cold ocean currents | Persistent cloud cover and humid air | *Clear skies and dry air
  x: Sub-tropical deserts around 20°–30° N have clear skies and dry air, permitting very high temperatures; the Equator does not record the highest temperatures merely because it receives strong insolation.
[n9635aca7212] sub1
  At the same latitude, insolation is generally higher over:
  Oceans than over continents | Polar seas than over tropical land | Oceans and continents equally | *Continents than over oceans
  x: Insolation declines towards the poles and, at the same latitude, is higher over continents than over oceans.
[n8ebc405c016] sub1
  In the Earth's heat budget, where is a heat surplus found?
  Antarctic region | Polar regions | Arctic Circle | *Tropics
  x: The tropics have a heat surplus and the poles a deficit; winds and ocean currents carry heat poleward.
[ngeneral-geography-7-33] sub1
  What type of the Sun's rays does the equator receive, causing it to be heated more than the poles?
  *direct | oblique | reflected | scattered
  x: Latitude sets the Sun's angle: the equator gets more direct rays and greater heating, while the poles get oblique rays and lower heating.

  x: The Earth is about 147 million km from the Sun at perihelion and about 152 million km at aphelion.
[f1d16358c4503] sub1
  How does insolation received at the Earth's surface generally change from the Equator towards the poles?
  increases | remains the same | *decreases | first decreases and then increases
  x: The Equator gets direct rays and the poles oblique rays, so insolation falls poleward.
[n40aec04c546] sub2
  According to recent assessments (Apr 2025), the Arctic is warming at about what rate compared with the global average?
  *3-4 times faster | About half as fast | At the same rate | 10 times faster
  x: The Arctic has warmed by at least 2 deg C and is warming 3-4 times faster than the global average (older estimates said about twice), driven by the ice-albedo feedback in which melting ice exposes dark ocean. It is not slower, equal or ten times faster.
[n27fe05dcf62] sub2

  *Sand | Grass | Forest | Water
  x: The descending albedo order is fresh snow, sand, grass, forest and water, so sand comes second.
[n319a424c6a3] sub2
  Which clouds tend to reflect incoming sunlight and produce cooling?
  High, thin clouds | Cirrostratus clouds | Cirrus clouds | *Low, thick clouds
  x: Low, thick clouds reflect more sunlight and cause cooling, whereas high, thin clouds tend to trap outgoing heat.
[n7113fb6c4a8] sub2
  What does the albedo of a surface refer to?
  *share of incoming radiation reflected by the surface | amount of heat stored below the surface | rate at which terrestrial radiation is emitted | amount of moisture absorbed by the surface
  x: Albedo is the proportion or share of incoming radiation that a surface reflects.
[nb8f3b9f39f8] sub2
  Why can melting of ice intensify warming?
  converts long-wave radiation into short-wave radiation | increases the albedo of the exposed ocean | *exposes a darker ocean surface that absorbs more heat | prevents the ocean from absorbing solar radiation
  x: Melting ice exposes dark ocean water, which has a lower albedo and absorbs more heat, producing a positive ice-albedo feedback.
[fb48293aed7c3] sub2
  What effect do high, thin clouds generally have?
  Reflect sunlight and cause cooling | *Trap heat and cause warming | Have no effect on temperature | Raise the Earth's albedo the most
  x: High, thin clouds trap heat (warming), while low, thick clouds reflect sunlight (cooling).
[f69a070d1b8c0] sub2
  What is the approximate albedo of fresh snow?
  20–40% | 15–25% | *75–95% | Below 10%
  x: Fresh snow reflects 75–95% of incoming radiation; dry sand 20–40%, crop land 15–25% and water below 10%.

[n617efcdebd2] sub4
  Why does temperature normally decrease with increasing altitude?

[f333eff8d84db] sub4

  x: Air is heated from below, not directly by the Sun; thinner air with less vapour and dust aloft makes temperature fall with height.

[na09cdb227ef] sub4

  x: The thermal equator is the line of highest mean temperature. It lies mostly north of the geographical Equator and shifts with the apparent movement of the Sun.

=== NOTES 4:16 | Atmospheric Pressure – Pressure Belts; Planetary, Periodic and Local Winds; Jet Streams
## SUB 0 | Local Winds of the World and India
[16:0:0] # Local winds – region and nature (asked 18 times)
[16:0:1] - Local winds: **short-lived, predictable, region-specific**; caused by local temperature and pressure differences and relief.
[16:0:2] TABLE head: Wind | Region | Nature
  [16:0:2.0] Foehn | Alps (Switzerland) | Warm, dry, downslope; melts snow
  [16:0:2.1] Chinook | East slopes of the Rockies (USA, Canada) | Warm, dry "snow eater"; blows in winter and early spring, raises winter temperature of the plains; benefits grazing – brings no rain
  [16:0:2.2] Zonda | Argentina (east slope of the Andes) | Foehn-type, warm, dry
  [16:0:2.3] Santa Ana | Southern California | Hot, dry; spreads wildfires
  [16:0:2.4] Samun (Simoom) | Kurdistan, Iran–Iraq | Hot, dry desert wind
  [16:0:2.5] Sirocco | Sahara → Mediterranean (Italy, Sicily) | Hot, dusty; red dust causes "blood rain" in Italy
  [16:0:2.6] Harmattan | West Africa – blows from the north-east and east to the west of the Sahara | Dry, dusty; "the doctor"
  [16:0:2.7] Khamsin | Egypt | Hot, dry, dusty
  [16:0:2.8] Haboob | Sudan | Dust storm
  [16:0:2.9] Shamal | Mesopotamia – Iraq, Persian Gulf | Hot, dry, dusty
  [16:0:2.10] Leveche | Spain | Hot, dry
  [16:0:2.11] Brickfielder | South-east Australia | Hot, dusty
  [16:0:2.12] Mistral | Rhone valley, France – not Australia | Cold, dry
  [16:0:2.13] Bora | Eastern shore of the Adriatic (Croatia, Slovenia, NE Italy) – not Siberia | Cold, dry, down from the mountains
  [16:0:2.14] Purga | Siberia (tundra) | Cold, snow-laden
  [16:0:2.15] Yamo | Japan | Warm, dry
  [16:0:2.16] Blizzard | Polar lands, Siberia, Canada, USA – not Chile | Snowstorm with strong winds
[16:0:3] - **Cold** local winds: **Mistral**, Bora, Purga, Blizzard; Santa Ana, Chinook, Loo are hot/warm (NDA 2020).

## SUB 1 | Pressure Belts – Doldrums, Horse Latitudes, ITCZ
[16:1:0] # The belts (asked 11 times)
[16:1:1] TABLE head: Belt | Latitude | Other name / nature
  [16:1:1.0] Equatorial low | 0–5° N and S, on both sides of the Equator | Doldrums – calm, rising air; NE and SE trades converge (ITCZ)
  [16:1:1.1] Subtropical high | 30–35° N and S | Horse latitudes – calm, sinking dry air, hot deserts; dynamically induced
  [16:1:1.2] Subpolar low | 60–65° | Westerlies meet polar easterlies; storms; dynamically induced
  [16:1:1.3] Polar high | Poles (90°) | Cold, dense, sinking air; thermally induced
[16:1:2] - **ITCZ** = low-pressure zone **at / near the Equator** where the **north-east and south-east trades converge** (APPSC Asst. Chemist; MPPCS 2018; CDS 2007) – not at the Tropics or poles.
[16:1:3] - **Doldrums** = the **equatorial low-pressure belt** (NDA 2007) with calm winds – **not** strong winds (APPSC Group-1: "doldrums are strong winds" and "NH trades blow from NW" are both wrong → **neither**).
[16:1:4] - **Horse latitudes** ~**30° (30–35°)** – sub-tropical high, **dynamically induced** by sinking air of the Hadley cell, calm (NDA 2012); sailors threw horses overboard when becalmed.
[16:1:5] - **Hadley cell**: air rises at the ITCZ and **descends at the subtropical high-pressure cells** (~30°) (CDS 2020).
[16:1:6] - Subpolar low at 60–65° instead of a high (IAS 2002): converging westerlies and polar easterlies; the lows are semi-permanent **over oceans** (Aleutian, Icelandic) – both true, but R does not explain A.
[16:1:7] - Belts **shift 5–10°** with the overhead Sun – **north in the NH summer**, south in winter.
[16:1:8] ~~ Sources: PMF Physical Geography 05 p.5-7; NCERT Fundamentals of Physical Geography ch.10; app notes 4:16 subs 2-3
## SUB 2 | Atmospheric Pressure – Causes, Gradient and Instruments
[16:2:0] # Pressure and weather (asked 10 times)
[16:2:1] - Atmospheric pressure = **weight of the air column**, held by **gravitational pull** (APPSC Panchayat Secretary).
[16:2:2] - Heated air **expands → density falls → low pressure**; cooled air contracts → high pressure.
[16:2:3] - Pressure **falls with altitude** → at high altitudes some people get **nose bleeding** (low pressure) (APPSC AE).
[16:2:4] - **Standard sea-level pressure 1013.25 mb (hPa)**; **isobars** join places of equal pressure.
[16:2:5] - **Pressure gradient** decides **wind velocity** (APPSC Group-II 2011): closely spaced isobars = steep gradient = strong wind. Air moves high → low.
[16:2:6] - **Sudden fall of the barometer** (mercury) = **stormy weather** (UKPSC 2002; IAS 2001); rising = fair weather.
[16:2:7] - A **low-pressure area** with converging winds = **cyclone**; high = anticyclone.
[16:2:8] # Instruments
[16:2:9] TABLE head: Instrument | Measures
  [16:2:9.0] Barometer (mercury / aneroid), barograph | Atmospheric pressure (APPSC; NDA 2018)
  [16:2:9.1] Aneroid barometer | No liquid – an evacuated metal box
  [16:2:9.2] Anemometer | Wind speed
  [16:2:9.3] Wind vane | Wind direction
[16:2:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket General Geography #7 p.51 (pressure); PMF Physical Geography 05 p.1-3; app notes 4:16 sub 0
## SUB 3 | Jet Streams and the Polar Vortex
[16:3:0] # Jet streams (asked 8 times)
[16:3:1] - Narrow bands of **high-velocity westerly winds** in the **upper troposphere near the tropopause** (8–15 km; generally **10–12 km**) (NDA 2011; CDS 2017).
[16:3:2] - Found in **both hemispheres** – not the NH only (UPSC 2020); NH jets stronger.
[16:3:3] - **Sub-tropical jet** forms at about **10–16 km** (option "10–20 km", APPSC AD 2017); polar front jet lower (6–9 km).
[16:3:4] - **Polar front jet is strongest in winter**, not summer (CDS 2017) – greatest temperature contrast.
[16:3:5] - Associated with the **monsoon** (APSLPRB SI 2023, 2018): they regulate onset and withdrawal.
[16:3:6] TABLE head: Jet | Position / season | Role
  [16:3:6.0] Sub-Tropical Westerly Jet | South of the Himalayas in winter, north in summer | Brings western disturbances; leaves before the monsoon "burst"; returns ~October
  [16:3:6.1] Tropical Easterly Jet | Summer, 5–20°N (South China Sea → East Africa) | Strengthens the SW monsoon
  [16:3:6.2] Somali (Findlater) Jet | Low-level, off East Africa | Boosts monsoon flow
[16:3:7] - NCERT: in winter the westerly jet blows across Asia **north of the Himalayas, parallel to the Tibetan highlands**; **Tibet splits it into two branches**; the **southern branch** (south of the Himalayas) controls India's winter weather – not the northern branch → "1 and 2" (State PSC).
[16:3:8] - First identified by **Wasaburo Ooishi** (Japan, 1920s); widely known in **World War II**.
[16:3:9] # Polar vortex
[16:3:10] - Cold **low** around the poles, **anticlockwise** (NH), strongest in **winter**. A **strong vortex keeps cold air up north** (APPSC 2018); when weakened (Rossby waves, sudden stratospheric warming) cold spells reach mid-latitudes.
[16:3:11] ~~ Sources: PMF Physical Geography 06 p.24-25; NextGen Indian Geography 06 p.10, 13 (jets and monsoon); NCERT India Physical Environment ch.4; app notes 4:16 sub 6
## SUB 4 | Planetary Winds and Wind Controls
[16:4:0] # Planetary winds (asked 7 times)
[16:4:1] TABLE head: Wind | From → to | NH | SH
  [16:4:1.0] Trade winds (easterlies) | Horse latitudes (subtropical high) → equatorial low | North-east (blow towards the south-west) | South-east
  [16:4:1.1] Westerlies | Subtropical high → subpolar low (~35–60°) | South-west | North-west
  [16:4:1.2] Polar easterlies | Polar high → subpolar low | North-east | South-east
[16:4:2] - **Trade winds = planetary winds**; monsoon is periodic; Chinook and Mistral are local (IAS 2009).
[16:4:3] - Order from Equator to pole: **doldrums → trade winds → westerlies → polar winds** (NDA 2014).
[16:4:4] - Westerlies blow between about 35° and 60° in **each** hemisphere – not "30°N to 60°S"; the **western disturbances** that give NW India winter rain come with the westerlies (UPSC 2015 → only II).
[16:4:5] - **NW European ports** stay ice-free all year because of the warm **North Atlantic Drift**; the south-westerlies do blow there all year, but are not the reason (UPPCS 2002: both true, R not the explanation).
[16:4:6] - Trades push tropical cyclones **west onto east coasts**; westerlies turn them north-east.
[16:4:7] # Wind controls (asked 4 times)
[16:4:8] - Surface horizontal wind = **pressure gradient + friction + Coriolis force** (CDS 2015).
[16:4:9] - **Coriolis force**: deflects **right in NH, left in SH** (**Ferrel's law**); **zero at the Equator, maximum at the poles**; grows with wind speed; depends on latitude, **not on hemisphere**.
[16:4:10] - **Geostrophic wind**: upper air, parallel to isobars, when **pressure gradient force = Coriolis force** (UKPSC 2024).
[16:4:11] - **SW monsoon** direction: SE trades crossing the Equator are deflected to the **right by the Coriolis force** (NDA 2011).
[16:4:12] - **Friction** slows surface winds, strongest over land, negligible aloft. No cyclones within ~5° of the Equator (Coriolis negligible).
[16:4:13] - **Walker circulation** = east–west Pacific cell; Hadley cell = meridional.
[16:4:14] ~~ Sources: PMF Physical Geography 05 p.11-14; NextGen Indian Geography 03 p.9 (Coriolis); NCERT Fundamentals of Physical Geography ch.10; app notes 4:16 subs 1, 4
## SUB 5 | Roaring Forties, Furious Fifties, Shrieking Sixties
[16:5:0] # The southern westerlies (asked 7 times)
[16:5:1] TABLE head: Name | Latitude
  [16:5:1.0] Roaring Forties | 40–50° S (strong ocean westerlies, "40–60° S" option)
  [16:5:1.1] Furious Fifties | 50–60° S
  [16:5:1.2] Shrieking Sixties | Around 60° S
[16:5:2] - They are the **westerlies of the Southern Hemisphere** (MPPCS 2015; State PSC) – stronger and steadier because the SH has **less landmass** (open ocean, little friction) (IAS 2011 → only I; Coriolis is not higher in the SH).
[16:5:3] - UPSC 2000: they blow with **great strength and constancy**, generally **from north-west to east (west to east)** in the SH, with **overcast skies, rain and raw weather** → **2, 3 and 4**; they do **not** blow uninterrupted in the NH (land breaks them).
[16:5:4] - NDA 2018: strong westerlies of the SH oceans (true); they blow **west to east**, not east to west, and there is **no** abundance of landmasses → **only I**.
[16:5:5] - Region: the southern oceans, incl. the **Indian Ocean** (of the options given).
[16:5:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Physical Geography 05 p.13; G.C. Leong ch.12; app notes 4:16 sub 5
## SUB 6 | Monsoon and Periodic Winds
[16:6:0] # Monsoon (asked 6 times)
[16:6:1] - Word from Arabic **"mausim" = season** (MPPCS 2013; APPSC ASO 2017).
[16:6:2] - **Seasonal reversal of winds** due to **differential heating of land and sea** (State PSC).
[16:6:3] - Summer: **high temperature and low pressure** over the subcontinent draw air from the Indian Ocean → **south-west monsoon** (UPSC 1996), flowing **from south-west to north-east** (MPPCS 2012).
[16:6:4] - Modern theory (**1957**): ITCZ shift + jet streams + Tibet Plateau + ENSO. Halley (1686): giant land–sea breeze.
[16:6:5] - Mediterranean (UPPCS 1992 key "monsoonal"): in winter air from the surrounding high-pressure lands flows towards the warmer sea, reversing in summer; its winter rain itself comes with the westerlies.
[16:6:6] - **ITCZ** moves north over the Indian plains in summer (monsoon trough) – this **helps** the monsoon; in winter it moves south and highs over **Tibet and Siberia** set up the **north-east monsoon**.
[16:6:7] - The **Himalayas** act as a **climatic divide**, giving India its distinct monsoon climate.
[16:6:8] - **El Niño** weakens the monsoon; **positive IOD** can offset it.
[16:6:9] - AP: SW monsoon 2026 entered via **Rayalaseema** (6 June 2026); IMD expected **below-normal** AP rain under El Niño. AP coastline **~1,053 km – third longest** (AP Socio-Economic Survey 2025-26).
[16:6:10] # Breezes
[16:6:11] TABLE head: Breeze | Time | Direction
  [16:6:11.0] Sea breeze | Day | Sea → land (land heats faster, lower pressure)
  [16:6:11.1] Land breeze | Night | Land → sea
  [16:6:11.2] Valley (anabatic) | Day | Uphill
  [16:6:11.3] Mountain (katabatic) | Night | Downhill; cold air in valleys → inversion, frost
[16:6:12] - Land and sea breezes are **daily**; they moderate **AP coastal** temperatures.
[16:6:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 06 p.13 (monsoon theories); NCERT India Physical Environment ch.4; app notes 4:16 sub 7
[16:6:14] - **Western disturbances** = winter rain-bearing lows from the Mediterranean carried east by the westerly jet (not a warm Indian Ocean); **Southern Oscillation** = sea-level pressure see-saw between the eastern Pacific and the Indian Ocean.

  1 and 2 only | 2 and 3 only | *1 and 3 only | 1, 2 and 3
  x: The Coriolis force deflects winds right in the NH and is maximum at the poles, but it grows with wind speed.
[f82c2b301b5bb] sub4

  *Land | Oceans | The upper air | Jet stream levels
  x: Friction is stronger over land and negligible aloft.

=== NOTES 4:17 | Humidity, Evaporation, Condensation, Clouds and Forms of Precipitation
## SUB 0 | Clouds – Families, Types and Thunderclouds
[17:0:0] # Cloud basics (asked 15 times)
[17:0:1] - **Cloud** = mass of minute water droplets or ice crystals formed by **condensation** of water vapour in free air around **hygroscopic nuclei**, mainly by **adiabatic cooling** of rising air below its dew point – clouds are the result of **condensation** (UKPSC 2016), not evaporation.
[17:0:2] - Clouds **float** because of their **low density** (UPSC 1995): the droplets are tiny, fall extremely slowly and are held up by gentle updrafts.
[17:0:3] - Four basic forms: **cirrus, cumulus, stratus, nimbus** ("nimbus" = rain-bearing; black or dark grey, dense, opaque).
[17:0:4] TABLE head: Family (height) | Cloud | Appearance | Weather
  [17:0:4.0] High (8,000–12,000 m; ice crystals) | Cirrus | Thin, detached, feathery, silky, always white | Fair; no rain
  [17:0:4.1] High | Cirrostratus | Thin milky sheet; produces the halo | Warm front coming
  [17:0:4.2] High | Cirrocumulus | Small globular masses, ripples ("mackerel sky") | Fair
  [17:0:4.3] Middle (2–6 km) | Altostratus / altocumulus | Grey-blue sheet; Sun as through ground glass | Light continuous rain
  [17:0:4.4] Low (below 2 km) | Stratus, stratocumulus, nimbostratus | Layered; nimbostratus dark, thick, shapeless | Stratus – drizzle; nimbostratus – steady, continuous rain
  [17:0:4.5] Vertical development | Cumulus | Heaped cauliflower, flat base, cotton wool (4,000–7,000 m) | Fair; convective; grows into Cb
  [17:0:4.6] Vertical development (to ~15 km) | Cumulonimbus | Towering, anvil top | Thunderstorm, heavy short rain, hail, cloudburst
[17:0:5] - APPSC Group-I 2024 match: **Cirrus – silky; Cirrostratus – milky; Cirrocumulus – small globular masses; Cumulus – cauliflower** (A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III).
[17:0:6] - **Cirrus clouds are composed of ice crystals** (UPSC 2004 correct statement); rising domes with flat base = cumulus, and cumulus is **not** a high cloud.
[17:0:7] - **Low cloud set: stratus, nimbus (nimbostratus), cumulus** (IAS 2004); **nimbostratus is a low cloud** (NDA 2007), cirro- = high, alto- = middle.
[17:0:8] - **Continuous precipitation = nimbostratus** (NDA 2018); **highly intense rain = cumulonimbus** (JPSC 2003).
[17:0:9] - Highest of a given set: **cirrostratus** is the only high cloud among altocumulus, altostratus, cumulus, cirrostratus (UP Lower 2009).
[17:0:10] - **Greatest vertical extent**, convectional rain with lightning and thunder = **cumulonimbus** (IAS 2003); rain-bearing clouds = **nimbostratus and cumulonimbus**.
[17:0:11] - **Tornadoes form from cumulonimbus** (supercell) clouds (APPSC FRO 2020); the funnel cloud and wall cloud are parts hanging from the Cb, not the parent cloud.
[17:0:12] - Rain clouds look **dark/black** because they are thick and dense with droplets, so very little sunlight gets through to the base (CDS 2012 – book key: the droplets **absorb** the sunlight; strictly the light is mostly scattered/reflected away).
[17:0:13] # Thunderclouds and thunder
[17:0:14] - Thundercloud (Cb) development needs **condensation, high temperature and humidity, orography and vertical winds – all four** (UPSC 2002; orographic thunderstorms are common).
[17:0:15] - **Thunder** is the sound of air **suddenly heated and expanded by lightning** (shock wave) – not clouds meeting, lightning "separating" clouds or upward air movement → **none of these** (IAS 2013).
[17:0:16] - **Waterspout**: funnel extending from a cumulus/cumulonimbus cloud **over water**; one recorded over the Brahmaputra in Barpeta, Assam (26 Aug 2026).
[17:0:17] ~~ Sources: PMF Physical Geography 05 p.27-29, 34, 36-43 (clouds, thunderstorm, lightning); NextGen Rocket General Geography #9 p.61 (cloud – disturbance link); NCERT Fundamentals of Physical Geography ch.11; app notes 4:17 sub 4
## SUB 1 | Evaporation, Latent Heat, Boiling Point and Adiabatic Change
[17:1:0] # Evaporation (asked 15 times)
[17:1:1] - **Evaporation / vaporisation** = change from liquid to gas (SSC 2019); it is a **physical change** (UPPSC 1992) and goes on at all temperatures from the surface.
[17:1:2] - Rate **rises with larger surface area** (CDS 2019), higher temperature, **lower humidity**, **stronger wind** and lower pressure; falls with salinity.
[17:1:3] - Oceans give **84%** of annual evaporation, continents 16%.
[17:1:4] # Latent heat
[17:1:5] - **Evaporation absorbs** latent heat; **condensation releases** it → powers **thunderstorms and cyclones**. Freezing (snow forming in clouds) also releases heat = **exothermic**; melting ice absorbs heat = **endothermic**.
[17:1:6] TABLE head: Change | Latent heat | Note
  [17:1:6.0] Fusion of ice | 80 cal/g (3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg) | Melts at 0°C; temperature constant
  [17:1:6.1] Vaporisation of water | 540 cal/g (2.26 × 10⁶ J/kg) | Boils at 100°C; temperature constant
[17:1:7] - Heat taken to turn liquid into gas **without change in temperature = latent heat of vaporisation** (NDA 2017); at the boiling point the **temperature remains constant** (SSC 2016).
[17:1:8] - Latent heat of vaporisation is **much greater** than that of fusion; **steam at 100°C holds more heat** than water at 100°C → **steam burns are worse** (SSC 2015) – it releases latent heat on condensing.
[17:1:9] - UPSC 2003: only "an air-conditioner extracts heat at the **evaporator** coils and rejects it at the **condenser** coils" is correct. **Refrigerator**: refrigerant absorbs heat on evaporation, releases it on condensation.
[17:1:10] # Pressure and boiling point
[17:1:11] - **Lower pressure lowers the boiling point** (Asst. Comm. 2018): at high altitude water boils below 100°C because **air pressure is less** (NDA 2017) → a **pressure cooker** raises pressure and boiling point (CDS 2010).
[17:1:12] # Adiabatic change and the uplift chain
[17:1:13] - **Adiabatic** temperature change = by **expansion (cooling) and compression (warming)** of air, without heat being added or removed (CDS 2018); compressing gas in a bicycle pump = **adiabatic heating**.
[17:1:14] - Air **descending** a mountain is compressed → **adiabatic warming** (AE 2017), as in the leeward rain shadow.
[17:1:15] - Uplift chain: warm air rises → **adiabatic cooling to the dew point** → **condensation** around nuclei → clouds → droplets grow and fall → precipitation. Rising air does **not** become warmer.
[17:1:16] ~~ Sources: PMF Physical Geography 05 p.22-24 (evaporation, condensation, adiabatic change); NextGen Rocket General Geography #7 p.52; NCERT Science (latent heat, boiling point); app notes 4:17 sub 1
## SUB 2 | Instruments and Isolines
[17:2:0] # Instruments (asked 14 times)
[17:2:1] TABLE head: Instrument / line | Measures / joins
  [17:2:1.0] Hygrometer | Humidity / moisture of air (APPSC Group-II 2008; APPSC Group-1; IAS 2017)
  [17:2:1.1] Sling psychrometer / wet and dry bulb thermometer | Humidity from the wet-bulb and dry-bulb difference (APPSC DL 2020; NDA 2009)
  [17:2:1.2] Lysimeter | Evapotranspiration / percolation
  [17:2:1.3] Rain gauge | Rainfall depth
  [17:2:1.4] Hydrometer | Density of a liquid (distractor)
  [17:2:1.5] Isohyet | Equal rainfall (MPPSC 2015)
  [17:2:1.6] Isoneph | Equal cloudiness (APPSC AD flashcard; OPSC 2018)
  [17:2:1.7] Isobar / isotherm | Equal pressure / temperature
  [17:2:1.8] Isogonic line | Equal magnetic declination (UP Lower 1998)
[17:2:2] - **Relative humidity is measured by a hygrometer** (three APPSC recruitment papers) – not anemometer, tachometer, manometer, hydrometer or lactometer.
[17:2:3] - A daily weather map with isobars = **isopleth map** (UPSC 1997) – lines joining equal values.
[17:2:4] - **Wet-bulb temperature** equals dry-bulb only at **100% RH**; above about **31.5°C** wet-bulb the body cannot cool by sweating.
[17:2:5] - Rain-gauge sequence: **Mauryan Arthashastra** → **Korea's Cheugugi (1441)** → **Castelli (1639)**.
[17:2:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Physical Geography 05 p.19 (hygrometer); NCERT Fundamentals of Physical Geography ch.11; app notes 4:17 sub 10
## SUB 3 | Precipitation – Forms and Types of Rainfall
[17:3:0] # Forms (asked 10 times)
[17:3:1] TABLE head: Form | Feature
  [17:3:1.0] Rain | Drops over 0.5 mm
  [17:3:1.1] Drizzle | Fine drops under 0.5 mm (APPSC FSO flashcard), mostly from stratus
  [17:3:1.2] Snow | Ice crystals formed below 0°C
  [17:3:1.3] Sleet | Rain frozen into pellets falling through cold air
  [17:3:1.4] Hail | Layered ice balls (5–50 mm) in cumulonimbus with strong updrafts
[17:3:2] - Raindrops grow by two processes: **collision–coalescence** in **warm clouds that do not extend beyond the freezing level** (CDS 2018) and the **ice-crystal (Bergeron)** process in clouds rising above it.
[17:3:3] - **Langmuir precipitation** = Langmuir's **chain reaction** of drop collision, break-up and coalescence in warm convective clouds, giving heavy showers – APPSC FSO key: **cloud burst**.
[17:3:4] - **Cloudburst**: about **100 mm/hour** or more over **20–30 sq km** from cumulonimbus; the stored water falls when **updrafts weaken**; Dharali, **Uttarkashi** (Aug 2025).
[17:3:5] - **Blood (coloured) rain**: dust or spores mixed with raindrops – Kerala's red rain (**2001**). 16th Finance Commission recommended adding **heatwaves and lightning** to notified disasters (Apr 2026).
[17:3:6] # Types of rainfall
[17:3:7] TABLE head: Type | Mechanism | Where
  [17:3:7.0] Convectional | Strong heating → air rises, cools → cumulonimbus; afternoon, short, heavy | Equatorial belt (Amazon, Congo, SE Asian islands); mango showers
  [17:3:7.1] Cyclonic / frontal | Warm air lifted over cold air along fronts – cyclonic activity (SSC 2011) | Temperate regions; western disturbances (10–15 cm winter rain, NW India)
  [17:3:7.2] Orographic (relief) | Moist wind forced up a mountain barrier | Western Ghats (Agumbe), Mawsynram; leeward = rain shadow
[17:3:8] - **Amazon basin** has convectional rainfall (IAS 2007); convectional rain occurs **daily in the afternoon** near the equator, is **short** and comes from **cumulonimbus** – all three true (NDA 2008).
[17:3:9] - Equatorial areas get rain **all year** because high temperature and humidity cause **afternoon convectional rain** – A and R true, R explains A (IAS 2003; UPSC 1996).
[17:3:10] - **Rain-shadow effect** and **inversion of rainfall** (rain increases with height only up to a level, then decreases) are features of **orographic rainfall** (NDA 2011; NDA 2019).
[17:3:11] - Rain-shadow area = dry **leeward** side; descending air warms and dries (Pune ~70 cm vs Mahabaleshwar 600 cm). **Eastern side of the Western Ghats** is leeward → peninsular rainfall **falls west to east**; **Aravallis** give little rain to Rajasthan as winds blow **parallel** to them.
[17:3:12] - AP: average rainfall ~**966 mm**, about **two-thirds from the SW monsoon**; **Rayalaseema** in rain shadow, **Hagari valley lowest**, **Sileru–Sabari valleys highest**; Sri Sathya Sai district 57% deficit (Aug 2026).
[17:3:13] ~~ Sources: PMF Physical Geography 05 p.31-35; NextGen Rocket General Geography #7 p.52; Langmuir (1948) chain-reaction theory (atmos.albany.edu precipitation processes notes); app notes 4:17 sub 5-7
## SUB 4 | Cloud Seeding and Acid Rain
[17:4:0] # Cloud seeding (asked 10 times)
[17:4:1] - Artificial rain uses **silver iodide (AgI)** – its crystal shape mimics ice (UPPCS 2008, 2013, Spl. 2008; APPSC flashcard); also **potassium iodide**, **sodium chloride**, **dry ice** (solid CO₂), liquid propane; not calcium carbonate.
[17:4:2] - Artificial rain to reduce air pollution: **silver iodide and potassium iodide** (UPSC 2025).
[17:4:3] - **AP cloud seeding (July 2004)**: **silver iodide–sodium chloride**.
[17:4:4] - Works **only when suitable clouds already exist**. Kazakhstan began seeding with UAE help (Aug 2026).
[17:4:5] # Acid rain
[17:4:6] - **Acid rain**: **pH below 5.6**, mainly from **SO₂ and NOx**; term coined by **Robert Angus Smith (1872)** in Manchester.
[17:4:7] - Coal thermal stations cause acid rain, but through **SO₂ and NOx**, not oxides of carbon → A and R true, R not the explanation (UPSC 2003).
[17:4:8] - UPPCS 2024: CO₂, SO₂ and NO₂ dissolve in rain to give acid rain, and air is polluted by these gases → **both true, R explains A**.
[17:4:9] - **Rain cleans a polluted environment** – it washes dust and gases out of the air (UP UDA/LDA 2013).
[17:4:10] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment (acid rain); UPSC 2025 key; app notes 4:17 sub 9
## SUB 5 | Hydrological Cycle and Transpiration
[17:5:0] # Water cycle (asked 9 times)
[17:5:1] - Continuous exchange of water by **evaporation, transpiration, condensation and precipitation**; correct sequence **evaporation → condensation → precipitation → infiltration** (NDA 2010).
[17:5:2] TABLE head: In the cycle | NOT in the cycle
  [17:5:2.0] Evaporation, transpiration (= evapotranspiration) | Photosynthesis
  [17:5:2.1] Sublimation, condensation, precipitation | Combustion
  [17:5:2.2] Infiltration/percolation, runoff, groundwater flow | Respiration, hydration
[17:5:3] - **Hydration** = water absorbed into minerals (a weathering process) – **not** part of the hydrological cycle (APPSC Group-1).
[17:5:4] - **Underground water may be connected to surface water** (CDS 2015); transpiration does contribute to clouds and rainfall recharges groundwater.
[17:5:5] - **Forests** control the hydrological cycle (UPRO 2023) – "water engineers": interception, transpiration, deep roots, groundwater recharge.
[17:5:6] # Transpiration
[17:5:7] - Plants lose water by **transpiration** (APPSC Group-1), mainly through **stomata**; it pulls water up, **cools the plant** = "**nature's air conditioner**", adds moisture to air and enhances rainfall – it does **not decrease humidity**.
[17:5:8] - Rate is **reduced by decreased light intensity** (stomata close), high humidity, low temperature and still air.
[17:5:9] - **Hydrometeorology** = transfer of water and energy between land surface and lower atmosphere. India: precipitation ~**4,000 BCM**/year; utilisable **1,139 BCM** (**690 surface + 449 groundwater**).
[17:5:10] ~~ Sources: PMF Physical Geography 05 p.19; NCERT Science Class 10 (transpiration); app notes 4:17 sub 2
## SUB 6 | Humidity and Dew Point
[17:6:0] # Measures of humidity (asked 7 times)
[17:6:1] - **Humidity** = water vapour present in the air – the result of the **presence of moisture in the air** (JPSC 2016); humid summer heat = **muggy** weather (UPUDA 2002).
[17:6:2] TABLE head: Measure | Meaning | Unit
  [17:6:2.0] Absolute humidity | Mass of water vapour per unit volume of air | g/m³
  [17:6:2.1] Specific humidity | Vapour per unit weight of air; unchanged by volume/temperature change | g/kg
  [17:6:2.2] Relative humidity (RH) | Actual vapour ÷ capacity at that temperature × 100 | %
  [17:6:2.3] Dew point | Temperature at which air becomes saturated; condensation begins below it | °C
[17:6:3] - When air temperature **equals the dew point, RH = 100%** (APPSC FSO flashcard) = saturation.
[17:6:4] - **Saturation deficit** = capacity minus actual vapour; **dew point** = temperature to which air must be cooled to saturate → both correct (NDA 2009).
[17:6:5] - Warmer air can hold **more** vapour – capacity **increases** with temperature (JPSC 2003); same vapour + warming → **RH falls**.
[17:6:6] - Water vapour: 0–4% of the air (up to **4%** in humid tropics), **decreases with height and latitude**; RH higher over oceans than continents.
[17:6:7] - AP: coastal Andhra RH **70–90%**; Rayalaseema below **30%** in peak summer.
[17:6:8] ~~ Sources: PMF Physical Geography 05 p.19-22; NextGen Rocket General Geography #7 p.52; app notes 4:17 sub 0
## SUB 7 | Optical Phenomena – Rainbow and Halo
[17:7:0] # Rainbow and halo (asked 7 times)
[17:7:1] TABLE head: Phenomenon | Cause
  [17:7:1.0] Rainbow | Refraction, dispersion and (total) internal reflection of sunlight in raindrops; Sun behind the observer
  [17:7:1.1] Halo | Refraction through hexagonal ice crystals of thin high cirrus/cirrostratus; ring of about 22°
  [17:7:1.2] Corona | Diffraction by small water droplets of thin clouds
[17:7:2] - Rainbow is formed by **reflection, refraction and dispersion** (APPSC ASO 2017; APPSC Group-1); if only one is offered, **dispersion** (APPSC ABCWO; NDA 2017).
[17:7:3] - **Primary rainbow**: one internal reflection, **red outside, violet inside** → terminal bands **violet and red** (UP Lower 2015). Secondary: two reflections, colours reversed.
[17:7:4] - APPSC Group-I 2024: Sun halo = refraction in hexagonal ice crystals (I) and a **22° ring** (II) correct; III wrong – the halo comes from thin **cirrostratus**, not cumulonimbus.
[17:7:5] - Sun's halo = refraction in **ice crystals in cirrus clouds** (IAS 2002).
[17:7:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Physical Geography 05 p.29-30; NCERT Science Class 10 ch.11; app notes 4:17 sub 8
## SUB 8 | Forms of Condensation – Dew, Frost, Fog and Mist
[17:8:0] # Dew, frost, fog, mist (asked 5 times)
[17:8:1] TABLE head: Form | Condition
  [17:8:1.0] Dew | Droplets on cool surfaces; dew point above 0°C
  [17:8:1.1] Frost | Dew point at or below 0°C; ice crystals (Lambasingi, AP)
  [17:8:1.2] Fog | Cloud at ground level; visibility under 1 km
  [17:8:1.3] Mist | More moisture per nucleus; visibility 1–2 km; a result of condensation (CDS 2008)
  [17:8:1.4] Smog | Fog + smoke; London smog sulphurous, Los Angeles photochemical (PAN)
[17:8:2] - Outside of a glass of cold water gets wet by **condensation of atmospheric water vapour** (APPSC ASWO screening).
[17:8:3] - Dew/frost need **clear sky, calm air, high RH, long cold nights**; no dew on windy nights.
[17:8:4] - **No dew on a cloudy night: clouds reflect back the Earth's radiation**, keeping the surface warm (UPSC 2019 ×3).
[17:8:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Physical Geography 05 p.24-27; app notes 4:17 sub 3

[n8fedae2d2f0] sub6
  Which one of the following regional humidity statements is correct?
  Rayalaseema records 70–90 per cent relative humidity in peak summer | Coastal Andhra generally records below 30 per cent relative humidity throughout the year | *Coastal Andhra generally records relative humidity of 70–90 per cent, whereas Rayalaseema may fall below 30 per cent in peak summer | Both coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema normally record identical relative humidity throughout the year
  x: Coastal Andhra has high relative humidity of about 70–90 per cent, contributing to a high heat index. Rayalaseema often records below 30 per cent in summer.
[f3286b5e66123] sub6
  Absolute humidity is the weight of water vapour per unit of what?
  Weight of air | *Volume of air | Area of land | Degree of temperature
  x: Absolute humidity is vapour per unit volume (g/m³); specific humidity is per unit weight (g/kg).
[fdfd8c1e620d0] sub6
  In the humid tropics, up to about what share of the air can water vapour make up?
  1% | 10% | *4% | 21%
  x: Water vapour reaches up to 4% in the humid tropics and is under 1% in deserts and polar areas.
[f765926227c4e] sub6
  Consider the following statements about humidity:
1. Relative humidity is higher over oceans than over continents.
2. Water vapour in the air increases with latitude.
3. Warm air can hold more water vapour than cold air.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
  1 and 2 only | 2 and 3 only | *1 and 3 only | 1, 2 and 3
  x: RH is higher over oceans and warm air holds more vapour; water vapour falls, not rises, with latitude.
[n2603d1e2a50] sub7
  How is a corona around the Sun or Moon mainly formed?
  dispersion in raindrops when the Sun is behind the observer | internal reflection in falling hailstones | *diffraction by small water droplets in thin clouds | refraction through large hexagonal ice crystals
  x: A corona consists of coloured rings close to the Sun or Moon and is produced by diffraction by small water droplets in thin clouds.
[nphysics-18-84] sub7
  In a primary rainbow, which colour appears on the outer side?
  Violet | Blue | Green | *Red
  x: Each wavelength refracts differently, so a primary rainbow has red on the outside and violet on the inside.
[nd40354897f1] sub7
  How is the sun halo generally observed?
  a semicircular arc produced by reflection from raindrops | *a ring of about 22° formed by refraction through ice crystals in high cirrostratus clouds | a coloured ring produced by diffraction near the Sun or Moon | a white ring caused by dust particles in the lower atmosphere
  x: A sun halo is typically a ring of about 22° produced when sunlight is refracted through millions of hexagonal ice crystals in thin, high cirrostratus clouds.
[nphysics-18-82] sub7
  When is a rainbow seen?
  The Sun is in front of the observer and water drops are behind | *The Sun is behind the observer and water drops are in front | The Sun is directly overhead at noon | The Sun and water drops are both behind the observer
  x: The viewing condition for a rainbow is the Sun behind the observer and water drops in front; the rainbow itself comes from refraction, dispersion and internal reflection in the drops.
[nphysics-18-83] sub7
  How many total internal reflections occur in each raindrop to form a secondary rainbow?
  One | *Two | Three | Four
  x: A secondary rainbow uses two reflections in each drop (a primary uses one), so its colours are reversed and it is fainter.
[f946af32706f7] sub7
  Consider the following statements about a sun halo:
1. It is caused by refraction of light through ice crystals.
2. It is seen through thin, high cirrostratus or cirrus clouds.
3. It is caused by diffraction of light by water droplets.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
  *1 and 2 only | 2 and 3 only | 1 and 3 only | 1, 2 and 3
  x: A halo is refraction through ice crystals in thin high clouds; diffraction by water droplets produces a corona.
[n2c136fce851] sub8
  Frost differs from dew because frost
  is a cloud at ground level with visibility below 1 km | forms only when the dew point is above 0°C | *forms as ice crystals when the dew point is at or below 0°C | consists of rain drops larger than 0.5 mm
  x: Frost forms as ice crystals when the dew point is at or below 0°C. Dew is liquid moisture condensed on cool surfaces with a dew point above 0°C.
[nd7dcdcd8fe7] sub8
  What is a cloud at ground level, with visibility under 1 km, formed when air cools below its dew point?
  Mist | Dew | *Fog | Frost
  x: Fog is a ground-level cloud with visibility under 1 km; mist is thinner and wetter, with visibility over 1 km.
[n9a348772e8c] sub8
  Los Angeles smog, which requires sunlight and can produce PAN, is of which nature?
  sulphurous | volcanic | *photochemical | radioactive
  x: Los Angeles smog is photochemical, needing sunlight and able to form PAN; London smog is sulphurous, cool and humid.
[nc517a32dd60] sub8
  Dew and frost are favoured by which combination of conditions?
  *Clear skies, calm air, high relative humidity and long cold nights | Continuous rainfall, turbulent winds and high atmospheric pressure | High daytime temperature, strong convection and dry air | Cloudy skies, strong winds, low humidity and short nights
  x: Clear and calm nights allow surfaces to cool efficiently, while high humidity and long cold nights favour dew or frost formation. Clouds and wind tend to prevent them.
[f979bee5e272d] sub8
  How does mist differ from fog?
  Allows visibility of under 1 km | *Allows visibility of over 1 km | Forms only above 2 km | Contains smoke and pollutants
  x: Fog cuts visibility to under 1 km; mist is thinner and wetter with visibility over 1 km.
[f0bea9a3cd543] sub8
  London smog, formed in cool, humid conditions, is of which nature?
  photochemical | volcanic | *sulphurous | radioactive
  x: London smog is sulphurous; Los Angeles smog is photochemical.
[f7ffcfa239ee5] sub8
  Which of the following does NOT favour the formation of dew?
  Clear sky | Calm air | High relative humidity | *Windy night
  x: Dew needs a clear sky, calm air and high RH; cloudy or windy nights prevent it.

=== NOTES 4:19 | Atmospheric Disturbances – Tropical Cyclones, Temperate Cyclones, Anticyclones, Thunderstorms, Tornadoes
## SUB 0 | Cyclones of India and Andhra Pradesh – Exposure and Major Cyclones
[19:0:0] # Exposure (asked 25 times)
[19:0:1] - India's coast is exposed to nearly **10%** of the world's tropical cyclones (APPSC-GS 2023; NDMA). Coastline: old **7,516.6 km**; remeasured 2023–24 = **11,098.81 km**; about 5,900 km directly exposed.
[19:0:2] - **Bay of Bengal : Arabian Sea ≈ 4 : 1** – the Bay has about **4 to 5 times** more cyclones (75–80% of the total) because it is **warmer (high SST)**, enclosed by land and receives **remnants of Pacific typhoons**; its funnel shape worsens storm surges.
[19:0:3] - **Arabian Sea**: fewer cyclones but becoming **more intense**; 2019 Arabian Sea storms = **Vayu, Hikka, Kyarr, Maha, Pavan** (Pabuk, Fani, Bulbul were Bay systems).
[19:0:4] - **East coast** (Odisha, AP, WB, TN) is more cyclone-prone than the west coast; **Odisha** faces the most cyclone disasters.
[19:0:5] - Season **bimodal**: main peak **Oct–Dec** (retreating monsoon), secondary **Apr–May**; some at monsoon onset (June) and withdrawal (Sept). A May (pre-monsoon) cyclone is linked to **local temperature variation** (strong local heating).
[19:0:6] - Bay of Bengal cyclones move **west, north-west or north**, recurving north/north-east later; some cross the peninsula into the Arabian Sea and revive.
[19:0:7] - **INCOIS (Hyderabad)** 1995–2019 study: El Nino may **reduce** post-monsoon Bay cyclones (15 in 9 El Nino years vs 33 in 11 La Nina years).
[19:0:8] # Andhra Pradesh
[19:0:9] - AP coastline **1,053 km** (3rd longest); **cyclones are AP's main hazard** (more than floods, landslides, earthquakes); hit mostly **Oct–Dec** (Hudhud, Titli, Michaung, Montha).
[19:0:10] - IMD record 1891–2017: AP coast hit **77 times** by cyclones (34 kt+), **31 of them severe** cyclonic storms.
[19:0:11] - **Montha** (Oct 2025, Kakinada): RTGS **AWARE 2.0** auto-evacuations, 423 drones, alerts to 3.60 crore people, only 15 deaths.
[19:0:12] # Major cyclones
[19:0:13] TABLE head: Cyclone | Year | Sea | Hit / note
  [19:0:13.0] Odisha Super Cyclone (unnamed) | 29 Oct 1999 | Bay | Odisha (Paradip); ~10,000 killed, 15 million affected in 12 districts; winds about 260 km/h sustained, 270–300 km/h in book keys
  [19:0:13.1] Gonu | June 2007 | Arabian Sea | Oman, Iran (not 2008)
  [19:0:13.2] Phailin | 2013 | Bay | Odisha, AP; 1 million+ evacuated; "zero casualty" approach since
  [19:0:13.3] Hudhud | 12 Oct 2014 | Bay | Visakhapatnam – first Indian city directly hit; M. Venkaiah Naidu wielded a broom there (24 Oct 2014, Swachh Bharat)
  [19:0:13.4] Ockhi | Nov 2017 | Arabian Sea (near Lakshadweep) | Kerala, TN fishermen
  [19:0:13.5] Titli | Oct 2018 | Bay | Landfall near Palasa – Srikakulam, Vizianagaram (AP), then south Odisha; RIMES: "rarest cyclone" (recurved inland, kept its force)
  [19:0:13.6] Gaja | Nov 2018 | Bay | Tamil Nadu (Nagapattinam)
  [19:0:13.7] Luban | Oct 2018 | Arabian Sea | Arabian Peninsula (Yemen, Oman)
  [19:0:13.8] Idai | Mar 2019 | SW Indian Ocean | Beira (Mozambique), Zimbabwe, Malawi
  [19:0:13.9] Fani | May 2019 | Bay | Odisha (Puri); extremely severe; ~1.2 million evacuated; 2019's most devastating disaster
  [19:0:13.10] Amphan | 2020 | Bay | West Bengal; super cyclonic
  [19:0:13.11] Tauktae | 14–19 May 2021 | Arabian Sea | Gujarat, Maharashtra (west coast); extremely severe
  [19:0:13.12] Biparjoy | 2023 | Arabian Sea | Gujarat; longest-lived Arabian Sea cyclone
  [19:0:13.13] Michaung | 2023 | Bay | AP coast; Chennai floods
  [19:0:13.14] Fengal | 2024 | Bay | TN–Puducherry
  [19:0:13.15] Shakti | 2025 | Arabian Sea | Maharashtra, TN alerts
  [19:0:13.16] Montha | Oct 2025 | Bay | Kakinada (AP)
  [19:0:13.17] Ditwah | Nov 2025 | Bay | Sri Lanka; India's Operation Sagar Bandhu
[19:0:14] - APPSC G1 2018 match: Ockhi – Kerala, Luban – Arabian Peninsula, Titli – AP (the paper put Gaja against Somalia; Somalia was hit by Cyclone **Sagar**, May 2018).
[19:0:15] > Odisha 1999: date **29-10-1999** – the APPSC options gave only August dates.
[19:0:16] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography Part 5 p.3; NextGen Rocket Disaster Management p.17, 36; NDMA; IMD/data.gov.in; RIMES (via GKToday, Nov 2018); app notes 4:19 sub 9
## SUB 1 | Measurement Scales and IMD Categories
[19:1:0] # Scales (asked 16 times)
[19:1:1] TABLE head: Scale | Measures | Range
  [19:1:1.0] Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale | Hurricanes – wind speed; estimates property damage and coastal flooding | Cat 1–5
  [19:1:1.1] Fujita / Enhanced Fujita (Ted Fujita) | Tornadoes – wind and damage; EF is the current standard (USA, 2007) | EF0–EF5 (6 categories)
  [19:1:1.2] Beaufort | Wind force | 0–12; gale = force 8 (about 62–74 km/h)
  [19:1:1.3] Richter (Charles Richter, 1935) | Quake magnitude | Logarithmic
  [19:1:1.4] Moment magnitude (Mw) | Quake magnitude (energy at source) | Modern standard
  [19:1:1.5] Modified Mercalli | Quake intensity (effects, damage); mainly USA | I–XII
  [19:1:1.6] MSK-64 | Quake intensity; India and Europe | I–XII
  [19:1:1.7] INES | Nuclear events (IAEA, 1990) | 0–7
[19:1:2] - Saffir-Simpson: Cat 1 **119–153**; Cat 2 154–177; Cat 3 178–208; Cat 4 209–251; Cat 5 **252+** km/h.
[19:1:3] - **"Gale force"** winds are a cyclone term.
[19:1:4] - Hurricane / typhoon / cyclone threshold: **74 mph (119 km/h, 64 knots)** – above 119 km/h a storm is "hurricane-strength" (old IMD: severe cyclonic storm with a core of hurricane winds; now Very Severe Cyclonic Storm).
[19:1:5] - **Super typhoon**: about 240 km/h (strong Cat 4–5); Super Typhoon **Bavi** = 3rd Cat-5 storm of 2026 (10 Jul 2026).
[19:1:6] # IMD categories (North Indian Ocean, Indian Cyclone Intensity Scale)
[19:1:7] TABLE head: Category | km/h | Knots
  [19:1:7.0] Low Pressure Area | < 31 | < 17
  [19:1:7.1] Depression | 31–49 | 17–27
  [19:1:7.2] Deep Depression | 50–61 | 28–33
  [19:1:7.3] Cyclonic Storm (named from here) | 62–88 | 34–47
  [19:1:7.4] Severe Cyclonic Storm | 89–117 | 48–63
  [19:1:7.5] Very Severe | 118–166 | 64–89
  [19:1:7.6] Extremely Severe (added 2015) | 167–221 | 90–119
  [19:1:7.7] Super Cyclonic Storm (highest) | 222+ | 120+
[19:1:8] - Tropical cyclone = winds **at or above 62 km/h** (APPSC 2021); Cyclonic Storm = **62–88 km/h** (APPSC AEE 2016; the 2018 option read 63–88).
[19:1:9] - From depression upwards the IMD has **7 classes** (6 before 2015). The IMD uses the **Indian Cyclone Intensity Scale**, not Saffir-Simpson.
[19:1:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Disaster Management p.14–17, 36; PMF Physical Geography 06 p.7, 10; app notes 4:19 sub 7

[19:2:0] # Names (asked 11 times)
[19:2:1] TABLE head: Name | Region
  [19:2:1.0] Hurricane | North Atlantic, Caribbean / West Indies, Gulf of Mexico, NE Pacific
  [19:2:1.1] Typhoon | NW Pacific, China Sea (China, Japan; 100°–180°E most at risk)
  [19:2:1.2] Cyclone | North Indian Ocean (India), South Pacific
  [19:2:1.3] Willy-willy | North-west Australia (UPSC 1995)
  [19:2:1.4] Baguio (Bagyo) | Philippines
  [19:2:1.5] Tornado | Small funnel over land – USA (Mississippi basin)
[19:2:2] - India gets tropical cyclones, **not hurricanes**.
