## SUB 3 | Tropical Cyclones – Formation and Where They Form
[19:3:0] # Conditions (asked 10 times)
[19:3:1] TABLE head: Condition | Role
  [19:3:1.0] Warm ocean, SST above 26.5–27°C over a large area | Heat and moisture – most essential
  [19:3:1.1] Large supply of warm, moist air | Latent heat of condensation = energy source
  [19:3:1.2] Coriolis force | Rotation; too weak within about 5° of the Equator
  [19:3:1.3] Unstable troposphere, high humidity | Vigorous convection
  [19:3:1.4] Low vertical wind shear | Keeps the vertical structure organised
  [19:3:1.5] Pre-existing disturbance; upper-level divergence | Seed low / cyclonic circulation
[19:3:2] - A cyclone is a **violent storm of strong wind and heavy rain**; form **only over warm oceans**, not rivers, lakes or ponds (APPSC-GS 2025).
[19:3:3] - Warm sea, high humidity and instability = **formative / initial stage** (NDA 2017).
[19:3:4] - **Moving away from the sea its force decreases** because the latent-heat (moisture) supply is cut off – weakens after **landfall** (A–R: both true, R explains A).
[19:3:5] # Where they form
[19:3:6] - Belt: **between 30°N and 30°S** (APPSC 2022); mainly **5°–30°** N and S, western parts of oceans; **not** in mid-latitudes and **none at the Equator** (no Coriolis).
[19:3:7] - **None in the South Atlantic and SE Pacific** – UPSC 2015 key: **ITCZ seldom occurs** there; also **cold currents** (Benguela, Humboldt) keep SST low.
[19:3:8] - Leong: typhoons at **6°–20° N and S**, most frequent **July–October**, winds **over 100 mph**, torrential rain with thunder and lightning.
[19:3:9] - Marine heatwaves raise cyclone winds by up to 20% and rain by up to 12% (2026 study).
[19:3:10] ~~ Sources: PMF Physical Geography 05 p.50, 06 p.48; NCERT Fundamentals ch.9 (OnlyIAS p.15–16); G.C. Leong ch.12 p.3; app notes 4:19 sub 1
## SUB 4 | Tornadoes, Thunderstorms and Pre-monsoon Local Storms
[19:4:0] # Tornadoes (asked 11 times)
[19:4:1] - Rotating funnel from a **cumulonimbus/supercell thunderstorm** to the ground; winds **105–322 km/h**; moves up to about 90–100 km/h; lasts **minutes** (rarely over 15–20).
[19:4:2] - **Land-based** (hurricanes, typhoons, willy-willies are ocean-born); much **smaller** than hurricanes – both are destructive rotating storms.
[19:4:3] - Air spiralling to the centre conserves angular momentum → **angular speed increases** towards the centre.
[19:4:4] - **Tornado Alley**: central US plains (**Mississippi plains / Great Plains**) where cold polar air meets warm, moist **Gulf of Mexico** air.
[19:4:5] - **India is least vulnerable to tornadoes** among major hazards (rare; pre-monsoon; Belda 1998).
[19:4:6] TABLE head: Feature | Tornado | Hurricane
  [19:4:6.0] Size, life | Small, minutes | Hundreds of km, days
  [19:4:6.1] Where | Land-based | Ocean-born
[19:4:7] - **Waterspout** = tornado over water; seen over the **Brahmaputra, Barpeta (Assam)**, 26 Aug 2026. An ordinary thunderstorm is a short-lived single-cell Cb; **supercells** spawn tornadoes.
[19:4:8] # Thunderstorms
[19:4:9] - Thundercloud (Cb, up to 15 km) needs **condensation, high temperature and humidity, orography and vertical winds – all four** (IAS 2002). **Thunder** = air expanding explosively after lightning heats it.
[19:4:10] - **Hailstorms**: instability, moisture, updrafts; **synoptic** causes = Western Disturbances and wind discontinuity lines.
[19:4:11] - **Damini App**: lightning alerts in 15 languages; 104 detection locations.
[19:4:12] # Pre-monsoon local storms of India
[19:4:13] TABLE head: Storm / shower | Season / region
  [19:4:13.0] Mango showers | End of summer (March–April); Kerala, coastal Karnataka, nearby TN; early ripening of mangoes
  [19:4:13.1] Blossom (cherry blossom) showers | Kerala and nearby; coffee flowering
  [19:4:13.2] Kaal Baisakhi / Nor'westers | West Bengal, Bihar, Odisha, Assam ("tea showers" in Assam); approach from NW
  [19:4:13.3] Aandhi (dust storm) | Summer; Uttar Pradesh, Punjab – dry plains of NW India
  [19:4:13.4] Loo | Hot dry wind of the northern plains
  [19:4:13.5] Cloudburst | Himalaya, June–August; about 100 mm/hour over 20–30 sq km
[19:4:14] - Hindi-medium key: mango showers = "rainfall in March–April in Bihar and Bengal" – strictly Kerala/Karnataka.
[19:4:15] - **Blizzard**: severe snowstorm, winds 35 mph (about 56 km/h)+, visibility a quarter mile or less for 3+ hours.
[19:4:16] ~~ Sources: G.C. Leong ch.12 p.3; NextGen Rocket Disaster Management p.14–16; NCERT India Physical Environment ch.4; app notes 4:19 sub 5
## SUB 5 | Structure, Rotation and Steering of Cyclones
[19:5:0] # Structure (asked 8 times)
[19:5:1] TABLE head: Part | Feature
  [19:5:1.0] Eye | Calm, clear, sinking air; lowest pressure; higher temperature (warm core); 20–50 km across
  [19:5:1.1] Eyewall | Ring of towering cumulonimbus; strongest winds, heaviest rain
  [19:5:1.2] Spiral rainbands | Curved bands of rain and wind – a mature cyclone shows a spiral pattern
[19:5:2] - Air moves **inward and rises**; rotation **anticlockwise (counter-clockwise) in NH, clockwise in SH** – spin from the **Coriolis effect**.
[19:5:3] - Approach of a cyclone = **falling** barometer.
[19:5:4] - Hurricanes usually **grow larger** poleward, and some are **under 150 km** across (Tracy 1974) – CDS 2010: only "spin from Coriolis" is right.
[19:5:5] - Steering: **trade winds** push tropical cyclones **west**; mature storms **recurve north-east** under the **westerlies**.
[19:5:6] - Threats: high winds, heavy rain, flooding, **storm surge** – abnormal rise of sea level, the **biggest killer**.
[19:5:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Physical Geography 06 p.4; NCERT Fundamentals ch.9; G.C. Leong ch.12 p.3; Environment Canada / NOAA JetStream (hurricane size); app notes 4:19 sub 2
## SUB 6 | Warnings, Detection and Naming
[19:6:0] # Warnings (asked 4 times)
[19:6:1] TABLE head: Stage (IMD four-stage warning) | Colour
  [19:6:1.0] Pre-Cyclone Watch | –
  [19:6:1.1] Cyclone Alert | Yellow
  [19:6:1.2] Cyclone Warning | Orange
  [19:6:1.3] Post-landfall Outlook | Red
[19:6:2] - General colour code: **green** no warning, **yellow** be aware, **orange** be prepared, **red take action**.
[19:6:3] - Detection: satellites and **coastal (Doppler) weather radars** of the IMD.
[19:6:4] - **Geo-informatics** (GIS, remote sensing) predicts track and intensity, maps vulnerability and supports evacuation and relief, but **cannot predict all impacts, such as death count**.
[19:6:5] # Naming
[19:6:6] TABLE head: Body | Role
  [19:6:6.0] WMO | 6 RSMCs + 5 TCWCs name cyclones worldwide
  [19:6:6.1] IMD (RSMC New Delhi) | Names Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea cyclones
  [19:6:6.2] WMO/ESCAP Panel | 13 countries; list of 169 names (2020); Shakti proposed by Sri Lanka
[19:6:7] ~~ Sources: IMD SOP for cyclone warnings; NextGen Rocket Disaster Management p.36; app notes 4:19 sub 8
## SUB 7 | Cyclones vs Anticyclones; Disturbances at a Glance
[19:7:0] # Cyclone vs anticyclone (asked 2 times)
[19:7:1] TABLE head: Basis | Cyclone | Anticyclone
  [19:7:1.0] Centre | Low pressure, surrounded by higher | High pressure, surrounded by lower
  [19:7:1.1] Air | Inward, rising | Outward, sinking (diverging)
  [19:7:1.2] Weather | Cloudy, stormy | Clear, dry, calm, settled
  [19:7:1.3] NH rotation | Anticlockwise | Clockwise
  [19:7:1.4] SH rotation | Clockwise | Anticlockwise
[19:7:2] - **Continually rising pressure = fine, settled weather** (anticyclone building).
[19:7:3] - **Heat dome**: a stalled warm high traps hot air (27 May 2026).
[19:7:4] # At a glance
[19:7:5] TABLE head: Disturbance | Nature | Clouds
  [19:7:5.0] Tropical cyclone | Large low over warm tropical oceans | Cumulonimbus, rainbands
  [19:7:5.1] Temperate cyclone | Large mid-latitude low from air-mass interaction, with fronts | Stratiform and cumuliform
  [19:7:5.2] Anticyclone | Large high, outward sinking air | Generally clear
  [19:7:5.3] Thunderstorm | Local violent convective storm with lightning, thunder | Cumulonimbus
  [19:7:5.4] Tornado | Very local rotating funnel | Cumulonimbus supercell
  [19:7:5.5] Cloudburst, squall | Very local intense rain / sudden gusty wind | –
[19:7:6] - **Fronts** belong to **temperate cyclones only**.
[19:7:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket General Geography #9; G.C. Leong ch.12; app notes 4:19 sub 0, 3
## SUB 8 | Temperate Cyclones and Western Disturbances
[19:8:0] # Temperate vs tropical (asked 1 time)
[19:8:1] TABLE head: Feature | Tropical | Temperate (extra-tropical)
  [19:8:1.0] Latitude | 5–30° | 35–65° (mid and high)
  [19:8:1.1] Origin | Only over warm seas | Land and sea
  [19:8:1.2] Fronts | None | Clear frontal system (warm, cold; occluded)
  [19:8:1.3] Size, winds | Smaller, very intense (100–500 km) | Larger area (300–2,000 km), gentler winds; long rain
  [19:8:1.4] Movement | East to west (trades) | West to east (westerlies)
[19:8:2] - APPSC G1: "Extra-tropical cyclones **do not have a clear frontal system**" is the **INCORRECT** statement.
[19:8:3] - **Western Disturbance**: extratropical low from the **Mediterranean**; reaches **NW India in winter** at the occluded stage; about **10–15 cm** rain for **rabi** crops, snow on the mountains.
[19:8:4] ~~ Sources: NCERT Fundamentals ch.9 (OnlyIAS p.16); PMF Physical Geography 06 p.48; NextGen Indian Geography Part 5 (westerly disturbance); app notes 4:19 sub 4

  *Anticlockwise and clockwise | Clockwise in both hemispheres | Anticlockwise in both hemispheres | Clockwise and anticlockwise
  x: Because of Coriolis deflection, tropical cyclones rotate anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.

  Spiral rainbands | *Centre (eye) | Outer periphery | Eyewall
  x: The centre of a cyclone has the lowest pressure; the eyewall has the strongest winds and the spiral rainbands bring rain and wind.

  x: Trade winds steer tropical cyclones westward; in mature systems the westerlies may recurve them towards the north-east.
[n23c0d36f4eb] sub5
  What is usually the biggest killer in a cyclone?

  x: Storm surge, the abnormal rise of sea water pushed ashore by cyclone winds and low pressure, is the biggest killer.
[n826716c8ca2] sub5
  In which part of a tropical cyclone do the strongest winds and heaviest rain occur?
  Eye | Outer rain bands | *Eyewall | Outer periphery
  x: The eyewall, a ring of towering cumulonimbus around the calm eye, has the strongest winds and heaviest rain.
[g4fe887fc5c9b] sub5
  Which winds make mature tropical cyclones recurve towards the north-east?
  Trade winds | *Westerlies | Polar easterlies | Monsoon winds
  x: Trade winds push tropical cyclones west; mature storms may then recurve north-east under the westerlies.
[g5bd993ad37c6] sub5

  x: The eye is calm and clear with sinking air and the lowest pressure; the strongest winds are in the eyewall around it.

=== NOTES 4:20 | Elements and Factors of Climate; World Climatic Classification (koeppen)
## SUB 0 | Forests and Biomes of the World
[20:0:0] # Biome basics (asked 29 times)
[20:0:1] - **Biome:** a large naturally occurring community of flora and fauna occupying a **major habitat**, shaped mainly by climate (APPSC Panchayat Secretary).
[20:0:2] - **Anthromes** (anthropogenic biomes): units shaped by sustained human use – croplands, villages, cities.
[20:0:3] - Geomorphic factors of plant and animal distribution: **slope angle, slope aspect and relative relief** (CDS 2020).
[20:0:4] TABLE head: Forest | Climate | Vegetation | Distribution
  [20:0:4.0] Tropical rainforest (selva) | Near the Equator (about 10°N–10°S); hot and wet all year, rain over 200 cm | Broadleaf evergreen (leaves not shed together); mahogany, ebony; climbers (lianas) and epiphytes | Amazon (Brazil), Congo Basin, Indonesia; Ivory Coast (Gulf of Guinea)
  [20:0:4.1] Tropical deciduous (monsoon) | 100–200 cm seasonal rain | Shed leaves in the dry season; teak, sal | Most extensive in Asia (India, Myanmar, Thailand); also Africa, S America, N Australia
  [20:0:4.2] Temperate deciduous | Mid latitudes between the tropics and the polar regions; four seasons (APPSC G2 Mains 2025) | Broadleaf, shed in autumn; oak, beech, maple | E USA, W Europe, E Asia
  [20:0:4.3] Taiga (boreal, temperate coniferous) | Long severe winters, short summers | Needle-leaved evergreen softwoods: spruce, fir, pine, cedar; little undergrowth; growing period 50–100 days | Canada, Alaska, Scandinavia, Siberia (N hemisphere only)
  [20:0:4.4] Mediterranean | Dry summer, wet winter | Evergreen oaks, cork oak, olive, shrubs (sclerophyll) | Med basin, California, Central Chile, SW Australia, Cape
  [20:0:4.5] Mangrove (tidal) | Tropical and subtropical saline coasts | Salt-tolerant; pneumatophores let roots breathe in waterlogged mud | Sundarbans; stabilise the shoreline, bulwark against the sea (UPSC 1996 A-R: both true, R explains A)
[20:0:5] # Tropical rainforest – what is asked
[20:0:6] - **Maximum biodiversity** of all biomes (over half of known species) – UPPCS 2012, 2014.
[20:0:7] - Luxuriant growth = **hot, wet climate all year + intense sunlight**; the soils are **not fertile** (leached) and there are **no seasons** (NDA 2015).
[20:0:8] - **Leaching** is the main soil problem (UPPCS 1998); leaf litter **decomposes faster than in any other biome**, so the forest floor is often bare; plants reach the canopy by climbing (lianas) or as **epiphytes** (UPSC 2021).
[20:0:9] - **Amazon** = "**lungs of the planet**"; **Amazon fires, 2019** (Brazil; INPE recorded a sharp rise in fires). **Congo Basin** = 2nd-largest rainforest.
[20:0:10] - Tropical rainforest has the **highest share of the world's forest area** among the forest types (APSC 2017; FAO: tropical forests ≈ 45% of all forest).
[20:0:11] - Equatorial region = **megathermal** (hot all year) with **aerial streamlets** (climbers/epiphytes, water dripping from the canopy); it is **not sclerophyll** and not a region of high development.
[20:0:12] # Taiga and tundra
[20:0:13] - **Taiga = largest land biome**; it has a **very wide** (not narrow) annual temperature range – **APPSC G1** "incorrect statement"; moderate precipitation, snow in winter; acidic **podzol**; lowest productivity of forests; northernmost temperate biome (UPPCS 2016: taiga = **temperate region**).
[20:0:14] - **Tundra:** mosses and lichens, no trees, permafrost; it is wet because **low temperatures make evaporation slow** and permafrost blocks drainage. **Alpine tundra** lies above the tree line.
[20:0:15] - **Tree line:** the altitude/latitude beyond which trees cannot grow. Himalaya: **lower in the west** (about 3,300–3,600 m) than in the east (3,600–3,800 m), because the Eastern Himalaya is **nearer the Equator and the sea** (Bay of Bengal moisture) – UPSC 1995, UPPCS 2005.
[20:0:16] # Adaptations
[20:0:17] - Dry regions: smaller leaves **reduce transpiration** (UPSC 2011). Deciduous trees shed leaves in winter/dry season **to conserve water** (APPSC G1). Desert animals = **xerocoles** (fossorial = burrowing; arboreal = tree-dwelling).
[20:0:18] # Biome wildlife
[20:0:19] TABLE head: Biome / realm | Animals
  [20:0:19.0] Rainforest | Apes, gorillas, orangutans, jaguars, macaws
  [20:0:19.1] Savanna | Elephants, lions, zebras, giraffes; elephant grass, guinea grass, baobab, acacia; fire-prone; "Land of Big Game"
  [20:0:19.2] Taiga | Moose, beavers, lynx, wolves
  [20:0:19.3] Tundra / polar | Polar bears, musk ox, krill, seals, walruses
  [20:0:19.4] Deserts | Camels, jackals, scorpions (xerocoles)
  [20:0:19.5] Australasian realm | Kangaroos, platypus – marsupials and monotremes (isolation)
  [20:0:19.6] New Zealand | Kiwi – flightless bird found only in New Zealand
  [20:0:19.7] Madagascar | Lemurs, tenrecs (endemism)
[20:0:20] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket World Geography p.29–30 (forest types, biomes); G.C. Leong ch.15, 23, 25; NCERT Fundamentals ch.11 (OnlyIAS Physical Geography 08); PMF Physical Geography 07; app notes 4:20 sub 5

## SUB 2 | World Climatic Regions – Identify the Type
[20:2:0] # Region table (asked 23 times)
[20:2:1] TABLE head: Region | Location | Climate | Vegetation
  [20:2:1.0] Equatorial | 0–10° N/S: Amazon, Congo, Gabon, Zaire, Indonesia (Ethiopia is NOT equatorial – a highland) | Hot, wet all year; mean ~27°C; annual range only 2–3°C; rain every month, double peak after the equinoxes; afternoon convectional thunder rain; no seasons | Evergreen hardwoods (mahogany, ebony)
  [20:2:1.1] Tropical monsoon | India, SE Asia, N Australia | Seasonal reversal of winds; summer rain 100–200 cm | Teak, sal
  [20:2:1.2] Savanna (Sudan type) | Sudan belt, E Africa, Llanos, Campos | Definite wet (summer) and dry (winter) seasons; 500–2,000 mm; no month below 20°C | Tall grass, scattered trees; "Land of Big Game"
  [20:2:1.3] Hot desert | 15–30°, western margins | Rain below 25 cm | Xerophytes
  [20:2:1.4] Mediterranean | 30–45°, western margins | Winter rain, dry summer | Evergreen oak, olive
  [20:2:1.5] China type (warm temperate eastern margin) | Central/S China, SE USA (Gulf type), S Brazil, Natal, E Australia | Rain all year, more in summer (modified monsoon) | Mixed forests
  [20:2:1.6] British / Marine West Coast | NW Europe (Norway, Netherlands), British Columbia, S Chile, New Zealand; 40–65°, westerlies | Mild; rain in all months, 50–250 cm; low annual and daily range | Oak, beech
  [20:2:1.7] Taiga (Siberian) | N North America, Eurasia | Severe winters, very large range | Conifers
  [20:2:1.8] Tundra | Arctic fringe; alpine above tree line | Permafrost | Mosses, lichens
[20:2:2] # Fixed facts
[20:2:3] - **Savanna trees are kept in check** by **fire, grazing herbivores and seasonal (dry-season) rainfall** – UPSC 2021 key (2, 3 and 4); termites and soil are not the answer.
[20:2:4] - Dense forests lie mostly **near the Equator**. Rain throughout the year: **equatorial region**. Monsoon rains: **tropical regions**.
[20:2:5] - **Equatorial passage** (UPSC 2015): clear morning, sea breeze, heat builds, dark clouds, rain with thunder in the afternoon, soon over.
[20:2:6] - UPSC 2002: equatorial regions do **not** have four seasons; Mediterranean summers are **dry**; China type has rain all year; **tropical highlands show vertical zonation** – only 3 and 4 are correct.
[20:2:7] - UPSC 2024: low annual and daily range + rain all year + 50–250 cm = **Marine West Coast**.
[20:2:8] - **Western Europe**: rain in all months, lies in the **westerlies** – both correct (UPPCS key).
[20:2:9] - **Norway** (west-coast type): rain all year with the maximum in autumn–winter; China, Brazil, Nigeria get summer rain.
[20:2:10] - **Monsoon climate** outside Asia: **SE United States** (Gulf type, slightly monsoonal); Pacific coast of Colombia is equatorial, Central California is Mediterranean.
[20:2:11] - Climate chart with cold winters (3.9°C), hot summers (27.8°C) and summer-maximum rain all year = **China type** (UPSC 1998).
[20:2:12] - **Zaire → Netherlands**: equatorial → hot desert → Mediterranean → West European (1, 3, 2, 4).
[20:2:13] - **Asia** has all climatic zones (Equator to near the North Pole).
[20:2:14] - Of the Earth's land, **humid regions** cover the largest share; drylands (arid, semi-arid, dry sub-humid, hyper-arid) together ≈ 41%.
[20:2:15] - Equatorial climate suits plants more than people (constant heat and humidity).
[20:2:16] - Order from the Equator to the poles: equatorial → tropical monsoon → temperate deciduous → tundra.
[20:2:17] ~~ Sources: G.C. Leong ch.15 (equatorial), 16 (monsoon), 17 (savanna), 21 (China and Gulf type), 22 (British type); NCERT Fundamentals ch.11 (OnlyIAS Physical Geography 08); PMF Physical Geography 07; UNCCD (drylands 41%); app notes 4:20 sub 3
## SUB 3 | Mediterranean Climate and Hot Deserts
[20:3:0] # Mediterranean (asked 16 times)
[20:3:1] - **Hot dry summers, mild wet winters** – **dry summer** is the most noticeable feature (CDS 2019); heavy rain in **winter**.
[20:3:2] - **Cause: seasonal shift of pressure and wind belts.** Summer: belts shift north, **subtropical high** and dry offshore (land) trade winds → drought. Winter (winter solstice, sun over the Tropic of Capricorn): belts shift **south**, **westerlies** and their depressions bring rain. (In the S hemisphere the shift is the reverse.)
[20:3:3] - UPPCS 2022 A-R (winter rain; summer under dry land winds): official key – **both true and R explains A**.
[20:3:4] - NOT Mediterranean features: **dry winter, no dry season, dry and very severe winter** (APPSC G1).
[20:3:5] - Vegetation: **evergreen oak**, cork oak, **olive** (most typical), chestnut, walnut; **teak is NOT** Mediterranean (it is monsoon forest).
[20:3:6] - Economy: "**orchard lands of the world**" – **citrus fruits**, grapes, wine; horticulture and market gardening (also in densely peopled temperate NW Europe, NE USA).
[20:3:7] TABLE head: Region | Towns
  [20:3:7.0] Mediterranean basin | Rome, Athens, Central Spain (Csa: dry hot summer)
  [20:3:7.1] California | Los Angeles, San Francisco
  [20:3:7.2] Central Chile | Santiago
  [20:3:7.3] SW Cape | Cape Town
  [20:3:7.4] SW and S Australia | Perth, Adelaide
[20:3:8] - NOT Mediterranean: **New York** (east coast), **Darwin / Northern Australia**, **Pampas** (humid temperate grassland).
[20:3:9] # Hot deserts
[20:3:10] - **Desert**: annual rainfall **below 25 cm**.
[20:3:11] - Hot deserts 15–30°, on **western margins**; most likely **near 23°** (Tropics): **subtropical high pressure + offshore trade winds + cold currents**. Sahara, Kalahari, Namib, Atacama, Arabian, Thar, Great Australian.
[20:3:12] - Temperate (cold) deserts: Patagonia, **Gobi**, Ladakh.
[20:3:13] ~~ Sources: G.C. Leong ch.18 (deserts), ch.19 (Mediterranean); NextGen Rocket World Geography p.23, 29–30; PMF Physical Geography 07; UPPCS 2022 official key (examrobot.com); app notes 4:20 sub 4
## SUB 4 | Elements and Controls of Climate
[20:4:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [20:4:0.0] Weather | State of the atmosphere at a particular place and time
  [20:4:0.1] Climate | Average weather over a long period; WMO normal = 30 years
  [20:4:0.2] Climograph | Monthly mean max/min temperature as a line + rainfall as bars (APSLPRB 2023)
  [20:4:0.3] Elements (measured) | Temperature, pressure, wind, humidity, cloudiness, precipitation, sunshine
  [20:4:0.4] Controls (factors) | Latitude (main factor), altitude, distance from the sea, pressure and wind belts, ocean currents, relief, land cover
[20:4:1] - **Distance from a river is NOT a control** of climate (APPSC Endowment, APPSC GS 2025). Cloudiness is an element, not a control.
[20:4:2] - **Latitude is the main factor** deciding climate: the climatic belts follow latitude.
[20:4:3] TABLE head: Control | How it works | Indian example
  [20:4:3.0] Latitude | Insolation falls towards the poles | Mainland 8°4′–37°6′ N; south of the Tropic of Cancer = tropical
  [20:4:3.1] Altitude | Normal lapse rate about 6.5°C per 1,000 m | Shimla cooler than Amritsar
  [20:4:3.2] Distance from sea | Coasts equable; interiors extreme (continental) | A&N Islands equable
  [20:4:3.3] Relief / mountain barriers | Windward wet, leeward rain-shadow | Himalayas block cold Central Asian air
  [20:4:3.4] Ocean currents | Cold currents make tropical west coasts cool and dry | –
  [20:4:3.5] Winds, pressure belts | Monsoons, westerlies, western disturbances | –
[20:4:4] - Tropic of Cancer crosses **8 states**: Gujarat, Rajasthan, MP, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura, Mizoram.
[20:4:5] - India has a **tropical monsoon** climate; IMD SW monsoon normal (Jun–Sep, 1971–2020) = **868.6 mm**.

## SUB 6 | Koeppen and Thornthwaite Classification
[20:6:0] - **Wladimir Koeppen**: empirical scheme on **mean temperature and precipitation**, closely linked to **natural vegetation** – "vegetation is the true index of climate" (UPPCS 2018).
[20:6:1] - **Thornthwaite (1931, revised 1948)**: **precipitation effectiveness** and **thermal efficiency**.
[20:6:2] TABLE head: Letter | Group | Criterion
  [20:6:2.0] A | Tropical humid | Coldest month above 18°C
  [20:6:2.1] B | Dry | Evaporation > precipitation (BS steppe, BW desert)
  [20:6:2.2] C | Warm temperate | Coldest month between –3 and 18°C
  [20:6:2.3] D | Cold snow-forest | Coldest month below –3°C
  [20:6:2.4] E | Polar | Warmest month below 10°C (ET tundra, EF ice cap)
  [20:6:2.5] H | Highland | Controlled by altitude
[20:6:3] - Second letters: **f** = no dry season; **m** = monsoon; **w** = dry winter; **s** = dry summer. Third letter **a** = hot summer: **Cfa = humid subtropical** (Af tropical wet, Aw tropical wet and dry, ET tundra).
[20:6:4] # Koeppen codes in India
[20:6:5] TABLE head: Code | Type | Area
  [20:6:5.0] Amw | Monsoon with short dry season | West coast south of Goa
  [20:6:5.1] As | Monsoon with dry summer (winter rain) | Coromandel coast of Tamil Nadu
  [20:6:5.2] Aw | Tropical savanna | Most of the Peninsular plateau south of the Tropic of Cancer; Andhra Pradesh
  [20:6:5.3] BShw | Semi-arid steppe | NW Gujarat, parts of W Rajasthan and Punjab
  [20:6:5.4] BWhw | Hot desert | Extreme western Rajasthan
  [20:6:5.5] Cwg | Monsoon with dry winter | Ganga plain, E Rajasthan, N MP, most of NE India
  [20:6:5.6] Dfc | Cold humid winter, short summer | Arunachal Pradesh
  [20:6:5.7] E | Polar type | J&K, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand (high Himalaya)
[20:6:6] - **APPSC G1** match: Amw–west coast; As–Coromandel; Cwg–NE India; BShw–NW Gujarat (A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV).
[20:6:7] - Number of Koeppen climates in India differs by book: NCERT **8** regions; PMF **9**; Wikipedia ("Climate of India") **4 major groups and 7 subtypes**.
[20:6:8] - **AP**: 12°41′–19°07′ N; mainly **Aw**; four climatic regions: humid coastal, deltaic, semi-arid **Rayalaseema**, hill micro-climates (Araku, Lambasingi, Horsley Hills). AP has **six agro-climatic zones**; India has **15**.
[20:6:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography Part 5 (appsc-07) p.6; NCERT India Physical Environment ch.4 (OnlyIAS Indian Geography 05 p.13); PMF Indian Physical Geography 03 p.37–38; NCERT Fundamentals ch.11; Wikipedia "Climate of India"; app notes 4:20 sub 2
## SUB 7 | Climatic Extremes
[20:7:0] TABLE head: Record | Place
  [20:7:0.0] Highest air temperature | Death Valley (Furnace Creek), California, 56.7°C (1913) – famous for excessive heat; WMO rejected Al Aziziya; lowest point of N America (–86 m)
  [20:7:0.1] Hottest land surface | Dasht-e-Lut (Iran), 70.7°C (NASA Aqua, 2005)
  [20:7:0.2] Lowest recorded | Vostok, Antarctica, –89.2°C (21 July 1983)
  [20:7:0.3] Cold Pole (inhabited) | Verkhoyansk (Siberia) –67.8°C (1892); Oymyakon –67.7°C (1933)
  [20:7:0.4] Driest | Atacama (northern Chile, west of the Andes); McMurdo Dry Valleys driest polar
  [20:7:0.5] Wettest | Mawsynram (mean ~1,187 cm), Cherrapunji – funnelling + orographic lift
  [20:7:0.6] Largest hot desert / largest desert | Sahara / Antarctica
  [20:7:0.7] India highest / lowest | Ganganagar ~50°C / Dras –45°C (1908)
[20:7:1] - Among Halifax, Chicago, Siachen and Verkhoyansk, the coldest is **Verkhoyansk** (Vostok is colder still).
[20:7:2] - 2025 (WMO): oceans held **over 90%** of excess heat. Bakhira Lake (UP) sediments: ~**25,000-year** monsoon record.
[20:7:3] ~~ Sources: WMO Weather and Climate Extremes Archive; G.C. Leong ch.23; app notes 4:20 sub 7

=== NOTES 4:21 | Climate Change – Evidence, Causes, Global Warming, Ipcc Assessments, Impacts
## SUB 0 | Evidence of Climate Change – Past Climates and Recent Warming
[21:0:0] # Past climates (asked 7 times)
[21:0:1] - **Tree rings (dendroclimatology)**: ring width is a fairly accurate index of a year's **precipitation** (water available in the growing season); old tree rings are the best record of a place's **past local climate over centuries** (weather logs cover only recent decades).
[21:0:2] - Other evidence: glacial landforms (advances and retreats), sediments of glacial lakes, archaeological finds (Rajasthan wet and cool about 8,000 BC).
[21:0:3] - **Great Ice Age = Pleistocene** (cooling began in the **Pliocene**) – APPSC G1 2002 key: "Pleistocene and Pliocene". Last glacial peak about 18,000 years ago; present interglacial began about 10,000 years ago.
[21:0:4] - **Glaciation of peninsular India** = the **Permo-Carboniferous (Carboniferous) ice age** of Gondwana, recorded in the **Talchir tillite** at the base of the Gondwana rocks; Pleistocene glaciers reached only the Himalaya.
[21:0:5] - **Little Ice Age**: about **1550–1850** (NCERT; others 1300–1850, glaciers greatest **1500–1850**); much colder winters in Europe and N America; among exam options **1650–1870** is the period given. 950–1250 AD = Medieval Warm Period.
[21:0:6] # Recent warming
[21:0:7] TABLE head: Indicator | Record
  [21:0:7.0] 2024 | Hottest year on record, about 1.55°C above pre-industrial
  [21:0:7.1] 2025 | 2nd/3rd warmest (~1.43°C); warmest La Nina year
  [21:0:7.2] 2015–2025 | The 11 warmest years (WMO State of the Global Climate 2025)
  [21:0:7.3] India | Warmed about 0.7°C since 1900 (less than global land, ~1.59°C); IMD: 2024 warmest year since 1901
  [21:0:7.4] Gangotri Glacier | Retreated about 1,700 m since 1935
  [21:0:7.5] Sea level | Up about 11 cm since 1993
[21:0:8] - **Global warming** = rise in global surface temperature, caused by rising greenhouse-gas concentrations (CDS 2017 A-R: both true, II explains I).
[21:0:9] - **Sea-level rise** = thermal expansion + melting ice; higher snow albedo is not a cause.
[21:0:10] ~~ Sources: NCERT Fundamentals ch.11 (OnlyIAS Physical Geography 08 p.7–8); PMF Physical Geography 01 p.68 (Carboniferous glaciation of Gondwana); Talchir Formation studies (J. Palaeogeography 2015); WMO; IMD; app notes 4:21 sub 0–1
## SUB 1 | Causes – Natural and Anthropogenic
[21:1:0] # Natural causes (asked 5 times)
[21:1:1] TABLE head: Cause | Meaning / effect
  [21:1:1.0] Eccentricity | Shape of Earth's orbit
  [21:1:1.1] Obliquity | Axial tilt
  [21:1:1.2] Precession (of the equinoxes) | Wobble of the rotational axis
  [21:1:1.3] Solar output (sunspots) | Satellites since 1978 show no net increase: the Sun does not explain recent warming
  [21:1:1.4] Volcanoes | SO2 + ash form aerosols that reflect sunlight: short-term cooling
[21:1:2] - **Milankovitch** (Serbian, **1920s**): astronomical theory – orbital forcing by eccentricity, tilt (shifting of the axis) and precession. **Solar irradiance is NOT a Milankovitch factor** (NCERT lists sunspots separately as a solar cause).
[21:1:3] # Anthropogenic causes
[21:1:4] - **Chief contributor** to warming in the last and present century = **anthropogenic impact** (IPCC AR6), not plate tectonics, volcanoes or Earth's rotation.
[21:1:5] - Fossil fuels (CO2), **land-use change** (deforestation removes sinks), **agriculture** (methane, N2O). CO2 causes about **three-quarters** of warming.
[21:1:6] - Rising GHGs → global warming, **CO2 fertilisation** of plants, stratospheric cooling linked to **ozone depletion**; there is **no "oxygen fertilisation effect"** (CDS 2007).
[21:1:7] - **Water vapour** = most abundant greenhouse gas (feedback).
[21:1:8] - **China** = largest CO2 emitter, and largest in the developing world; India 3rd (after China and USA).
[21:1:9] TABLE head: Gas | GWP (100 yr, AR6) | Main sources
  [21:1:9.0] CO2 | 1 | Fossil fuels, deforestation, cement
  [21:1:9.1] Methane | ~27–30 | Rice paddies, livestock (enteric fermentation), landfills
  [21:1:9.2] Nitrous oxide | ~273 | Fertilisers (largest farm source), manure
  [21:1:9.3] CFCs / HFCs | Very high | Refrigeration, air conditioning (synthetic)
  [21:1:9.4] SF6 | ~25,200 (highest) | Electrical switchgear (entirely synthetic)
[21:1:10] # Short-lived climate pollutants (SLCPs)
[21:1:11] - Stay in the air **days to a few decades** – far **shorter** than CO2.
[21:1:12] - **Black carbon** = **soot**; **tropospheric ozone** is not emitted directly (sunlight on methane, CO, VOCs, NOx); methane; HFCs.
[21:1:13] - **Climate and Clean Air Coalition**: UNEP + **six countries**, 16 Feb 2012.
[21:1:14] ~~ Sources: NCERT Fundamentals ch.11 (OnlyIAS Physical Geography 08 p.8); IPCC AR6 WG I; Global Carbon Project; app notes 4:21 sub 1–3
## SUB 2 | Impacts of Global Warming
[21:2:0] - IPCC: warming raises the frequency and severity of **cyclones, storms and hurricanes – all of these**, plus floods, droughts, glacier melt (UPPCS 2018).
[21:2:1] - **Melting polar ice and sea-level rise** = the most cited effect; Uttarakhand 2002 PYQ keyed statements 1, 3 and 4 (coral islands submerged, Fiji by 2044) – these were alarmist forecasts, not facts (as of 2026 Fiji is not submerged).
[21:2:2] TABLE head: Area | Effect
  [21:2:2.0] Sea level | Uninhabited Kiribati islets Tebua Tarawa, Abanuea submerged 1999; Tuvalu at risk
  [21:2:2.1] Coral reefs | 1.2°C warm-water reef tipping point already crossed (UN brief, Jun 2026)
  [21:2:2.2] Amazon | Beyond ~2°C parts may turn savanna and a carbon source
  [21:2:2.3] Oceans, species | Acidity up 30% since the Industrial Revolution; up to 25% of mountain species face extinction (AR6)
  [21:2:2.4] Disease | Warmer, wetter conditions spread vector-borne malaria, dengue
[21:2:3] - **AP**: heatwaves in Palnadu, Kurnool, Anantapur; **coastal erosion at Uppada (Kakinada)**.
[21:2:4] - **COP31**: **Türkiye (Antalya), November 2026**.
[21:2:5] ~~ Sources: IPCC AR6; Shankar Environment ch.17, 20; WMO; app notes 4:21 sub 6
## SUB 3 | Geoengineering – Reducing Global Warming
[21:3:0] TABLE head: Proposal | Meaning | Note
  [21:3:0.0] Stratospheric sulphate aerosol injection | SO2 forms reflective aerosols; copies volcanic cooling | Termination shock if stopped suddenly
  [21:3:0.1] Cirrus cloud thinning | Seeding high cirrus so they thin and more outgoing heat escapes | –
  [21:3:0.2] Marine cloud brightening | Sea-salt spray as cloud condensation nuclei | –
[21:3:1] - UPSC 2019: cirrus thinning and sulphate injection are proposed for **reducing global warming** – not artificial rain, cyclones or solar wind.
[21:3:2] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment 05 (geoengineering); Shankar Environment ch.21; app notes 4:21 sub 7
## SUB 4 | IPCC, Reports and Recognition
[21:4:0] - **195 members**; **assesses existing literature**, does **no research** of its own; **Nobel Peace Prize 2007** with **Al Gore**.
[21:4:1] TABLE head: Working Group | Subject
  [21:4:1.0] WG I | Physical science basis
  [21:4:1.1] WG II | Impacts, adaptation, vulnerability
  [21:4:1.2] WG III | Mitigation
[21:4:2] - **AR7** cycle began **July 2023**.
[21:4:3] TABLE head: Report | Finding
  [21:4:3.0] SR1.5 (2018) | 1.5°C likely between 2030 and 2052; CO2 to fall 45% from 2010 by 2030, net zero ~2050
  [21:4:3.1] AR6 Synthesis (20 Mar 2023) | 1.1°C reached in 2011–2020; emissions to peak before 2025
  [21:4:3.2] UNEP Emissions Gap 2025 | Current policies → ~2.8°C
  [21:4:3.3] WMO State of the Global Climate 2025 | Released 23 Mar 2026 (World Meteorological Day)
[21:4:4] - **CMIP7** scenarios drop **SSP5-8.5**. **Net zero**: human emissions balanced by removals (sinks or capture).
[21:4:5] - **Nobel Physics 2021**: **Syukuro Manabe and Klaus Hasselmann** (shared) for physical modelling of Earth's climate, quantifying variability and reliably predicting global warming; other half to Giorgio Parisi. (David Julius = Medicine 2021; Benjamin List = Chemistry 2021.)
[21:4:6] ~~ Sources: IPCC; nobelprize.org (Physics 2021); UNEP; WMO; app notes 4:21 sub 4–5

=== NOTES 4:22 | Oceans – Relief of the Ocean Floor, Continental Shelf, Ridges, Trenches
## SUB 0 | Trenches, Deeps and Ridges
[22:0:0] # Trenches and deeps (asked 9 times with ridges)
[22:0:1] TABLE head: Trench / deep | Ocean | Exam point
  [22:0:1.0] Mariana (Challenger Deep) | Western Pacific, near the Northern Mariana Islands | Deepest on Earth, about 11 km (11,022 m, NCERT); deepest of Tonga, Puerto Rico, Izu-Bonin
  [22:0:1.1] Tonga, Kermadec | SW Pacific | Deep, but shallower than Mariana
  [22:0:1.2] Aleutian | North Pacific | –
  [22:0:1.3] Sunda (Java) | Indian | Deepest of the Indian Ocean
  [22:0:1.4] Diamantina | SE Indian Ocean, about 1,500 km west of Perth | Fracture zone (UPSC 2006, asked twice)
  [22:0:1.5] Puerto Rico (Milwaukee Deep) | Atlantic | Deepest of the Atlantic
  [22:0:1.6] South Sandwich | Southern Ocean | –
[22:0:2] - **Milwaukee Deep, Java Trench, Challenger Deep** = the deepest points of the **Atlantic, Indian and Pacific** respectively (CDS 2011).
[22:0:3] - Trenches lie at **subduction zones**, at the base of continental slopes and along island arcs; **most deeps are in the Pacific** (57 explored: 32 Pacific, 19 Atlantic, 6 Indian – NCERT); tsunamis too are most common in the Pacific.
[22:0:4] # Ridges and plateaus
[22:0:5] TABLE head: Ridge / plateau | Ocean
  [22:0:5.0] Mid-Atlantic Ridge | Atlantic; S-shaped; Iceland and the Azores rise above it
  [22:0:5.1] Telegraph Plateau | North Atlantic (not Indian), south of Iceland between Newfoundland and Ireland; part of the North Atlantic Ridge; route of the first transatlantic cables
  [22:0:5.2] Walvis Ridge | South Atlantic, off Namibia
  [22:0:5.3] East Pacific Rise | Pacific
  [22:0:5.4] Cocos Ridge | Pacific, off Central America (not Indian)
  [22:0:5.5] Ninety East Ridge | Indian Ocean, along 90°E; about 5,000 km from 34°S to 10°N, about 200 km wide (asked twice)
  [22:0:5.6] Carlsberg Ridge | NW Indian Ocean (Arabian Sea); India sought exploration rights, 2024
  [22:0:5.7] Agulhas Basin | Indian Ocean (SE of Africa)
[22:0:6] - MPPSC 2019 wrong pair: **Telegraph Plateau – Indian Ocean**. India's polymetallic-sulphide licence on the Indian Ocean Ridge (ISA) runs to **Sept 2031**.
[22:0:7] ~~ Sources: NCERT Fundamentals ch.12 (OnlyIAS Physical Geography 08 p.16, 19); G.C. Leong ch.12 (gc-leong-geography-10.1); PMF Physical Geography 07 (ocean relief); app notes 4:22 sub 4
## SUB 1 | Relief Divisions of the Ocean Floor and Ocean Deposits
[22:1:0] # Four major divisions (NCERT)
[22:1:1] TABLE head: Division | Depth | Key feature
  [22:1:1.0] Continental shelf | To about 200 m (100-fathom isobath); average width about 80 km | "Submerged prolongation of land"; gradient 1° or less; massive sedimentary deposits → source of fossil fuels (most offshore oil); richest fishing
  [22:1:1.1] Continental slope | 200–3,000 m | Gradient 2°–5°; canyons and trenches; marks the end of the continent
  [22:1:1.2] Continental rise | Foot of the slope | Apron of sediment
  [22:1:1.3] Deep-sea (abyssal) plain | 3,000–6,000 m | Most extensive (over 76% of ocean basins); flattest, smoothest; fine-grained sediments (clay, silt); polymetallic nodules
  [22:1:1.4] Oceanic deeps / trenches | Deepest | Active volcanoes and strong earthquakes; 3–5 km deeper than the surrounding floor
[22:1:2] - **APPSC G2 2024 match**: shelf – massive sedimentary deposits (III); slope – canyons and trenches (I); deep-sea plain – fine-grained sediments (IV); deeps – volcanoes and earthquakes (II) = **a-III, b-I, c-IV, d-II**. Wrong pair: deep-sea plain – volcanoes and earthquakes.
[22:1:3] - Depth order: deeps > deep-sea plains > slope > shelf. The deep sea below 200 m is the **oldest and largest biome**.
[22:1:4] - **NDA 2012 shelf statements**: it is **submerged** and its average depth is about **100 fathoms** – true; the largest share of shelf is NOT in the Pacific (the **Atlantic** has the most; widest single shelf = **Siberian shelf**, about 1,500 km); the shelf is **narrow, not wide, where high mountains run close and parallel to the coast** (Chile, west Sumatra).
[22:1:5] - **Marine sediments by volume**: about **90%** lie on the continental margins (shelf, slope, rise), which cover only about a quarter of the floor; the deep-ocean floor holds the least (Britannica). APPSC FSO key (increasing): deep-ocean floor, shelves, rises, slopes.
[22:1:6] # Ocean deposits (APPSC G1 2024)
[22:1:7] - **Terrigenous** deposits come **from land** (gravel, sand, silt, **mud**) and lie mainly on **shelves and slopes**; they get **finer (not coarser) away from the shore**; **muds are the finest** terrigenous material; mud **colour depends on chemical content** (blue, red, green muds). Key: **I, III and IV**.
[22:1:8] TABLE head: Pelagic deposit | Make-up
  [22:1:8.0] Calcareous ooze | Lime shells (globigerina, pteropods)
  [22:1:8.1] Siliceous ooze | Silica skeletons (diatoms, radiolarians); colder, deeper water
  [22:1:8.2] Red clay | Fine inorganic clay + volcanic dust; most widespread deep-sea deposit, largest in the deep Pacific; not from lime shells
[22:1:9] - **Coastal gravel** is terrigenous, not pelagic.
[22:1:10] # Continental shelf of India
[22:1:11] TABLE head: Coast | Shelf
  [22:1:11.0] West | Wide; broadest off Gujarat (and part of Maharashtra); Mumbai High oilfield on it, about 160 km off Mumbai (ONGC)
  [22:1:11.1] East | Narrow
[22:1:12] - East coast has **fewer ports**: **shallow** near-shore water / shelf choked with delta silt and a straight coastline, and frequent **cyclones and storm surges** (AP paper key: statements 1 and 2).
[22:1:13] - **40th Amendment, 1976**: minerals of the shelf and EEZ vest in the **Union**. **2025**: India widened its central Arabian Sea shelf claim by about **10,000 sq km** before the UN **CLCS** (data: NCPOR Goa).
[22:1:14] - **AP**: **1,053 km** coast (3rd longest) on the narrow east-coast shelf; **Visakhapatnam** = only major port.
[22:1:15] ~~ Sources: NCERT Fundamentals ch.12 Table 12.1 (OnlyIAS Physical Geography 08 p.19); G.C. Leong ch.12 (gc-leong-geography-10.1); Britannica "Marine sediment"; APPSC G2 2024 and G1 2024 keys; app notes 4:22 sub 2, 5, 6
## SUB 2 | Measuring Depth and Ocean Zones
[22:2:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [22:2:0.0] Bathymetry | Measuring ocean depth and mapping the sea floor; narrower than oceanography
  [22:2:0.1] Fathom | Unit of depth = 6 feet (about 1.83 m)
  [22:2:0.2] Nautical mile | 1,852 m exactly (international definition)
  [22:2:0.3] Isobath | Line joining points of equal depth
  [22:2:0.4] Hypsometric curve | Share of Earth's surface at each height and depth; shows the bottom topography of the ocean
  [22:2:0.5] Echo sounding / SONAR | Reflection of ultrasonic waves; depth = speed of sound × half the echo time
[22:2:1] - SONAR uses: **fish location (fishing)**, submarine detection, depth measurement, sea-bed mapping.
[22:2:2] TABLE head: Zone | Extent
  [22:2:2.0] Neritic | Water over the continental shelf
  [22:2:2.1] Pelagic | Open ocean beyond the shelf
  [22:2:2.2] Epipelagic | 0–200 m (sunlit)
  [22:2:2.3] Mesopelagic ("twilight zone") | 200–1,000 m; drives the biological carbon pump
  [22:2:2.4] Bathypelagic / Abyssopelagic | 1,000–4,000 m / 4,000–6,000 m
  [22:2:2.5] Hadopelagic | Deep water in the oceanic trenches (below about 6,000 m)
  [22:2:2.6] Benthic | The sea floor
[22:2:3] ~~ Sources: NCERT Fundamentals ch.12; G.C. Leong ch.12 (isobaths, fathoms); BIPM SI Brochure (nautical mile = 1,852 m); NOAA Ocean Service (ocean zones); app notes 4:22 sub 1
## SUB 3 | Oceans – Size and Basic Facts
[22:3:0] - Size order: **Pacific > Atlantic > Indian > Southern > Arctic**; **Arctic = smallest** (asked 3 times), Indian = third largest.
[22:3:1] - **Pacific** = the largest (about one-third of Earth) and deepest ocean, the **major ocean of the world**; larger than all land combined; has the **most islands** (about 25,000).
[22:3:2] - Atlantic: S-shaped, highly indented coast; Indian: only ocean named after a country, triangular, lies **south of the Indian subcontinent** (Arabian Sea to the west, Bay of Bengal to the east).
[22:3:3] - Oceans cover about **70–71%** of Earth's surface.
[22:3:4] ~~ Sources: NCERT Fundamentals ch.12 (OnlyIAS Physical Geography 08 p.18); app notes 4:22 sub 0
## SUB 4 | Minor Relief – Seamounts, Guyots, Canyons and Atolls
[22:4:0] TABLE head: Feature | Description
  [22:4:0.0] Seamount | Volcanic peak rising from the floor that does not reach the surface; cobalt-rich crusts
  [22:4:0.1] Guyot | Flat-topped seamount, planed by waves, then sunk
  [22:4:0.2] Submarine canyon | Deep, steep-sided valley cut across shelf and slope, often off river mouths; Hudson Canyon best known
  [22:4:0.3] Atoll | Low ring- or horseshoe-shaped coral reef round a central lagoon (Lakshadweep, Maldives)
[22:4:1] - **Addu Atoll** = southernmost atoll of the **Maldives**, **Indian Ocean**.
[22:4:2] - **Canyons off Visakhapatnam**: E.C. LaFond (1963) mapped three canyon systems between Visakhapatnam and Bheemunipatnam, named **Andhra** (after Andhra University), **Mahadevan** (after Prof. C. Mahadevan, "father of Indian geology") and **Krishna**; CSIR-**NIO** (RV Sindhu Sankalp, 2017) mapped them and a new canyon system off **Kovvada** (Srikakulam). There is no "Visakha Canyon".
[22:4:3] - **Raman Seamount** ("Raman Sagar mountain"): about **1,505 m** high, Arabian Sea floor about 455 km WSW of Mumbai, found by Indian oceanographers, named after C.V. Raman.
[22:4:4] - **Deep Ocean Mission** surveys: about **25 seamounts** in the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal.
[22:4:5] ~~ Sources: NCERT Fundamentals ch.12 Table 12.2 (OnlyIAS Physical Geography 08 p.20); Rocket General Geography p.66 (atoll, Addu); The Hans India 10 Mar 2017 (Vizag canyons); app notes 4:22 sub 3

=== NOTES 4:23 | Physical and Chemical Characteristics of Ocean Water – Temperature and Salinity Distribution
## SUB 0 | Salinity – Meaning, Factors and Distribution
[23:0:0] # Basics
[23:0:1] - **Salinity** = total dissolved salts in sea water: grams of salt per **1,000 g (1 kg)** of water, in **‰ / ppt** or PSU. **Average 35‰** (35 g per kg); open ocean 33–37‰; **Indian Ocean average 35‰**, Atlantic about 36‰.
[23:0:2] - **Isohaline** = line joining places of equal salinity. Brackish water: about 5–35 ppt (NCERT upper limit 24.7‰).
[23:0:3] - **Main source of salts = land** (weathered rocks), **carried by rivers**; volcanoes add a little. Salinity **reduces evaporation**.
[23:0:4] TABLE head: Factor | Effect
  [23:0:4.0] Evaporation | Raises
  [23:0:4.1] Freezing (salt left behind) | Raises
  [23:0:4.2] Precipitation | Lowers
  [23:0:4.3] River inflow | Lowers (Black Sea: Danube, Dnieper, Dniester)
  [23:0:4.4] Ice melting | Lowers
  [23:0:4.5] Currents, winds | Redistribute
[23:0:5] # Horizontal distribution
[23:0:6] TABLE head: Region | Salinity | Reason
  [23:0:6.0] Equator | Relatively lower | Heavy rain
  [23:0:6.1] Subtropics (about 20°–30°/40° N and S) | Highest – near the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn | Strong evaporation, little rain (UPPSC 2023 true statement)
  [23:0:6.2] Polar seas | Lower | Low evaporation, ice melt, rivers – so "salinity is high in polar regions" is false, though freezing does raise the salinity of the water left (CDS 2009: A false, R true)
[23:0:7] # Seas and lakes
[23:0:8] TABLE head: Water body | Salinity | Reason
  [23:0:8.0] Lake Van (Turkey) | ~330‰ | Closed soda lake
  [23:0:8.1] Dead Sea | ~238‰ (often given as ~340 g/l) | Closed basin, intense evaporation
  [23:0:8.2] Great Salt Lake (Utah) | ~220‰ | Closed basin (Utah Lake is fresh)
  [23:0:8.3] Red Sea | ~41‰ – saltiest sea | High evaporation, little rain, few rivers; narrow Bab-el-Mandeb link
  [23:0:8.4] Gulf of California, Persian Gulf, Mediterranean | High | Hot, dry, evaporation
  [23:0:8.5] Arabian Sea | ~36‰ | High evaporation, low freshwater inflow
  [23:0:8.6] Bay of Bengal | ~30‰ | Ganga–Brahmaputra and other rivers dilute
  [23:0:8.7] Arctic | Low (<32‰) | Cold, ice melt
  [23:0:8.8] Black Sea | 17–18‰ | Rivers pour in
  [23:0:8.9] Baltic | Lowest (under ~10‰) | Many rivers, cold
[23:0:9] - Orders asked: **Lake Van > Dead Sea > Great Salt Lake** (APPSC G2); ascending **Baltic < Black Sea < Red Sea < Dead Sea** (APPSC FSO); **Baltic < Arctic < Gulf of California < Red Sea** (CDS 2012); **Arabian Sea saltier than the Bay of Bengal**.
[23:0:10] - Most saline among Dead Sea, Caspian, Utah Lake, Red Lake = **Dead Sea** (APPSC G1 2002).
[23:0:11] # Dissolved salts
[23:0:12] TABLE head: Salt | Share
  [23:0:12.0] Sodium chloride | 77.8%
  [23:0:12.1] Magnesium chloride | 10.9%
  [23:0:12.2] Magnesium sulphate | 4.7%
  [23:0:12.3] Calcium sulphate | 3.6%
  [23:0:12.4] Potassium sulphate | 2.5%
  [23:0:12.5] Calcium carbonate / magnesium bromide | 0.3% / 0.2%
[23:0:13] - By ions **chloride and sodium** dominate.
[23:0:14] ~~ Sources: Rocket General Geography p.63–64; NCERT Fundamentals ch.12 (OnlyIAS Physical Geography 08 p.22–24); G.C. Leong ch.12 (gc-leong-geography-10.1); app notes 4:23 sub 1–4
## SUB 1 | Distribution of Earth's Water
[23:1:0] TABLE head: Store | Share of all water | Rank
  [23:1:0.0] Oceans | About 97% (96.5%) | 1
  [23:1:0.1] Polar ice and glaciers | About 1.74% (about 68–70% of fresh water) | 2
  [23:1:0.2] Groundwater | About 1.7% (a little over 30% of fresh water) | 3
  [23:1:0.3] Lakes, soil moisture, atmosphere | Tiny | 4
  [23:1:0.4] Rivers | 0.0002% (smallest) | Last
[23:1:1] - Descending order: **oceans > ice and glaciers > groundwater > rivers** (UPPSC 2025: 1, 3, 4, 2).
[23:1:2] - **Largest fresh-water store = glaciers and ice caps**; of the rest, the **largest = groundwater** (UPSC 2013, asked twice); groundwater far exceeds lakes and rivers, and **ice caps hold more than groundwater** (UPSC 2021: statement 2 only).
[23:1:3] - Fresh water = about 2.5–3%; usable fresh water under 1%. The **total amount of water on Earth is constant** (water cycle); it is not vanishing and the oceans are not getting saltier because they are drying.
[23:1:4] - **2003** = UN International Year of Freshwater.
[23:1:5] ~~ Sources: NCERT Fundamentals ch.12 (OnlyIAS Physical Geography 08 p.16–17); USGS Water Science School; UN General Assembly res. 55/196 (2003); app notes 4:23 sub 0
## SUB 2 | Density, Clines and Water's Anomalous Behaviour
[23:2:0] - Water is **densest at 4°C**: a lake freezes at the **top** while the bottom stays liquid at about 4°C (UPSC 2011: density maximum at 4°C).
[23:2:1] - **Density of sea water rises** as **temperature falls**, **salinity rises**, and **pressure (depth)** increases; colder and saltier water sinks and drives deep currents.
[23:2:2] - **Sea water is denser than fresh water**: swimming is easier in sea water (CDS 2008: A and R true, R explains A); an egg sinks in tap water but **floats in strong salt solution** because the solution is denser than the egg; people float in the Dead Sea.
[23:2:3] TABLE head: Layer | Rapid change with depth in
  [23:2:3.0] Thermocline | Temperature
  [23:2:3.1] Halocline | Salinity (salinity gradient; asked twice)
  [23:2:3.2] Pycnocline | Density; drives deep circulation
  [23:2:3.3] Chemocline | Chemistry; Black Sea (layers rarely mix)
[23:2:4] - Every cline is a **barrier to vertical mixing**.
[23:2:5] ~~ Sources: Rocket General Geography p.62; NCERT Fundamentals ch.12 (OnlyIAS Physical Geography 08 p.24); app notes 4:23 sub 0, 6
## SUB 3 | Temperature of Ocean Water
[23:3:0] - Oceans are **store-houses** of solar energy: they heat and cool slowly and absorb **over 90%** of the excess heat of global warming, and about a quarter of human CO2 (ocean **pH ~8.1** and falling).
[23:3:1] - **Horizontal**: falls from equator to poles (about 0.5°C per degree of latitude); highest just north of the equator; **NH oceans warmer** (more land; averages 19°C vs 16°C).
[23:3:2] - **Tropics: western side warmer** (trade winds pile warm water west); **temperate zone: eastern side warmer** (westerlies, North Atlantic Drift) – UPSC 2021: **both statements correct**.
[23:3:3] - **Annual range smaller in the Pacific** than the Atlantic (vast) and **greater in the Northern Hemisphere** than the Southern (UPSC 2007: only II).
[23:3:4] - **Vertical, three layers**: warm surface layer (about **500 m**, 20–25°C) → **thermocline** (**500–1,000 m**, rapid fall) → cold deep layer (**0–4°C**); about 90% of ocean water lies below the thermocline.
[23:3:5] - **Blue colour of sea water** = water absorbs red light and **scatters** blue (molecular scattering, C.V. Raman 1921), not interference.
[23:3:6] - **2025**: record ocean heat content; about **90%** of the ocean surface saw marine heatwaves (WMO). **AP**: NIOT's station at **Nellore** runs **OMNI buoys** (temperature, salinity, currents).
[23:3:7] ~~ Sources: NCERT Fundamentals ch.12 (OnlyIAS Physical Geography 08 p.20–22); Rocket General Geography p.62; Nobel Prize Physics 1930 citation (Raman); WMO State of the Climate 2025; app notes 4:23 sub 5, 7

=== NOTES 4:25 | Ocean-atmosphere Interaction – El Nino, La Nina, Enso, Iod, Walker Circulation
## SUB 0 | El Nino – Meaning, Mechanism and Effects
[25:0:0] # What El Nino is (asked 9 times)
[25:0:1] - **El Nino** = an **abnormally warm ocean current** that appears off the coast of **Peru and Ecuador** in the **eastern (and central) tropical Pacific** and flows south along the west coast of South America, **replacing the cold Peruvian (Humboldt) current**. It is an **ocean** event, not an air mass, a wind or a low-pressure centre (CDS 2011).
[25:0:2] - **Ocean:** El Nino develops only in the **Pacific Ocean** – not in the Indian Ocean, Bay of Bengal, Atlantic or Mediterranean.
[25:0:3] - **Name:** Spanish for **"the little boy / Christ child"**, because it appears around **Christmas (December)**.
[25:0:4] - **Recurrence:** **irregular**, about every **3–7 years** (2–7 in some books); it does **not occur every year** (MPPSC 2024 wrong statement).
[25:0:5] - The El Nino current carries **warmer, less saline** water (the warm, rain-freshened pool of the western Pacific spreads east) – NDA 2010 "all four" statements.
[25:0:6] - **Atmospheric counterpart = the Southern Oscillation**; together they are **ENSO**.
[25:0:7] # Mechanism
[25:0:8] TABLE head: Step | Normal year | El Nino year
  [25:0:8.0] Pressure | Low over Indonesia / N Australia, high off Peru | Pressure falls over the central/eastern Pacific; a weak high forms in the west
  [25:0:8.1] Trade winds | Strong easterlies push warm water west | Weaken or even reverse
  [25:0:8.2] Peru coast | Cold, nutrient-rich upwelling – rich fishing | Equatorial counter current piles warm water off Peru; thermocline drops; upwelling stops
  [25:0:8.3] Peru sea temperature | Cold | Warms by up to about 10°C
  [25:0:8.4] Plankton and fish | Abundant (anchoveta) | Plankton falls; fish catch collapses – the warm water does not increase plankton (UPPSC 2023: statement 2 false)
[25:0:9] # World effects
[25:0:10] TABLE head: Region | El Nino effect
  [25:0:10.0] Peru, Ecuador, coastal Colombia, N Chile | Heavy rain and flooding of the normally arid coast (APPSC FSO "planetary climatic event")
  [25:0:10.1] Indonesia, northern Australia | Drought, drier
  [25:0:10.2] Central Pacific | Convective storms, hurricanes
  [25:0:10.3] India | Delayed, weak monsoon; drought (e.g. 2014 deficit, about 12% below normal; 2014–16 El Nino droughts)
[25:0:11] - APPSC Group 1: Peru warm current + "Christ child" + 2014 Indian rainfall deficit = **all three correct**.
[25:0:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 06 p.10, p.14 (book p.80, 84); PMF Physical Geography 06 p.49-51 (book p.412-415); ScienceDaily 30 Jan 2003 (NASA, warm fresher western Pacific water); app notes 4:25 sub 0
## SUB 1 | ENSO, La Nina and the Indian Monsoon
[25:1:0] # Southern Oscillation and ENSO
[25:1:1] - **Southern Oscillation** = a **pressure seesaw between the Pacific and Indian Oceans** – **Tahiti (French Polynesia) vs Port Darwin (N Australia)**; first described by **Sir Gilbert Walker (1920s)**.
[25:1:2] - **SOI** = Tahiti minus Darwin pressure. **Positive SOI** (high at Tahiti, low at Darwin) = good Indian monsoon, **La Nina**-like; sustained **negative SOI = El Nino**, bad monsoon.
[25:1:3] - **ENSO** = El Nino + Southern Oscillation; detected and used for **short-term (seasonal) climate prediction** of **weak Indian monsoon** years (UPSC 2002, asked twice).
[25:1:4] - **Monsoon and ENSO are inversely related** (APPSC Fisheries ADF).
[25:1:5] # El Nino vs La Nina
[25:1:6] TABLE head: Feature | El Nino | La Nina
  [25:1:6.0] Central/east Pacific sea temperature | Warmer | Cooler (strong upwelling)
  [25:1:6.1] Trade winds | Weak / reversed | Stronger than usual
  [25:1:6.2] Walker circulation | Weakens, shifts east | Strengthens
  [25:1:6.3] Indian monsoon | Weak, below normal – drought | Normal to above normal – good rain
  [25:1:6.4] North India winter | – | Colder, frequent cold waves (e.g. January 2012)
  [25:1:6.5] Bay of Bengal | Fewer post-monsoon cyclones (INCOIS study) | More floods, severe cyclones
  [25:1:6.6] Australia / Indonesia | Drier | Heavy rain, floods (2010–11 Australian floods)
[25:1:7] - **La Nina** is a cooling of the **central/eastern equatorial Pacific** – **not the Indian Ocean** – and it **does affect** the monsoon (favourably). So both statements of UPSC 2011 are **wrong**.
[25:1:8] - Over India, El Nino = harbinger of drought; **La Nina brings rain** (APPSC Group 1). A **positive IOD** can also offset El Nino, but the Pacific opposite of El Nino is La Nina.
[25:1:9] - Factor affecting India's climate among El Nino, Gulf Stream, western intensification, North Atlantic Oscillation = **El Nino**.
[25:1:10] - Not every El Nino year is a drought year: about **6 of 10** El Nino years brought depressed Indian rainfall; 1997–98 strong El Nino, no drought (positive IOD); moderate 2002 El Nino, severe drought.
[25:1:11] - El Nino and La Nina are **climate patterns, not storms**. Last global El Nino: **2023–24**; **2025** = warmest La Nina year on record.
[25:1:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 06 p.14 (book p.84); PMF Physical Geography 06 p.49, 51 (book p.413, 415); Rocket General Geography p.54; app notes 4:25 sub 1, 4
## SUB 2 | Walker Circulation, El Nino Types and ENSO Monitoring
[25:2:0] # Walker circulation (normal year)
[25:2:1] - East–west (zonal) loop over the tropical Pacific: air **rises over the warm western Pacific / Indonesia**, flows east aloft, **sinks over the cool eastern Pacific**; surface **easterly trade winds** return west. Driven by **high pressure over the eastern Pacific and low over Indonesia**; linked to the Peru upwelling.
[25:2:2] - El Nino **weakens** (sometimes reverses) the Walker cell and shifts it east; La Nina strengthens it.
[25:2:3] - **Bjerknes feedback:** weaker trades → warm water shifts east → winds weaken further → air sinks over the Indian Ocean (high pressure) → **late or weak Indian monsoon**.
[25:2:4] # Types of El Nino
[25:2:5] TABLE head: Type | Maximum warming
  [25:2:5.0] Canonical (conventional) | Eastern Pacific, near Peru
  [25:2:5.1] El Nino Modoki (Japanese: "similar but different") | Central Pacific, with cooler water on both the eastern and western sides (two-cell Walker circulation)
[25:2:6] # Monitoring and 2026 outlook
[25:2:7] - **Nino 3.4 region:** **5°N–5°S, 120°W–170°W** (central equatorial Pacific).
[25:2:8] - **NOAA:** El Nino when the **Oceanic Nino Index** (3-month SST anomaly in Nino 3.4) is **≥ +0.5°C** for **5 consecutive overlapping seasons**. IOD is measured by the **Dipole Mode Index (DMI)**.
[25:2:9] - **IMD, 13 April 2026:** southwest monsoon forecast **92% of LPA (±5%)** – below normal – as **El Nino** was expected to develop during the season (LPA 87 cm).
[25:2:10] ~~ Sources: PMF Physical Geography 06 p.48-50 (book p.412-414); newsonair.gov.in, "IMD forecasts below normal southwest monsoon rainfall this year" (13 Apr 2026); app notes 4:25 sub 2, 3, 5
## SUB 3 | Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) and Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO)
[25:3:0] # Indian Ocean Dipole ("Indian Nino")
[25:3:1] - **IOD** = difference in **sea-surface temperature** between **two poles of the tropical Indian Ocean**: a **western pole (Arabian Sea / off Africa)** and an **eastern pole (south of Indonesia)** – **not the eastern Pacific** (UPSC 2017 statement 1 false).
[25:3:2] - Identified in **1999** (Saji et al., IISc); develops from about April, peaks in October; atmospheric part = **EQUINOO**.
[25:3:3] TABLE head: IOD phase | West (Arabian Sea) | East (south of Indonesia) | India
  [25:3:3.0] Positive | Warmer | Cooler, dry | More monsoon rain; can offset El Nino (1983, 1994, 1997); more Arabian Sea cyclones
  [25:3:3.1] Negative | Cooler | Warmer, rainy | Reduced rainfall; more Bay of Bengal cyclones
[25:3:4] - **An IOD can influence an El Nino's impact on the monsoon** (UPSC 2017 statement 2 true → answer **2 only**). In **1997** a strong **positive IOD** saved India from drought despite a **Super El Nino**.
[25:3:5] - The IOD is a separate Indian Ocean mode that **runs independently of ENSO** but interacts with it; positive IOD events often develop in El Nino years. (NextGen's notes pair the positive phase with La Nina – PMF and Rocket give the effect on India as above.)
[25:3:6] # Madden-Julian Oscillation
[25:3:7] - Identified by **Roland Madden and Paul Julian (1971–72)**: an **eastward**-moving pulse of clouds and rain that starts over the warm **tropical Indian Ocean** and fades in the eastern Pacific.
[25:3:8] - Recurs every **30–60 days**; convection up to about 10 km; causes **active and break spells** of the monsoon.
[25:3:9] ~~ Sources: PMF Physical Geography 06 p.51-52 (book p.415-416); NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 06 p.11, 07 p.1 (book p.81, 85); Rocket General Geography p.54; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Ocean_Dipole (Saji et al. 1999, Nature); app notes 4:25 sub 6, 7

=== NOTES 4:26 | Biological Characteristics of Oceans – Marine Ecosystems, Coral Reefs, Bleaching, Upwelling
## SUB 0 | Coral Reef Places – World and India
[26:0:0] # Great Barrier Reef (asked 9 times)
[26:0:1] - **World's largest coral reef system** and largest structure built by living organisms: off **Queensland, north-eastern Australia**, in the **Coral Sea (Pacific Ocean)** – not New Zealand, Finland, Greenland or Ireland.
[26:0:2] - Length about **2,300 km** (PMF; G.C. Leong gives 1,200 miles) – so "more than 2,500 km" is **false** (UPRO/ARO 2023: only statement 1). Over **2,900 reefs**; dugong and green turtle habitat; **UNESCO World Heritage Site 1981**.
[26:0:3] - APPSC Group 1 2004: became the world's biggest protected marine sanctuary (July 2004). Next largest system: **Mesoamerican Barrier Reef**.
[26:0:4] # World distribution
[26:0:5] - **Most reefs lie in tropical waters** (between the **Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn**, mostly 25°N–25°S, up to 30°); **more than one-third** are in **Australia, Indonesia and the Philippines**; reefs host **far more animal phyla** than tropical rainforests – all three statements of UPSC 2018 (asked 3 times) are **correct**.
[26:0:6] - Few reefs on the **west coasts** of tropical continents (cold currents, upwelling).
[26:0:7] # India's reefs
[26:0:8] TABLE head: Reef area | Point asked
  [26:0:8.0] Gulf of Mannar (Tamil Nadu) | Known for coral reefs; Marine National Park (1980/86): 21 islets between Rameswaram and Tuticorin (Thoothukudi); Biosphere Reserve 1989 – India's (and South Asia's) first marine BR: islands, estuaries, beaches, seagrass, reefs, salt marshes, mangroves; dugong
  [26:0:8.1] Gulf of Kachchh (Gujarat) | Reefs (northernmost)
  [26:0:8.2] Andaman & Nicobar | Reefs; highest diversity; National Coral Reef Research Institute, Chidiyatapu
  [26:0:8.3] Lakshadweep | Coral islands – built by accumulation of coral reefs; atolls (Shankar also lists Nicobar atolls)
  [26:0:8.4] Malvan (Maharashtra) | Patchy reefs
[26:0:9] - Have reefs: **A&N, Gulf of Kachchh, Gulf of Mannar** – **not the Sundarbans** (mangroves) (UPSC 2014, asked twice).
[26:0:10] - **No reefs: Gulf of Cambay / Khambhat** (silt, freshwater; asked twice), Sundarbans, most of the east coast – **West Bengal, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh**. AP fisheries depend on Bay of Bengal plankton, threatened by marine heatwaves.
[26:0:11] - **Hope Spots** (IUCN-linked **Mission Blue** network of special marine areas) in India: **Lakshadweep and the Andaman & Nicobar Islands**.
[26:0:12] - **Feb 2026:** NGT cleared the **₹92,000-crore Great Nicobar project**, directing the Environment Ministry to **protect and regenerate corals**.
[26:0:13] # Marine protection targets
[26:0:14] TABLE head: Target | Provision
  [26:0:14.0] Aichi Target 11 (CBD, 2011–2020) | 10% of coastal and marine areas by 2020
  [26:0:14.1] 30x30 (Target 3, Kunming-Montreal GBF, COP15, Dec 2022) | 30% of land + 30% of oceans by 2030
[26:0:15] - About **10%** of ocean and coastal areas protected (April 2026); only **2.8%** fully or highly protected.
[26:0:16] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment 05 p.94, 97 (book p.442, 446); PMF Species & PAN 03 p.27, 39 (Gulf of Mannar NP, BR); PMF Environment 03 p.21 (Hope Spots); Shankar Environment ch.4 (shankar-environment-05 p.14); G.C. Leong ch.11 (gc-leong-geography-09.2); Rocket General Geography p.65-66; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Mannar_Marine_National_Park (21 islets, Thoothukudi to Dhanushkodi/Rameswaram); app notes 4:26 sub 6, 9
## SUB 1 | Coral Reefs – Nature, Conditions and Types
[26:1:0] # Nature
[26:1:1] - Built from the **calcium carbonate** skeletons of tiny colonial **coral polyps** (phylum **Cnidaria**); the CaCO3 is **aragonite**. **Oyster shells** too are **calcium carbonate**.
[26:1:2] - **Mutualism with zooxanthellae** (single-celled dinoflagellate algae): the algae photosynthesise and give the coral **food and colour**; the coral gives **shelter and CO2/nutrients**.
[26:1:3] - **"Rainforests of the Sea"** – the marine counterpart of **tropical rain forests** – because of exceptional **species richness**: under **1%** of the ocean floor, over **25%** of marine species.
[26:1:4] - Reefs **break storm waves** and prevent coastal erosion; also nurseries, fisheries, tourism. APPSC Group 1: both statements true, but wave-breaking does **not explain** the epithet.
[26:1:5] - **Biorock (mineral accretion)**: a small electric current on a steel frame precipitates CaCO3 – used to **restore damaged reefs** (ZSI trial, Gulf of Kachchh) (UPSC 2022).
[26:1:6] # Growth conditions
[26:1:7] TABLE head: Condition | Requirement
  [26:1:7.0] Temperature | Not below about 20°C (20–21°C minimum); optimum 23–25°C; tropical seas
  [26:1:7.1] Light | Photic, shallow water – under about 50 m (Leong: not over 180 ft; ideal under 100 ft)
  [26:1:7.2] Water | Clean, sediment-free, normal sea salinity (about 3.5%, not 6%); freshwater and very saline water harm growth
  [26:1:7.3] Avoid | Muddy river mouths, cold currents
[26:1:8] - Astt. Comm. 2017: photic + clean water + 20–21°C = **I, II and IV**; "salinity of 6%" is wrong.
[26:1:9] # Reef types
[26:1:10] TABLE head: Type | Feature | Example
  [26:1:10.0] Fringing | Close to shore; shallow lagoon or none; commonest in India | Andamans, Gulf of Mannar
  [26:1:10.1] Barrier | Parallel to the coast, separated by a wide, deep lagoon | Great Barrier Reef
  [26:1:10.2] Atoll | Ring / horseshoe reef enclosing a lagoon, no central land | Lakshadweep
[26:1:11] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment 05 p.94-95, 97-98 (book p.442-447); G.C. Leong ch.11 (gc-leong-geography-09.2 p.2); Shankar Environment ch.4 (shankar-environment-05 p.13-14); Rocket General Geography p.65-66; app notes 4:26 sub 4, 5
## SUB 2 | Marine Life, Ocean Zones and Productivity
[26:2:0] # Ocean zones
[26:2:1] TABLE head: Zone | Extent / feature
  [26:2:1.0] Littoral / intertidal | Between high- and low-tide marks
  [26:2:1.1] Neritic | From the high-water line over the continental shelf to about 200 m; richest fishing zone
  [26:2:1.2] Photic (euphotic) | Sunlit layer (to about 200 m); photosynthesis
  [26:2:1.3] Epipelagic (sunlit) | Highest share of marine habitats and life
  [26:2:1.4] Disphotic (twilight) | Above the aphotic zone; light too weak for photosynthesis
  [26:2:1.5] Aphotic | Dark; no photosynthesis
  [26:2:1.6] Pelagic / benthic | Open water column / sea floor
  [26:2:1.7] Abyssal, hadal | Deep floor and trenches
[26:2:2] - Marine ecosystems cover about **71%** of Earth's surface; **hydrothermal vents** support **chemosynthetic** life. Rivers and freshwater lakes are **freshwater**, not marine, ecosystems.
[26:2:3] # Organisms and oxygen
[26:2:4] TABLE head: Group | Feature
  [26:2:4.0] Plankton | Drift with water: phytoplankton (plants) + zooplankton (animals)
  [26:2:4.1] Nekton | Swim actively (fish, squid, marine mammals)
  [26:2:4.2] Benthos | Live on or in the bottom
[26:2:5] - **Phytoplankton** (diatoms, dinoflagellates, cyanobacteria) = **main primary producers** of the sea (not seaweeds or marine angiosperms).
[26:2:6] - Marine phytoplankton and photosynthetic bacteria produce **about 50%** of the world's oxygen – **more than rainforests**; air holds **far more oxygen** than even well-oxygenated water (about 25–35 times per litre) – UPSC 2025: **2 only**.
[26:2:7] - If phytoplankton were destroyed: the **carbon sink** and **food chains** would suffer; water density would not change (UPSC 2012: I and II).
[26:2:8] # Upwelling
[26:2:9] - Winds push surface water **offshore** → cold, **nutrient-rich** water rises → plankton boom → rich fisheries. Upwelling raises productivity by bringing **nutrients** to the surface – not decomposers or bottom organisms (UPSC 2011: only II).
[26:2:10] TABLE head: Upwelling zone | Current / fishery
  [26:2:10.0] Peru–Chile | Humboldt – anchoveta; suppressed by El Nino → fisheries fail
  [26:2:10.1] Namibia | Benguela
  [26:2:10.2] Somalia | Findlater jet, SW monsoon
  [26:2:10.3] Kerala / SW India | SW monsoon – oil sardine, mackerel
[26:2:11] # Algal blooms and red tides
[26:2:12] - **Red tide** = bloom of a **pigmented dinoflagellate** that discolours estuarine or coastal water (UPSC 1998).
[26:2:13] - **Harmful algal blooms in Indian seas:** **nutrient discharge from estuaries**, **monsoon land run-off** and **upwelling** (also mud banks) – all three (UPSC 2011). Excess N and P → eutrophication → **dead zones** (Gulf of Mexico – **Mississippi** run-off). **INCOIS** issues algal-bloom and coral-bleaching alerts.
[26:2:14] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment 02 p.40-42 (book p.75-76); PMF Physical Geography 07 (productivity, upwelling); Rocket General Geography p.65; Shankar Environment ch.4 (shankar-environment-05, red tide 4.4.3); app notes 4:26 sub 0-3, 8
## SUB 3 | Coral Bleaching and Ocean Acidification
[26:3:0] # Coral bleaching
[26:3:1] - **Meaning:** stressed polyps **expel (eject) their zooxanthellae** and lose pigment, turning **white**; a bleached coral is **stressed, not necessarily dead** (it can recover if conditions improve).
[26:3:2] - **Most significant cause:** **global warming** – rising sea-surface temperature, **marine heatwaves** (1°C above normal for weeks can trigger it); also UV, turbidity, pollution, salinity change, **extreme low tides**, **ocean acidification**, El Nino – **not** more carbonate, not mining or disease as the main cause.
[26:3:3] TABLE head: Global bleaching event | Period | Note
  [26:3:3.0] 1st | 1998 | Strong El Nino
  [26:3:3.1] 2nd | 2010 | –
  [26:3:3.2] 3rd | 2014–2017 | 68.2% of reef areas
  [26:3:3.3] 4th | 2023 – about mid-2025 | About 84% of reefs, 83 countries (NOAA–ICRI)
[26:3:4] - Every strong El Nino since 1998 came with a global bleaching event; recovery takes **more than 15 years**. GCRMN 2026: major disturbances now every **4–6 years**; **87%** of reefs faced heat stress in 2024. **Andaman** mass bleaching linked to about a **2°C** rise in Indian Ocean temperature.
[26:3:5] # Ocean acidification
[26:3:6] - CO2 + water → **carbonic acid** → bicarbonate + hydrogen (hydronium) ions → **pH falls** (sea water about **8.1**, alkaline) → **carbonate ions fall** → corals, calcareous plankton and shellfish **form shells less easily** (it does not strengthen reefs).
[26:3:7] - Oceans absorb about **30–40%** of human CO2; worst in **cold seas** (higher CO2 solubility). Nicknames: **"evil twin of global warming"**, "the other CO2 problem".
[26:3:8] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment 05 p.93-96 (book p.441-445); NextGen Environment - APPSC Exams 14 p.3, 7-8; Rocket General Geography p.66; app notes 4:26 sub 7, 8
