=== NOTES 4:27 | Hydrological Disasters – Floods, Flash Floods, Cloudbursts, Droughts, Tsunamis, Storm Surges
## SUB 0 | Floods – Extent, Causes and Management
[27:0:0] # Nature and extent (asked 18 times)
[27:0:1] - Flood = overflow of water onto normally dry land when rivers or other water bodies cannot contain it; **rapid-onset**; the **most frequent / most common natural disaster in India**; can be **mitigated through early warning**.
[27:0:2] - **Rashtriya Barh Ayog (National Flood Commission)**, set up **1976**, report **1980**: of India's **329 mha**, **more than 40 mha** (about **12%** of the area) is flood-prone; a recent estimate is about **49 mha**. About **10%** of India's area is actually flood-affected.
[27:0:3] - Worst-affected states: **Assam and Bihar**, then **Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal**; **most flood-prone state: Bihar** (UPPCS 2000). Tamil Nadu floods in Nov–Jan (retreating monsoon).
[27:0:4] - About **200 million** people are exposed to recurring floods every year (APPSC Group 1 2012 key).
[27:0:5] - **Flood control is a State subject**; the Centre helps through **FMBAP** (Flood Management and Border Areas Programme, 2021–26).
[27:0:6] # Causes
[27:0:7] TABLE head: Cause | Effect
  [27:0:7.0] Heavy / prolonged rainfall | Primary cause of riverine flooding in low-lying areas
  [27:0:7.1] Cloudburst | Very intense rain over a small area
  [27:0:7.2] Snowmelt | Sudden rise in river flow
  [27:0:7.3] Siltation (from soil erosion) | Reduces channel depth and capacity
  [27:0:7.4] Embankment breach | Water escapes the channel
  [27:0:7.5] Deforestation | Human factor: increases runoff
  [27:0:7.6] Floodplain encroachment | Raises exposure
  [27:0:7.7] Poor drainage | Water accumulates
  [27:0:7.8] Dam failure | Sudden downstream discharge; overtopping = water spills over the crest
[27:0:8] - Major causes in India = **heavy rainfall, poor drainage, deforestation and dam failure** (not high temperature, windstorms or ocean acidification).
[27:0:9] - A landslide can **block a river**: **Pareechu river (Tibet)**, August **2004** landslide lake – flood threat on the **Sutlej** in Himachal Pradesh.
[27:0:10] # Management
[27:0:11] TABLE head: Structural | Non-structural
  [27:0:11.0] Embankments, dams and reservoirs, channel and drainage improvement, diversion channels | Flood-plain zoning, flood insurance, flood-proofing, forecasting and warning, watershed management
[27:0:12] - **Afforestation** of flood-prone areas / catchments = **flood control (mitigation)** – forests **increase infiltration and interception**; wetlands and floodplains store water; mangroves buffer coasts.
[27:0:13] - **Watershed structures** (check dams, percolation tanks) mitigate both **drought and flood** – not tornadoes or fire.
[27:0:14] - **Forecasting**: **Central Water Commission (CWC)** (Jal Shakti) runs flood forecasting – using **GIS, radar** (Doppler) and **remote sensing / satellite** data (not the Richter or Pascal scale or MRI).
[27:0:15] - In flood response, high-resolution satellite imagery and GIS map the **inundated area**, from which the **number of people affected** and damage are estimated.
[27:0:16] - **Odisha Flood Hazard Atlas**: built from satellite images of historic flood inundation **2001–2018** (Rocket: 2000–2018).
[27:0:17] # Committees and programmes
[27:0:18] TABLE head: Body | Year | Role
  [27:0:18.0] National Flood Control Programme / National Flood Policy | 1954 | Launched after the 1954 floods
  [27:0:18.1] Rashtriya Barh Ayog | 1976 (report 1980) | Assessed about 40 mha flood-prone
  [27:0:18.2] Expert Committee for Scientific Assessment of Flood-Prone Areas | July 2012 | Set up by Ministry of Water Resources, under the CWC Chairman
  [27:0:18.3] NDMA Guidelines | 2008 (floods), 2010 (urban floods) | Policy
[27:0:19] ~~ Sources: Rocket Disaster Management p.27-31; PMF Internal Security & DM 02 p.55-56 (book p.130-131); NCERT summary (OnlyIAS Indian Geography 05) p.25-27; CAG Report No.10 of 2017 ch.6 (Expert Committee, July 2012), via web search; app notes 4:27 sub 2, 3
## SUB 1 | Tsunamis – Meaning, Causes, Behaviour and the 2004 Tsunami
[27:1:0] # Meaning (asked 17 times)
[27:1:1] - **Tsunami** = Japanese word: **"tsu" = harbour + "nami" = wave** ("harbour wave") – **not Latin, Arabic or Hebrew** (UKPSC 2005; CDS 2017 "Latin word" = the wrong statement).
[27:1:2] - A **series of waves** of very long wavelength (over 500 km) and long period (10 minutes to 2 hours) – **not a single wave**; the **first wave is often not the largest**, later waves can be bigger.
[27:1:3] - A **natural disaster**; can strike at **any time of day or night**. **Not a "tidal wave"** – tides (gravity of Moon and Sun) play **no role** in generating it (CDS 2012).
[27:1:4] # Causes
[27:1:5] TABLE head: Cause | Note
  [27:1:5.0] Undersea earthquakes | Main / most common cause – sudden vertical displacement of the sea floor at subduction zones (shocks above about 7.5)
  [27:1:5.1] Submarine or coastal landslides | Displace water
  [27:1:5.2] Volcanic eruptions | E.g. Krakatoa 1883 (about 40 m wave), Anak Krakatau 2018
  [27:1:5.3] Explosions, meteorite (bolide) impacts | Rare
[27:1:6] - **Not caused by hurricanes / cyclones** (they raise **storm surges**) or deserts (CDS 2010, asked twice).
[27:1:7] - Most tsunamis occur in the **Pacific Ocean** (Ring of Fire – Alaska, Japan, Philippines, Indonesia).
[27:1:8] - **Coastal States/UTs** of India are vulnerable to **tsunamis** (not volcanic eruptions).
[27:1:9] # Behaviour
[27:1:10] TABLE head: Deep ocean | Near the coast
  [27:1:10.0] Very long wavelength; height under 1 m ("slight swell" about 30 cm); speed hundreds of km/h (about 700–850 km/h at 4,000–6,000 m depth) | Slows down (speed depends on depth); wavelength shortens, height rises sharply (shoaling) – 15 m or more; on coastal plains it moves at roughly 50 km/h
[27:1:11] - Impact is **less over the open ocean, more near the coast**; ships at sea hardly notice it.
[27:1:12] - **Warning sign: drawdown** – the sea **suddenly recedes** (sea level falls quickly) before the wave hits; also strong quake shaking.
[27:1:13] # 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami
[27:1:14] - **26 December 2004**; **Sumatra-Andaman earthquake, Mw about 9.1** (Indian plate under the Burma plate); speed about 800 km/h, falling to under 70 km/h near shore.
[27:1:15] - Hit **Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Puducherry, Kerala, Andaman & Nicobar** – **not Gujarat**; **worst-hit state Tamil Nadu**, worst district **Nagapattinam**; India: over **12,000 deaths**; Indira Point submerged.
[27:1:16] - **Mangroves** acted as a safety hedge: their **extensive prop roots** (and pneumatophores) are **not uprooted by storms and tides** and absorb wave energy (UPSC 2011). Sand dunes and coastal cliffs also block waves; **open water bodies give no protection**.
[27:1:17] - **Fukushima (Japan), 11 March 2011**: Mw 9.0 Tohoku earthquake + tsunami → nuclear radiation.
[27:1:18] # Risk zones and warning
[27:1:19] TABLE head: Risk | States/UTs
  [27:1:19.0] Very high | Andaman & Nicobar (near the Sunda subduction zone)
  [27:1:19.1] High | Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Puducherry, Odisha
  [27:1:19.2] Moderate | Kerala, Karnataka, Goa, Maharashtra, Gujarat
[27:1:20] - Sources for India: **Sunda-Andaman** subduction zone (east) and the **Makran** zone (west coast).
[27:1:21] - **Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre (ITEWC)** at **INCOIS, Hyderabad** (MoES): detects tsunamigenic quakes within **10 minutes** and can warn **25 Indian Ocean countries**; **NIOT (Nellore)** OMNI buoys feed it. International Tsunami Information Centre: **Honolulu**. World Tsunami Awareness Day: **5 November**.
[27:1:22] > Traps: Japanese (not Latin); tides play no role; hurricanes do not cause tsunamis; the wave slows near the shore; the first wave may not be the largest.
[27:1:23] ~~ Sources: Rocket Disaster Management p.10-13; PMF Internal Security & DM 02 p.53-54 (book p.127-128); PMF Physical Geography 02 p.101-103 (book p.192-194); NCERT summary (OnlyIAS Indian Geography 05) p.20-21; app notes 4:27 sub 7
## SUB 2 | Disasters – Meaning, Classification and Onset
[27:2:0] # Meaning (asked 15 times)
[27:2:1] - **Disaster = Hazard × Vulnerability** (with low capacity to cope); French "desastre" = "bad star".
[27:2:2] - Natural disasters cause most damage in **developing countries**; the **Bhopal gas tragedy** was **man-made**; **India is not disaster-free**; **mangroves reduce cyclone impact** → UPPCS 2018 (asked twice): **1, 2 and 4**.
[27:2:3] - Globally **drought (and famine)** are the **deadliest** weather/climate disasters, followed by **floods** (NCERT); **floods** cause the largest economic losses over the long run and affect the most people.
[27:2:4] # Classification
[27:2:5] TABLE head: Class | Examples
  [27:2:5.0] Geological | Earthquakes, tsunamis, landslides, volcanic eruptions, dam burst, mine fire
  [27:2:5.1] Hydrological / hydro-meteorological | Floods, flash floods, cloudbursts, storm surges, cyclones
  [27:2:5.2] Climatological | Droughts, heatwaves, cold waves
  [27:2:5.3] Biological | Epidemics, pest attacks, food poisoning
  [27:2:5.4] Accident-related (HPC 1999) | Urban/forest fires, road/rail/air accidents, building collapse, mine flooding
  [27:2:5.5] Man-made: chemical, industrial, nuclear | Bhopal gas tragedy, Chernobyl
[27:2:6] - **Drought is not geological** (it is climatological).
[27:2:7] - **Mine flooding** = **accident-related** disaster (not geological or water-and-climate).
[27:2:8] - **Avalanche** = classed as a **hydro-geological** disaster (snow + steep slope) in Indian keys; international (EM-DAT) lists it as hydrological.
[27:2:9] - **Socio-natural hazards** = natural + human factors: floods worsened by deforestation, **landslides due to unscientific construction**.
[27:2:10] - **Man-made hazard**: **fires** (not landslides, avalanches or droughts); **not man-made: mud slides** (natural) – deforestation and food poisoning come from human action.
[27:2:11] - **Chennai floods (2015)** = the most human-induced (wetland and lake encroachment); the Chennai tsunami, Anantapur low rainfall and Kedarnath flood had natural triggers.
[27:2:12] # Onset
[27:2:13] TABLE head: Rapid-onset | Slow-onset
  [27:2:13.0] Cyclone, flood, tsunami, earthquake, flash flood, cloudburst | Drought ("creeping emergency / creeping hazard"), pest infestation, environmental degradation
[27:2:14] ~~ Sources: Rocket Disaster Management p.40, 47-48; NCERT summary (OnlyIAS Indian Geography 05) p.15-17; PMF Internal Security & DM 02 p.42-43 (book p.116-117); UNDRR/ScienceDaily 2016 natural-disaster losses study (via web search); app notes 4:27 sub 0
## SUB 3 | Flash Floods, Cloudbursts and GLOFs
[27:3:0] # Flash floods (asked 10 times)
[27:3:1] - A flood that **occurs suddenly, unexpectedly and for a short duration** – from **local precipitation of high intensity** (intense rain, cloudbursts), or dam / glacial-lake / landslide-lake bursts; little warning time; main danger is **debris**; also landslides.
[27:3:2] - Heavy rain, urban settings or blocked drains are only possible causes – not the definition.
[27:3:3] - Vulnerable: **mountains, steep catchments and urban areas**. **IMD** gives flash-flood guidance for India + **Bangladesh, Bhutan, Nepal**.
[27:3:4] # Cloudburst
[27:3:5] - **Sudden, extremely heavy rainfall for a short period over a small area** (CDS 2012: copious rain lasting a few minutes) – **IMD: at least 100 mm (10 cm) in one hour over about 20–30 sq km**.
[27:3:6] - Localised, with **thunder and lightning**; **mostly in hilly areas** (1,000–2,500 m; orographic lifting); can give **250–300 mm in a couple of hours**; occurs **day or night** → CDS 2017: **I, II and III**.
[27:3:7] - Highly localised → very hard to forecast (Doppler radar, nowcasting). **HKH "monsoon paradox"**: erratic seasonal rain plus more short, intense cloudbursts.
[27:3:8] TABLE head: Region | Areas | Why
  [27:3:8.0] Himalaya | Uttarakhand, HP, J&K, Ladakh, Sikkim | Steep slopes, orographic effect
  [27:3:8.1] Western Ghats | Kerala, Karnataka, Maharashtra | Intense rain on the windward side
  [27:3:8.2] AP Eastern Ghats agency areas | Narrow valleys | Cloudburst flash floods
[27:3:9] # GLOFs and events
[27:3:10] - **GLOF**: glacier retreat enlarges a **proglacial (moraine-dammed) lake**, whose dam bursts. **NDMA GLOF Guidelines (October 2020)**: population risk highest in **Sikkim and Jammu & Kashmir**.
[27:3:11] TABLE head: Event | Year | Note
  [27:3:11.0] Leh cloudburst | 2010 | Ladakh
  [27:3:11.1] Kedarnath | June 2013 | Cloudburst + GLOF; Chorabari (Chaurabari) Glacier in Uttarakhand, north of the temple; lake Gandhi Sarovar
  [27:3:11.2] Operation Phuktal | 2015 | Army + NDMA blasted a landslide-debris lake on the Phuktal river (Zanskar, Kargil) to prevent flash floods
  [27:3:11.3] Chamoli glacier burst | 2021 | Uttarakhand
  [27:3:11.4] South Lhonak GLOF | Oct 2023 | Sikkim (Teesta III dam)
  [27:3:11.5] HP flash floods | 2023 | Unregulated slope construction
  [27:3:11.6] Mandi (HP) | 2025 | Nearly 20 times normal rain
  [27:3:11.7] Dharali-Harsil (Uttarkashi) | 5 Aug 2025 | Flash flood; ice-patch collapse on the Srikanta glacier (ISRO)
  [27:3:11.8] Nepal GLOF floods | 26 Aug 2026 | 26 GLOFs since the 1970s (UNDP)
[27:3:12] ~~ Sources: Rocket Disaster Management p.45-46; PMF Internal Security & DM 02 p.57-59 (book p.132-134); PMF Indian Physical Geography 01 p.54 (Chorabari, Rudraprayag); NDMA GLOF Guidelines Oct 2020 (nidm.gov.in/PDF/pubs/NDMA/29.pdf, via web search); app notes 4:27 sub 4
## SUB 4 | India's Vulnerability Profile
[27:4:0] # Hazard exposure (asked 8 times)
[27:4:1] TABLE head: Hazard | Exposure | Region
  [27:4:1.0] Earthquake | 58.6% of landmass (moderate to very high intensity; PMF rounds to 59%) | Himalaya, Kutch
  [27:4:1.1] Flood | >40 mha (about 12%) | Brahmaputra-Ganga plains
  [27:4:1.2] Drought | About 68% of cultivable area | Rajasthan, Deccan interior
  [27:4:1.3] Cyclone / tsunami / storm surge | About 5,700 km of the about 7,516 km coastline (about 76%, not 50%) | East coast
  [27:4:1.4] Landslide | About 12.6% of land (about 0.42 million sq km) | Himalaya, Western Ghats (not Thar)
[27:4:2] - APPSC DAO: the **incorrect** statement is "50% of the coastline is prone to cyclones and tsunamis" → **only D**.
[27:4:3] - **27 of 35** (now 36) States/UTs are **disaster-prone** (NIDM / NDMA); some older books give 25.
[27:4:4] - Cyclones affect **13 coastal States/UTs** and **84 coastal districts**.
[27:4:5] - **1980–2010**: **1,43,039** people killed by natural disasters in India (APPSC Group 1 key; UNISDR/EM-DAT figures).
[27:4:6] - **Odisha** (Bay of Bengal coast) faces the **most natural disasters** – cyclones, floods and droughts (UP Lower 2002).
[27:4:7] - India loses about **0.4% of GDP** a year to disasters (1990–2024). **World Risk Index 2025**: India **2nd** most vulnerable, after the **Philippines**.
[27:4:8] - **2025**: about 331 days of climate impacts, **over 4,000 deaths**; heaviest toll in **Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand**.
[27:4:9] # Displacement data (IDMC)
[27:4:10] - **IDMC** (Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre, **Geneva**) publishes the **Global Report on Internal Displacement (GRID)**.
[27:4:11] - APPSC key: India **seventh** worst climate-disaster-hit country (2020 to May 2021, IDMC).
[27:4:12] - **GRID 2025**: India **5.4 million** disaster displacements in **2024**; over **2015–2024** **32.3 million**, **3rd** after China and the Philippines.
[27:4:13] ~~ Sources: PMF Internal Security & DM 02 p.44 (book p.118); Rocket Disaster Management p.22; NIDM IEC material (27 of 35, via web search); app notes 4:27 sub 1
## SUB 5 | Droughts
[27:5:0] # Nature and types (asked 8 times)
[27:5:1] - Prolonged deficiency of rainfall or moisture → water scarcity; **slow-onset**; in India drought is **coterminous with the monsoon** (its failure or delay) – **irregular or delayed monsoons** raise drought chances; >80% of rain falls in under 100 days of the SW monsoon.
[27:5:2] TABLE head: Type | Indicator | Time lag
  [27:5:2.0] Meteorological | Prolonged inadequate rainfall, maldistributed over time and space; rain ≥ 25% below LPA (degree of dryness + length of dry period) | Immediate
  [27:5:2.1] Agricultural | Soil-moisture deficit → crop failure | Intermediate
  [27:5:2.2] Hydrological | Fall in reservoirs, rivers, aquifers | Weeks to months
  [27:5:2.3] Socio-economic | Demand exceeds supply; water/food shortage hits livelihoods and markets | Long-term
  [27:5:2.4] Ecological | Ecosystem productivity collapses | —
[27:5:3] - **IMD**: deficiency **26–50%** of LPA = **moderate**; **over 50%** = **severe** drought (no separate "extreme" category).
[27:5:4] # Local names of drought (NCERT)
[27:5:5] TABLE head: Scarcity | Name
  [27:5:5.0] Food grains | Akal
  [27:5:5.1] Fodder | Trinkal
  [27:5:5.2] Water | Jalkal
  [27:5:5.3] All three | Trikal (most devastating)
[27:5:6] # Triggers, consequences, regions
[27:5:7] - Triggers: delayed/erratic monsoon, breaks, heat and evaporation; **El Nino**. Normal SW-monsoon rain **868.6 mm** (1971–2020).
[27:5:8] - Long-term consequences of recurrent drought: **groundwater depletion, land degradation, desertification, distress (rural) migration**, debt, lower farm output.
[27:5:9] - Drought is a **recurrent** hazard that can **regularly affect all regions** of India (APPSC key); 68% of cultivable area is vulnerable.
[27:5:10] - Regions: **Western Rajasthan, Kutch-Saurashtra, Marathwada-Vidarbha, interior Karnataka, Rayalaseema (AP)** – not Lower Assam. **Rayalaseema**: **deep borewells** worsen groundwater loss.
[27:5:11] - Management: NDMA Guidelines 2010; Manual for Drought Management 2016 (Agriculture); nodal ministry **Agriculture**.
[27:5:12] ~~ Sources: Rocket Disaster Management p.22-23; NCERT summary (OnlyIAS Indian Geography 05) p.27-28; PMF Internal Security & DM 02 p.64 (book p.136); NCERT India Physical Environment ch.7 (jalkal, trikal – general knowledge, not checked); app notes 4:27 sub 6
## SUB 6 | Urban Floods and Major Floods
[27:6:0] # Urban flooding
[27:6:1] - Causes: intense rain, cloudbursts, cyclone rain; **encroached drains and lakes**, **wetland destruction**, impervious surfaces, **floodplain construction**, poor storm drains, **high tides**. **Wetland restoration** reduces it. Nodal ministry: **Housing and Urban Affairs**.
[27:6:2] TABLE head: Flood | Year | Cause
  [27:6:2.0] Mumbai | 26 July 2005 | 944 mm in 24 h; drainage failure
  [27:6:2.1] Bihar (Kosi) | 2008 | Embankment breach
  [27:6:2.2] Chennai | Dec 2015 | Extreme rain; wetland destruction
  [27:6:2.3] Kerala | Aug 2018 | Heavy rain; dam releases
[27:6:3] - **AP**: **Vijayawada – Budameru** rivulet. **AP City Flood Alert (July 2026)**: AI platform (RTGS + APSDMA + IIT Gandhinagar), first in **Vijayawada**.
[27:6:4] # Types of flood
[27:6:5] TABLE head: Type | Cause | Typical impact
  [27:6:5.0] River (riverine) | Discharge exceeds channel capacity | Crop damage, bank erosion
  [27:6:5.1] Flash | Sudden intense rain, cloudbursts | Debris, landslides
  [27:6:5.2] Urban | Rain + poor drainage | Infrastructure collapse
  [27:6:5.3] Coastal | Storm surge, cyclones, high tides | Inundation, salinity intrusion
  [27:6:5.4] GLOF | Proglacial lake burst | Downstream flash flood
  [27:6:5.5] Dam failure | Breach | Downstream flash flooding
[27:6:6] ~~ Sources: Rocket Disaster Management p.28-29; PMF Internal Security & DM 02 p.56-57 (book p.131-132); app notes 4:27 sub 0, 2, 5
## SUB 7 | Storm Surges and the Coastline
[27:7:0] - **Storm surge** = abnormal sea rise pushed by **cyclone winds and low pressure**; a **high tide** raises the baseline; **sea-level rise** worsens surge flooding (more, not less, exposure); heavy coastal rain causes drainage congestion; brings **salinity**.
[27:7:1] - **East coast** gets far more cyclones than the west (Bay of Bengal : Arabian Sea about 4 : 1).
[27:7:2] - Coastal defence: **mangroves, shelter belts, dune stabilisation, seawalls**.
[27:7:3] - **Coastline remeasured (2023–24)** by the **National Hydrographic Office with the Survey of India**, reported Dec 2024: **11,098.81 km**; **Gujarat** 1st (2,340.62 km), Tamil Nadu 2nd, **Andhra Pradesh 3rd (1,053.07 km)**.
[27:7:4] - **AP pattern**: coastal belt – cyclones and storm surges; deltas – floods; **Rayalaseema – drought**.
[27:7:5] ~~ Sources: NCERT summary (OnlyIAS Indian Geography 05) p.24; Rocket Disaster Management p.35; app notes 4:27 sub 8
## SUB 8 | Related Hazards – Landslides, Avalanches, Nodal Ministries and Major Disasters
[27:8:0] # Landslides
[27:8:1] - **Mass movement of rocks, debris or earth down mountain slopes or riverbanks** under gravity; both **geological and hydro-meteorological**; **prolonged rainfall** is the main trigger. About **12.6%** of land landslide-prone.
[27:8:2] - Zones: Himalaya; **Western Ghats** (the other major zone); NE Himalaya (**jhum cultivation**); Eastern Ghats – **Araku region** (AP). Rising frequency: **unregulated construction on unstable slopes**, road widening.
[27:8:3] - **GSI** = nodal agency; **National Landslide Forecasting Centre**; **NDMA Guidelines 2009** (landslides and snow avalanches); **National Landslide Risk Management Strategy 2019**; nodal ministry **Mines**. **Wayanad (Kerala) 2024** = landslide.
[27:8:4] # Avalanches
[27:8:5] TABLE head: Type | Feature
  [27:8:5.0] Slab | Large cohesive slab breaks off – most dangerous
  [27:8:5.1] Loose snow (sluff) | Small dry slide
  [27:8:5.2] Ice | Ice masses from glaciers
  [27:8:5.3] Rock/debris | Rock, soil and snow
[27:8:6] - **Rapid flow of snow, ice and debris down a mountain slope**; slopes **30°–45°**; human triggers: **skiing, mountaineering**, explosives. **J&K most affected**; **Lahaul-Spiti, Kinnaur – Himachal Pradesh**.
[27:8:7] - Nodal **Ministry of Defence**; **DGRE** (earlier **SASE**, DRDO) issues **daily winter bulletins**; **BRO** builds roads and protection structures. NDMA guidelines: **structural** (snow nets, bridges, galleries) **and non-structural** (**hazard zonation**) measures.
[27:8:8] - **Mana avalanche (28 Feb 2025)**: BRO camp near **Mana** village (Badrinath); 54 workers, 46 rescued, **8 died**.
[27:8:9] # Nodal ministries
[27:8:10] TABLE head: Hazard | Nodal ministry
  [27:8:10.0] Earthquake, cyclone, tsunami | Earth Sciences
  [27:8:10.1] Flood, GLOF | Jal Shakti
  [27:8:10.2] Urban flood | Housing and Urban Affairs
  [27:8:10.3] Drought, hailstorm, pest attack | Agriculture
  [27:8:10.4] Landslide | Mines
  [27:8:10.5] Avalanche | Defence
  [27:8:10.6] Forest fire; industrial and chemical | Environment, Forest and Climate Change
  [27:8:10.7] Rail accidents | Railways (road – Road Transport)
  [27:8:10.8] Oil spills | Defence (Coast Guard)
[27:8:11] - **Aug 2026**: **heatwaves and lightning** added – notified disasters **12 → 14** (2026–31) on the **16th Finance Commission**'s recommendation. Earthquake indoors: **"Drop, cover and hold on"**.
[27:8:12] # Major disasters
[27:8:13] TABLE head: Disaster | Date | Note
  [27:8:13.0] Bhopal gas leak | 2–3 Dec 1984 | Methyl isocyanate, Union Carbide pesticide plant
  [27:8:13.1] Chernobyl | 26 Apr 1986 | Ukraine (then USSR)
  [27:8:13.2] Latur (Killari) earthquake | 30 Sep 1993 | Maharashtra
  [27:8:13.3] Odisha super cyclone | Oct 1999 | Near Paradip
  [27:8:13.4] Bhuj earthquake | 26 Jan 2001 | Kutch, Gujarat
  [27:8:13.5] Fukushima Daiichi | 11 Mar 2011 | Earthquake + tsunami
  [27:8:13.6] Bhola cyclone | 1970 | Bangladesh (then East Pakistan)
  [27:8:13.7] Yellow River flood / Crete tsunami / Tohoku | 1931 / 365 CE / 2011 | China / Greece / Japan
[27:8:14] - Nuclear hazards: plant accidents + **improper disposal of radioactive waste**. **NIDM Southern Campus, Kondapalli (AP)**: **safety audits for chemical corridors and port clusters**.
[27:8:15] ~~ Sources: Rocket Disaster Management p.19-20, 41-44, 63, 66-67; PMF Internal Security & DM 02 p.59-60 (book p.134-135); app notes 4:27 sub 9, 10, 11

=== NOTES 4:28 | Disaster Management Framework – Dm Act 2005, Ndma, Ndrf, Early Warning Systems
## SUB 0 | Disaster Management Cycle – Phases and Measures
[28:0:0] # Phases (asked about 45 times)
[28:0:1] TABLE head: Phase | Stage | Measures
  [28:0:1.0] Prevention | Pre-disaster | Proactive, long-term; stops a hazard becoming a disaster: land-use zoning, regulating deforestation, control of industrial siting
  [28:0:1.1] Mitigation | Pre-disaster | Reduces the damaging effects / risk (lowers the likelihood of a disaster); most cost-effective phase: quake-resistant buildings, building codes, embankments, afforestation, insurance, hazard maps, retrofitting; vulnerability analysis and risk assessment
  [28:0:1.2] Preparedness | Pre-disaster | "First and critical step": early warning (CAP-SACHET), public education on evacuation routes, mock / evacuation drills (practise escape routes), stockpiling food, water and supplies, Aapda Mitra, Emergency Operation Centres, contingency plans
  [28:0:1.3] Response | During / just after | Time-critical: search and rescue (the major post-disaster operation), evacuation, first aid, temporary shelter, food and water, law and order
  [28:0:1.4] Relief | During / post | Providing food, shelter and medical help to victims
  [28:0:1.5] Recovery (rehabilitation + reconstruction) | Post-disaster | Rebuilding infrastructure and restoring normalcy – restore the area to its pre-disaster state, livelihoods, compensation, psycho-social care, Build Back Better
[28:0:2] - **Four phases** of the DM cycle (generally **4**): **Mitigation, Preparedness, Response, Recovery** (Rocket: "Mitigation, Preparation, Response, Recovery"). **Eradication**, rescue-only or risk-assessment lists are not the cycle.
[28:0:3] - **Stages**: **Pre-disaster = prevention + mitigation + preparedness**; **during = response**; **post-disaster = recovery, rehabilitation, reconstruction**. **Recovery / reconstruction are NOT pre-disaster**; **prevention and mitigation are NOT post-disaster**.
[28:0:4] - After a disaster the phases are **sequential and sometimes simultaneous**; the cycle is **continuous** – lessons from recovery feed prevention.
[28:0:5] - Sequences: during – early warning → evacuation → rescue → shelters → emergency medical / water; after – **relief → restoration → reconstruction → resilient rebuilding**.
[28:0:6] - DM needs a **proactive strategy** (not reactive); its main aim is **saving lives and reducing damage**; a contingency plan for people should be in **simple language with basic information and steps**.
[28:0:7] # Mitigation – types and examples
[28:0:8] TABLE head: Strategy | Example / meaning
  [28:0:8.0] Structural mitigation | Seismic-resistant buildings, flood barriers, embankments, cyclone shelters; earthquakes – building codes; cyclones – planting trees along the coast
  [28:0:8.1] Non-structural mitigation | Public awareness campaigns / public education, community awareness, early warning, land-use rules
  [28:0:8.2] Early warning system | Tsunami detection buoys; a crucial component of mitigation because it gives timely information for preparedness and response (A and R true, R explains A)
  [28:0:8.3] Seismic retrofitting | Strengthening existing (old) buildings to withstand earthquakes
  [28:0:8.4] Floodplain zoning | Regulating land use to restrict construction in flood-prone areas
  [28:0:8.5] Afforestation | Planting trees to reduce landslide and flood risk
  [28:0:8.6] Disaster-resistant design | Materials and techniques that minimise damage
[28:0:9] - Mitigation **does not** mean evolving a **single strategy for all disasters**; it gives rapid recovery, fewer deaths and lower financial impact. It involves **community action** (CBDM – involving local people in preparedness and response).
[28:0:10] - Cyclone pre-disaster mitigation: revamp drainage, **conserve wetlands**, cyclone shelters – **removing coastal trees/forests is NOT** mitigation.
[28:0:11] - Educated communities are more likely to **follow land-use rules and early-warning instructions** (education → long-term mitigation).
[28:0:12] - Types of mitigation: **avoidance, minimization, compensatory**; hazard-specific control activity – e.g. **flood levees**.
[28:0:13] - Terms: **HAZOP** study = assessment of the **adequacy of safety measures**; **MAT** = **Mitigation Assessment Team**; **hazard map** = identifies **areas at risk for specific disasters**.
[28:0:14] - **First responder**: the **community**. Urban response = civic bodies + fire brigade + police; the **district administration** has basic responsibility (Collector pivotal).
[28:0:15] - Search and rescue principles (APPSC key): **Search, Find, Rescue**.
[28:0:16] > Traps: mitigation, not prevention, is the phase "reducing likelihood/effects" when prevention is not offered; preparedness = drills, stockpiling, evacuation education; response = during the disaster.
[28:0:17] ~~ Sources: Rocket Disaster Management p.4-6, 31; PMF Internal Security & DM 02 p.43 (book p.116); app notes 4:28 sub 7
[28:0:18] - **Incident Command System (ICS)**: a standard management system for incidents of **all kinds and sizes**; India uses it as the **Incident Response System (IRS)** (NDMA guidelines 2010).
[28:0:19] - Phase definitions (FEMA): **mitigation** – minimising the effects of disaster; **preparedness** – planning how to respond; **response** – efforts to minimise the hazards created by a disaster; **recovery** – returning the community to normal.
## SUB 1 | Disaster Management Act, 2005 and the Authorities
[28:1:0] # The Act (asked about 25 times)
[28:1:1] - **Act No. 53 of 2005**; **Presidential assent 23 December 2005** (= "passed / enacted" date in exams); published in the **Gazette of India on 26 December 2005**; in force progressively from 2006; **11 Chapters, 79 Sections**; whole of India.
[28:1:2] - Enacted after the **2004 Indian Ocean tsunami**; gives the legal and institutional framework at national, state and district levels.
[28:1:3] - s.2(d) **disaster** = catastrophe, mishap, calamity or grave occurrence from natural or man-made causes, accident or negligence, **beyond the coping capacity of the community of the affected area**. Mitigation = measures to **reduce the risk, impact or effects** of a disaster.
[28:1:4] # Key Sections and Chapters
[28:1:5] TABLE head: Section | Provides for
  [28:1:5.0] 3 (Chapter II) | NDMA
  [28:1:5.1] 8 | National Executive Committee (NEC)
  [28:1:5.2] 14 (Chapter III) | SDMA – s.14(1): "every State Government shall … establish" it (books and keys: "Governor establishes", i.e. in the Governor's name)
  [28:1:5.3] 25 (Chapter IV) | DDMA
  [28:1:5.4] 35 / 37 | Hazard-specific plans of Union ministries / Ministry DM Plans
  [28:1:5.5] 42 | NIDM (statutory)
  [28:1:5.6] 44 | National Disaster Response Force (specialised response to natural and man-made disasters)
  [28:1:5.7] 46 | National Disaster Response Fund
  [28:1:5.8] 47 | National Disaster Mitigation Fund
  [28:1:5.9] 48 | State Disaster Response Fund (s.48(1)(a))
[28:1:6] - "**NDRF**" = both the **Force (s.44)** and the **Fund (s.46)**; the Act's force is the **National Disaster Response Force** (not "Relief Force").
[28:1:7] # Authorities – who heads what
[28:1:8] TABLE head: Body | Head | Note
  [28:1:8.0] NDMA | Prime Minister (ex officio) | Apex policy body under MHA; max 9 members incl. Vice-Chairperson; set up by executive order 30 May 2005, notified under the Act 27 September 2006
  [28:1:8.1] NEC | Union Home Secretary | Prepares the National Plan
  [28:1:8.2] SDMA | Chief Minister | Apex statutory state body: state policy, approves State Plan, coordinates with NDMA and DDMAs
  [28:1:8.3] SEC | Chief Secretary | Runs the SDRF
  [28:1:8.4] DDMA | Collector / District Magistrate / Deputy Commissioner ("any of them") | Elected local head (Zilla Parishad chair) = co-chairperson
  [28:1:8.5] NCMC | Cabinet Secretary | Highest coordination body in major crises; statutory since 2025
  [28:1:8.6] State Crisis Management Committee | Chief Secretary | —
  [28:1:8.7] High Level Committee | Union Home Minister | Approves aid from national funds (does not prepare the National Plan)
  [28:1:8.8] Cabinet Committee on Security | Prime Minister | Nuclear, biological, chemical emergencies
  [28:1:8.9] Cabinet Committee on Natural Calamities | — | Takes important policy decisions
  [28:1:8.10] National Advisory Committee | Under NDMA | Expert advice
  [28:1:8.11] NPDRR | Union Home Minister | Multi-stakeholder DRR platform
  [28:1:8.12] Crisis Management Group (nuclear) | Department of Atomic Energy | —
[28:1:9] - **NDMA and NIDM**: NDMA (PM) = national policy and coordination; NIDM = apex national institute for **training, capacity building and research** under NDMA's guidelines.
[28:1:10] - **NCMC** (natural calamities): Cabinet Secretary with Secretaries of ministries concerned with relief (Home, Agriculture, Defence, Health, Rural Development …); the **Secretary, Department of Atomic Energy is not a member** (APPSC key).
[28:1:11] - **Chain of command** = the hierarchy of officials and organisations responsible for decisions in a disaster.
[28:1:12] - **Uttarakhand**: first State with a separate **Ministry of Disaster Management**.
[28:1:13] # DM (Amendment) Act, 2025
[28:1:14] - **Urban Disaster Management Authorities (UDMA)** in State capitals and Municipal Corporation cities, **except Delhi and Chandigarh**; headed by the **Municipal Commissioner** (not the Mayor).
[28:1:15] - **Statutory status to NCMC and HLC**; national and state **disaster databases**; definitions of risk, resilience, recovery; aligned with Sendai; unified early warning.
[28:1:16] - **June 2026 – "Resilient India 2047"**: NDMA asks Union ministries for hazard-specific plans (**s.35**) and Ministry DM Plans (**s.37**).

## SUB 3 | Nodal Ministries, Early Warning Agencies and Relief Responsibility
[28:3:0] # Who is responsible (asked about 17 times)
[28:3:1] - **Ministry of Home Affairs** = nodal ministry for disaster management (natural and man-made; since **2002**, shifted from Agriculture after the 2001 Gujarat quake) – **except drought, hailstorm, pest attack (Agriculture) and epidemics (Health)**.
[28:3:2] - **Primary responsibility** for rescue, relief and rehabilitation = **State Government**; the Centre supports with resources, early warning and coordination (also under the National Policy).
[28:3:3] - **Central Relief Commissioner** (MHA) = nodal officer coordinating relief for natural disasters.
[28:3:4] - States follow **State Relief Manuals / Codes** that set each officer's role in natural disasters.
[28:3:5] TABLE head: Disaster | Nodal ministry / department
  [28:3:5.0] Drought, hailstorm, cold wave, pest attack | Ministry of Agriculture (& Farmers Welfare)
  [28:3:5.1] Epidemics / biological | Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
  [28:3:5.2] Flood | Ministry of Jal Shakti; urban flood – Housing and Urban Affairs
  [28:3:5.3] Earthquake, cyclone, tsunami | Ministry of Earth Sciences
  [28:3:5.4] Landslide | Ministry of Mines; avalanche – Defence
  [28:3:5.5] Forest fire, industrial and chemical | MoEFCC
  [28:3:5.6] Nuclear and radiological | Department of Atomic Energy
  [28:3:5.7] Air (civil aviation) accidents | Ministry of Civil Aviation; rail – Railways; road – MoRTH
[28:3:6] # Early warning → agency
[28:3:7] TABLE head: Hazard | Agency | Detail
  [28:3:7.0] Cyclone | IMD (RSMC New Delhi) | Forecasts, tracks, names cyclones; 7 cyclone warning centres incl. Visakhapatnam
  [28:3:7.1] Flood | Central Water Commission (New Delhi) | Scientific flood forecasting began 1958 (then Central Water & Power Commission), first forecasting centre at Delhi on the Yamuna
  [28:3:7.2] Landslide | Geological Survey of India (Kolkata) | Inventory, susceptibility, hazard zonation, Landslide Atlas

[28:4:2] # High Powered Committee (1999)
[28:4:3] - Constituted **August 1999**; first chairman **J.C. Pant**; reported **2001**; theme **"Building a Culture of Prevention"**; first natural disasters only, later man-made too.
[28:4:4] - Identified **31 types of disasters** in **five broad categories**; recommended a **separate Department of DM** in GoI.
[28:4:5] - Levels: **L0 = normal times (normalcy)**, **L1 = district level**, **L2 = State level**, **L3 = national level** (used in NDMP 2016).
[28:4:6] # National Policy (NPDM 2009) and NDMP
[28:4:7] - **NPDM**: approved by the Union Cabinet **22 October 2009** (exam answer for "approved / enforced"); prepared by NDMA under the DM Act; vision **"safe and disaster-resilient India"**; mainstreaming DRR into development, partnership with the **media**, identification and monitoring of risks. **NOT an objective**: "preparedness only after a disaster occurs". Primary responsibility: **State Government**.
[28:4:8] - **NDMP 2016**: India's first national plan, all phases of the cycle, aligned with Sendai; time frames **short 5, medium 10, long 15 years**; revised 2019. Mainstreaming DRR is part of the **PM's 10-Point Agenda** (2016).
[28:4:9] # International frameworks

  [28:4:10.0] IDNDR | 1990s (1990–1999); UNGA res. 44/236 (1989) | UN decade; India set up a DM Cell

  [28:4:10.2] Hyogo Framework | 2005–2015 | Adopted at Kobe, Jan 2005
  [28:4:10.3] Sendai Framework | 2015–2030 | 4 priorities – understanding risk (first), risk governance, investing in DRR, preparedness and "Build Back Better"; 7 global targets
  [28:4:10.4] CDRI | 2019 | Launched by India at the UN Climate Action Summit, New York; secretariat New Delhi
[28:4:11] - **Build Back Better** = the current UN approach to post-disaster recovery and reconstruction.
[28:4:12] - India ranks **second after China** in natural disasters (UNISDR data cited in exams).
[28:4:13] - **Shift in approach**: pre-2005 **3 Rs** (rescue, relief, rehabilitation) – relief-centric, reactive → post-2005 **3 Ps** (**prevention, preparedness, proofing/mitigation**) – holistic, proactive, continuous cycle.

## SUB 5 | NDRF, SDRF and Disaster Funds
[28:5:0] # National Disaster Response Force (asked about 13 times)
[28:5:1] - **NDRF = National Disaster Response Force** (not "Relief / Rescue / Reserve Force"); constituted under **s.44** of the DM Act for specialised response to **natural and man-made disasters (incl. CBRN)**; raised / operational **2006**; **Raising Day 19 January**; world's largest dedicated response force.
[28:5:2] - Under **MHA**; superintendence of **NDMA**; DG from the senior **IPS** cadre; HQ **New Delhi**; motto **"Aapada Seva Sadaiv Sarvatra"**.
[28:5:3] - Battalions: initial **8** → **12** (2018–19 keys; "as of December 2019" = 12) → **16** now; ~1,149 personnel each; **18** search-and-rescue teams per battalion.
[28:5:4] - Parent forces (deputation): **BSF, CRPF, CISF, ITBP, SSB, Assam Rifles** (central paramilitary forces).
[28:5:5] - Skills: **CSSR** (Collapsed Structure Search and Rescue), flood and mountain rescue, medical first response, CBRN; teams placed by **vulnerability profile**.
[28:5:6] - **AP**: **10th Battalion**; regional HQ for **AP, Telangana and Karnataka = Vijayawada**.
[28:5:7] - **Budget estimate 2021-22: ₹1,209 crore** (₹1,209.41 crore; RE ₹1,313 crore).
[28:5:8] - **NDRF Academy**: **Nagpur (2018)**.
[28:5:9] # State Disaster Response Force
[28:5:10] - Raised by States/UTs; first responder for the first 24–48 hours; **trained by NDRF/NDRF Academy**; **battalion** model; drawn from **State Police, Armed Police, Fire Services, Home Guards, Civil Defence**. Not yet in all states → strain on NDRF.
[28:5:11] # Funds
[28:5:12] TABLE head: Fund | Section | Use
  [28:5:12.0] State Disaster Response Fund | 48 | First fund for immediate relief to victims of notified disasters; run by SEC; not for compensation or long-term rebuilding
  [28:5:12.1] National Disaster Response Fund | 46 | Central fund that tops up SDRF in severe calamities
  [28:5:12.2] NDMF / SDMF | 47 | Mitigation (long-term risk reduction), operationalised on the 15th Finance Commission's recommendations; ₹4,645 crore approved for 9 states incl. AP
[28:5:13] - SDRF share (Centre : State): general **75:25**, NE/Himalayan **90:10**. **From 1 April 2018** the Centre raised its SDRF contribution **from 75% to 90%** for all states (Sept 2018 decision); later reverted to **75:25** for general states.
[28:5:14] - **14th Finance Commission**: SDRF for **Andhra Pradesh, 2015-20 = ₹2,429 crore** (440 + 462 + 485 + 509 + 534).
[28:5:15] - Up to **10%** of SDRF for **state-specific disasters**. **Finance Commission** recommends; **MHA notifies**.
[28:5:16] - Notified list: cyclone, drought, earthquake, fire, flood, tsunami, hailstorm, landslide, avalanche, cloudburst, **pest attack**, **frost and cold wave**; **Aug 2026**: heatwaves and lightning added (12 → 14, 2026–31, 16th FC).
[28:5:17] - Drought support: **PMFBY** (crop insurance), MGNREGA. AP: ₹277.63 crore (2025-26) released under SDRF/NDRF.
[28:5:18] ~~ Sources: Rocket Disaster Management p.7, 37-38, 49, 54; PMF Internal Security & DM 02 p.47, 49 (book p.120, 122); Fourteenth Finance Commission Report, Annex 10.1 (NITI digital library copy); indiabudget.gov.in Expenditure Budget 2022-23 sbe49 (NDRF line); web search (Centre's SDRF share 90% from 1 April 2018, later 75:25); app notes 4:28 sub 4, 5
## SUB 6 | Key Concepts – Hazard, Disaster, Vulnerability, Types
[28:6:0] # Terms (asked about 10 times)
[28:6:1] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [28:6:1.0] Hazard | Dangerous condition or event with the potential to harm; an earthquake in an uninhabited desert is not a disaster – a hazard / natural event
  [28:6:1.1] Disaster | Occurs when people are unable to cope with the impact of a hazard: Hazard × Vulnerability with low capacity; French "desastre" = bad star
  [28:6:1.2] Vulnerability | Conditions raising susceptibility: limited health care, elderly / disabled residents, poverty, weak housing
  [28:6:1.3] Capacity | Strengths that reduce risk: strong social networks and community cohesion, volunteerism (communities recover better), early warning
  [28:6:1.4] Risk | Likelihood of loss; rises with hazard, exposure, vulnerability; falls with coping capacity
[28:6:2] - **Least** contributor to vulnerability: **strong social networks and community cohesion** (a capacity).
[28:6:3] - Vulnerability types: **physical** (weak houses), **social** (age, gender, caste, disability), **economic** (poverty, daily wage), **environmental** (mangrove loss, deforestation), **systemic/institutional** (weak governance, poor coordination, weak early warning). Community factors: kutcha housing, thin health infrastructure, weak early warning; **high crop-insurance coverage reduces** vulnerability.
[28:6:4] # Types of disasters
[28:6:5] TABLE head: Type | Examples
  [28:6:5.0] Geological | Earthquakes, landslides, tsunamis, volcanoes
  [28:6:5.1] Hydro-meteorological (water and climate) | Cyclones, floods, droughts, cloudbursts, heat waves
  [28:6:5.2] Biological | Epidemics, pest attacks
  [28:6:5.3] Man-made (chemical / industrial, accidents, societal) | Bhopal gas leak (MIC, 2–3 Dec 1984), car accidents, stampedes, fires
[28:6:6] - Four broad emergency types: **natural disasters, environmental emergencies, complex emergencies, pandemic emergencies** – **pandemic emergency** = **sudden onset of contagious disease** that affects health, disrupts services and businesses, with high economic and social cost.
[28:6:7] - Natural disasters cause most damage in **developing countries**; deaths from natural disasters in India 1980–2010: **1,43,039**.
[28:6:8] ~~ Sources: NCERT summary (OnlyIAS Indian Geography 05) p.15-17 (book p.49-50); PMF Internal Security & DM 02 p.42-44 (book p.115-117); Rocket Disaster Management p.40, 47-48, 68; general knowledge (four emergency types); app notes 4:28 sub 0
## SUB 7 | Technology – GIS and Remote Sensing
[28:7:0] # GIS in disaster management
[28:7:1] - **GIS** stores, analyses and presents **spatial data**; maps hazard zones and vulnerable people; in floods it **analyses flood patterns and topography**; it cannot give details of individual victims.
[28:7:2] TABLE head: Phase / hazard | GIS use
  [28:7:2.0] Prevention / mitigation | Hazard zonation, vulnerability and risk mapping
  [28:7:2.1] Preparedness | Evacuation route planning, resource mapping
  [28:7:2.2] Response / recovery | Real-time damage assessment; Build Back Better
  [28:7:2.3] Cyclone | Track monitoring, storm surge modelling
  [28:7:2.4] Landslide | Susceptibility mapping (GSI NLSM)
  [28:7:2.5] Drought | NADAMS
  [28:7:2.6] Tsunami | Inundation modelling (INCOIS)
  [28:7:2.7] Tools | INSAT-3D/3DR track cyclones; NDEM (ISRO) GIS repository; Google Earth Engine – rapid flood mapping from large satellite archives
[28:7:3] - **Landslide Hazard Zonation**: divides hill areas into homogeneous zones by **degree of susceptibility, hazard or risk**.
[28:7:4] ~~ Sources: Rocket Disaster Management p.57-58; app notes 4:28 sub 10
[28:7:5] - **DEM = Digital Elevation Model**: digital terrain/elevation surface used in GIS for flood, inundation and landslide modelling.
## SUB 8 | Andhra Pradesh – APSDMA, Cyclones and Awards
[28:8:0] # APSDMA
[28:8:1] - **APSDMA** = apex statutory DM body of AP, **chaired by the Chief Minister**, constituted in **2007** under the **AP DM Rules 2007** (G.O.Ms.1436, Revenue, 14.11.2007; effective 1 Aug 2007); formulates policy, approves the State Plan, coordinates with NDMA and DDMAs (not an NGO, not under MoEF, covers natural and man-made disasters).
[28:8:2] - Runs the **State Emergency Operations Centre** (Kunchanapalli); alert systems **Vajrapath, Varuna, Red Message**. AP shifted from **relief-centric to mitigation-centric**.
[28:8:3] - Cyclone measures: IMD warnings, cyclone shelters, evacuation, shelter belts, mangroves; about **13–14** Bay of Bengal low-pressure systems a year.
[28:8:4] TABLE head: Cyclone | Year | Landfall
  [28:8:4.0] Hudhud | Oct 2014 | Visakhapatnam
  [28:8:4.1] Titli | Oct 2018 | Near Palasa, Srikakulam
  [28:8:4.2] Michaung | Dec 2023 | Near Bapatla
[28:8:5] # Awards and exercises in the news
[28:8:6] - **SKOCH Award 2018** (disaster management): **Odisha** SDMA (OSDMA).
[28:8:7] - **January 2019**: Coast Guards of India and Japan held disaster-control and SAR exercises off **Yokohama**, Japan.
[28:8:8] - **Prakampana**: super-cyclone exercise at Visakhapatnam by the **Eastern Naval Command**; first forest-fire DM exercise: **Uttarakhand, April 2017**; **Subhash Chandra Bose Aapda Prabandhan Puraskar 2020**: Uttarakhand's Disaster Mitigation & Management Centre.
[28:8:9] - **Tsunami Ready** villages: target **100**; **12 indicators**; renewed every **4 years**. **CBDRR through PRIs**: ₹507.37 crore, **MoPR + NDMA**.
[28:8:10] - **IMD colours**: green all well – yellow be aware – **orange be prepared** – red take action.
[28:8:11] - Safety: earthquake – **Drop, Cover, Hold**; cyclone – go to a shelter, **never stand under trees**; flood – higher ground, avoid flowing water; tsunami – **sudden sea recession** → move inland/uphill.
[28:8:12] ~~ Sources: Rocket Disaster Management p.8, 36, 53; web search (AP DM Rules 2007, G.O.Ms.1436; OSDMA SKOCH 2018 – Business Standard/GKToday; ICG–JCG exercise Yokohama 23 Jan 2019 – ANI/Siasat); app notes 4:28 sub 8, 11
[28:8:13] - **2nd BIMSTEC DMEx-2020** (11-13 Feb 2020, NDRF nodal): inaugurated at **Bhubaneswar**, field exercise at Puri (Odisha); the 1st (2017) was in New Delhi-NCR.
[28:8:14] - **Lightning:** **do not stand under trees** or in open fields; go indoors or crouch low; alerts via the **Damini** (IMD) and AP **Vajrapath** apps.
[28:8:15] - **Vajrapath** (July 2017): APSDMA **lightning** alert app built with **ISRO**, warns about **45 minutes** ahead.
[28:8:16] - **Earthquake indoors:** take cover **under a strong table** (Drop, Cover, Hold); keep away from **windows, balconies and staircases**.

=== NOTES 4:29 | Marine Resources – Fisheries, Minerals, Polymetallic Nodules, Eez, Blue Economy
## SUB 0 | Indian Fisheries – Blue Revolution, National Fish, Fisheries Days
[29:0:0] # Blue Revolution (asked 3 times)
[29:0:1] - **Blue Revolution = fisheries / fish production / aquaculture** (APPSC Sociology 2002 "Aquaculture"; UPUDA 2010 and UKPSC 2006 "Fisheries / Fishing") – not agriculture, irrigation, dairy (**White**), silk, poultry, bees or iron and steel.
[29:0:2] TABLE head: Revolution | Sector
  [29:0:2.0] Green | Food grains
  [29:0:2.1] White | Milk / dairy
  [29:0:2.2] Blue | Fish / fisheries / aquaculture
  [29:0:2.3] Yellow | Oilseeds
  [29:0:2.4] Golden | Horticulture, honey
  [29:0:2.5] Black | Petroleum
  [29:0:2.6] Red | Meat, tomato
[29:0:3] - Flagship scheme: **PMMSY (2020)** – Ministry of **Fisheries, Animal Husbandry & Dairying**; subsidy **40%** general, **60%** women / SC / ST.
[29:0:4] # National fish and national aquatic animal (asked 2 times)
[29:0:5] - **National fish = Indian Mackerel** (bangda) – the answer books and APPSC keys give (APPSC Group 2 2019; APPSC Mains 2018) – not Pomfret, Hilsa or Rohu. It was **never formally notified**; Golden Mahseer is sometimes cited but is a **state fish** (Arunachal, Uttarakhand, Himachal …).
[29:0:6] - **National aquatic animal = Gangetic river dolphin** (declared **2009**).
[29:0:7] # Fisheries days (asked 2 times)
[29:0:8] TABLE head: Day | Date | Why
  [29:0:8.0] World Fisheries Day | 21 November | Global day of fishing communities
  [29:0:8.1] National Fish Farmers' Day | 10 July | Induced breeding of carps, 10 July 1957, by Dr Hiralal Chaudhuri and Dr K.H. Alikunhi
[29:0:9] # India's fish economy
[29:0:10] - India = **2nd** fish producer after **China** (~8–9% of world output); **inland fisheries >75%** of production; seafood exports **₹62,408 crore (FY 2024-25)**, led by **frozen shrimp**.
[29:0:11] TABLE head: Waters | Rule
  [29:0:11.0] 0–12 nm | State subject; annual 61-day ban on mechanised fishing
  [29:0:11.1] 12–200 nm (EEZ) | Centre; EEZ Rules 2025 – Access Pass for vessels ≥24 m via ReALCraft, zero fee; traditional crafts exempt
[29:0:12] > Blue Revolution is never dairy (White) or oilseeds (Yellow); national fish ≠ national aquatic animal.
[29:0:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Indian Geography p.53 (revolutions); Praveen CA360 July 2026 one-liners p.25 (Fish Farmers' Day); Daily CA 26 Oct 2026 p.4 (World Fisheries Day); PMF Environment 03 p.98 (Gangetic dolphin); web: Assam Tribune / NBFGR (mahseer state fish); app notes 4:29 sub 4
## SUB 1 | Blue Economy and SAGAR
[29:1:0] # What the blue economy is (asked 3 times)
[29:1:1] - **Blue economy = sustainable use of ocean (marine) resources** – ocean, coastal and inland waters – for growth, livelihoods/jobs and ecosystem conservation (APPSC FSO "Sustainable use of ocean resources"; APPSC AEE ×2 "Ocean Resources") – not water purification, space-based mapping, sky/agricultural resources or "deep-sea mining only".
[29:1:2] - India: **Draft Blue Economy Policy Framework, 2021 – Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES)**.
[29:1:3] - **SAGAR** = "**Security and Growth for All in the Region**" – PM, **2015, Mauritius**; expanded as **MAHASAGAR (2025)** to the wider Global South.
[29:1:4] ~~ Sources: Praveen CA360 June 2026 magazine p.77 (blue economy); PMF Lens July 2026 p.39 (SAGAR → MAHASAGAR); app notes 4:29 sub 5
## SUB 2 | World Fisheries – Grounds, Fishing Nations, Pearls
[29:2:0] # Fishing nations (asked 1 time)
[29:2:1] - **Norway** and **Japan** depend most on fishing – hilly/rugged land, harsh winters, little farmland; fish is their main food. Fishing is "particularly important in Britain, **Norway** and British Columbia" (Leong). APPSC Group 2 2011: "fishing is the main occupation of" → **Norway** (not New Zealand – meat and dairy). **Iceland**'s exports lean most heavily on fish.
[29:2:2] # Pearls (asked 1 time)
[29:2:3] - **Japan** = the standard answer for **largest producer of (cultured) pearls** (APPSC Group 2 Mains 2019): cultured pearls invented in Japan (**1913**, Mikimoto, **Akoya** oyster). By **volume China** now leads (freshwater pearls).
[29:2:4] # Fishing grounds
[29:2:5] TABLE head: Ground | Location
  [29:2:5.0] Grand Banks (world's largest) | Off Newfoundland, NW Atlantic – Gulf Stream meets Labrador
  [29:2:5.1] NW Pacific | Off Japan – Kuroshio meets Oyashio
  [29:2:5.2] Dogger Bank | Shallow sandbank, North Sea, ~100 km off eastern England
[29:2:6] - Favourable: **wide shallow continental shelves**, **mixing of warm and cold currents**, **upwelling** (Peru), cold waters (plankton), indented coasts.
[29:2:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Human & Economic Geography 05 p.95-97 (Norway, Japan, Grand Banks, pearls); G.C. Leong ch.18 (Part 18.2 ocr p.1); web: GIA 4Cs "Meet the mollusks" (freshwater pearls mainly China); app notes 4:29 sub 3
## SUB 3 | UNCLOS Maritime Zones and India's EEZ
[29:3:0] # India's EEZ (asked 1 time)
[29:3:1] - **India's EEZ ≈ 2.37 million sq km** (APPSC Polytechnic Lecturers) – exclusive right to all living and non-living resources; world's **18th largest**; much of it from **Andaman-Nicobar and Lakshadweep**. Coastline **11,098.81 km**.
[29:3:2] TABLE head: Zone (from baseline) | Limit | Coastal-state rights
  [29:3:2.0] Territorial sea | 12 nm | Full sovereignty (innocent passage for others)
  [29:3:2.1] Contiguous zone | 24 nm | Customs, fiscal, immigration, sanitary laws
  [29:3:2.2] EEZ | 200 nm | Sovereign rights over living and non-living resources only
  [29:3:2.3] Continental shelf | Up to 350 nm | Seabed and subsoil
  [29:3:2.4] High seas | Beyond | Freedom of navigation
[29:3:3] - **UNCLOS** adopted **1982**, in force **1994**; set up the **International Seabed Authority (ISA)**.
[29:3:4] - Indian law: **Maritime Zones Act, 1976** (Territorial Waters, Continental Shelf, EEZ and Other Maritime Zones).
[29:3:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Internal Security & DM 02 p.19 (EEZ 2.37 million sq km, coastline); PMF Science & Tech 06; app notes 4:29 sub 0
## SUB 4 | Marine Resources of Andhra Pradesh
[29:4:0] # Why the coast matters (asked 1 time)
[29:4:1] - Residuary AP (2014) has little coal and leans on its **974 km coastline (2nd longest)** – **offshore resources** (fish, aquaculture, oil and gas, ports, beach minerals) (APPSC Panchayat Secretary).
[29:4:2] - ~**30%** of India's fish, **31%** of shrimp exports (**Vannamei**); aquaculture districts: **West Godavari**, Eluru, Krishna, Bapatla, Nellore, Konaseema, Kakinada.
[29:4:3] - **10 fishing harbours** (₹3,699.09 crore) under **PMMSY, not Sagarmala**.
[29:4:4] - Oil and gas: **Krishna-Godavari (KG) basin**; beach sand minerals: **Srikakulam–Bhimunipatnam** coast.
[29:4:5] - **Centre of Excellence on Blue Economy**: **Vignan's University, Vadlamudi (Guntur)**, Aug 2026.
[29:4:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP Geography 01 p.7 (974 km, 2nd longest); app notes 4:29 sub 6
## SUB 5 | Seabed Minerals, Deep Ocean Mission and Offshore Minerals
[29:5:0] # Seabed minerals
[29:5:1] TABLE head: Mineral | Where | Metals
  [29:5:1.0] Polymetallic nodules | Central Indian Ocean Basin (CIOB) | Nickel, copper, cobalt, manganese
  [29:5:1.1] Polymetallic sulphides | Hydrothermal vents, mid-ocean ridges | Copper, zinc, lead, iron, silver, gold, platinum
  [29:5:1.2] Gas hydrates | Methane ice in seabed sediments – KG basin, Mahanadi, Andaman (National Gas Hydrate Programme) | —
[29:5:2] - **India's seabed contracts** are granted by the **ISA**:
[29:5:3] TABLE head: Year | India and the ISA
  [29:5:3.0] 1987 | India first Pioneer Investor, CIOB
  [29:5:3.1] 2002 | Contract 1: nodules, CIOB (75,000 km²)
  [29:5:3.2] 2016 | Contract 2: sulphides, Central and South West Indian Ridge
  [29:5:3.3] 15 Sep 2025 | Contract 3: sulphides, Carlsberg Ridge
[29:5:4] - Three ISA contracts now cover ~95,000 km² (as of 2026); ISA has approved only exploration – exploitation rules pending.
[29:5:5] # Deep Ocean Mission and offshore blocks
[29:5:6] - **Deep Ocean Mission**: **Ministry of Earth Sciences** (not Ports/Shipping); approved **June 2021**; **₹4,077 crore**, 5 years; one of the nine PM-STIAC missions; covers deep-sea mining and a manned submersible, ocean climate services, biodiversity, ocean survey, **energy and freshwater**, marine biology.
[29:5:7] - **Samudrayaan – Matsya 6000**: indigenous submersible, **3 crew to 6,000 m**.
[29:5:8] - **OAMDR Act 2002** (amended 2023): first tranche of **13 offshore blocks**, **28 Nov 2024**, composite licence.
[29:5:9] TABLE head: Resource | Places
  [29:5:9.0] Oil and gas | Mumbai High, Krishna-Godavari, Cauvery, Gulf of Khambhat
  [29:5:9.1] Beach placers: monazite (thorium), ilmenite (titanium) | Chavara (Kerala), Manavalakurichi (TN), Chatrapur (Odisha), AP
[29:5:10] > Chavara is a placer site, not an oil basin; nodules = Ni, Cu, Co, Mn.
[29:5:11] ~~ Sources: PMF Lens Sep 2026 p.27 (ISA contracts, Deep Ocean Mission, Matsya 6000); app notes 4:29 sub 1-2

=== NOTES 4:30 | Continental Resources – Land, Forest, Water, Mineral and Energy Resources; Conservation
## SUB 0 | Dams and Multipurpose Projects

[30:0:4] # Project Facts
[30:0:5] - **Sardar Sarovar:** part of the Narmada Valley Project; **MP gets the largest share of power (57%)**, Gujarat most of the irrigation; **Medha Patkar** founded the **Narmada Bachao Andolan**, which opposed raising its height.
[30:0:6] - **Chambal Project:** **Rajasthan and MP** (Gandhi Sagar, Rana Pratap Sagar, Jawahar Sagar, Kota barrage); Chambal is the main tributary of the Yamuna, so the Chambal Canal project belongs to the **Yamuna basin**.
[30:0:7] - **Beas Project:** Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan; **Pong** dam keeps water flowing to the **Indira Gandhi Canal**. **Mahi Bajaj Sagar:** Rajasthan and Gujarat.
[30:0:8] - A dam on the Sutlej in Himachal Pradesh above Bhakra was built to **check silt** flowing into the Bhakra reservoir.
[30:0:9] - **DVC (1948):** statutory body run jointly by the **Centre and the governments of West Bengal and Jharkhand**.
[30:0:10] - **States by number of large dams (NRLD):** **Maharashtra (most) > Madhya Pradesh > Gujarat**; Rajasthan comes before Telangana.
[30:0:11] - **After bifurcation (2014):** AP looks after Srisailam, Pulichintala and Prakasam barrage; **Telangana claims Nagarjuna Sagar and Jurala**.
[30:0:12] > Most-asked: dam → river and dam → state matches; Bhakra states; Sardar Sarovar river/states/NBA; Hirakud longest.

[30:3:2] # Interlinking of Rivers
[30:3:3] - **Garland Canal:** proposed by **Captain Dinshaw J. Dastur**; interlinking first proposed by **M. Visvesvaraya**, later **K. L. Rao** (Ganga–Cauvery link).
[30:3:4] - **National Perspective Plan (1980):** **30 links** (14 Himalayan, 16 Peninsular); implemented by **NWDA**; flagship **Ken-Betwa**.
[30:3:5] - **Pattiseema lift:** **Godavari → Krishna** (AP); also Kurnool-Cuddapah canal.
[30:3:6] - Book: "**Interlinking of Indian Rivers**" – **Radhakanta Bharati**.
[30:3:7] - Criticism: monsoons and climate change make "surplus" basins unreliable.

## SUB 4 | Watershed Management and Water Schemes
[30:4:0] - **Watershed development** = soil and moisture conservation of a whole catchment: **earthworks, soil conservation and tree planting** to conserve moisture and raise groundwater recharge – its hallmark in semi-arid India (UPSC 1994).
[30:4:1] - **IWMP** (2009-10): run by the **Department of Land Resources** (MoRD); **merged DPAP, DDP and IWDP**; key objective – **agricultural productivity and water conservation**.
[30:4:2] - IWMP/IWDP benefits: **prevents soil run-off, rainwater harvesting, groundwater recharge, regenerates vegetation** – NOT linking perennial and seasonal rivers.
[30:4:3] - **DPAP and DDP** = Department of Land Resources (MoRD), not Agriculture or Environment; **NWDPRA** = **Ministry of Agriculture**, not Rural Development (so none of the UPSC 2014 pairs is correct).
[30:4:4] - IWMP merged into **PMKSY (2015)** as the **Watershed Development Component**; CAD&WM is a PMKSY component.
[30:4:5] - **Hermann Bacher** (Swiss priest, WOTR) – **Father of community-led watershed development** in India.
[30:4:6] - **Neeranchal** – World Bank-assisted watershed project; **Watershed Development Fund** – NABARD.
[30:4:7] TABLE head: Scheme | Key facts
  [30:4:7.0] Hariyali (27 Jan 2003) | Vajpayee; Centrally sponsored watershed and wasteland development through Panchayati Raj Institutions – for the rural population, not urban
  [30:4:7.1] PMKSY (2015-16) | AIBP = faster completion of major/medium projects; Har Khet Ko Pani = CAD&WM, minor irrigation, RRR of water bodies
  [30:4:7.2] Jal Shakti Abhiyan (2019) | Water conservation and water security campaign; Phase 1: 1 Jul–15 Sep 2019; Phase 2: 1 Oct–30 Nov 2019 for states of the NE (retreating) monsoon – AP, Karnataka, Puducherry, TN
  [30:4:7.3] Atal Bhujal Yojana | First community-led CSS on demand-side groundwater management
  [30:4:7.4] Namami Gange (2014); NRCP (1995) | Ganga main stem; other rivers
[30:4:8] - Ganga pollution: mainly **urban waste rich in organic matter**.
[30:4:9] - **Rashtriya Barh Ayog** (1976; report 1980): flood-prone area about **40 million ha**; XII Plan Working Group (2011): maximum flood-affected area **49.815 million ha**.
[30:4:10] - AP (Aug 2026): Pattiseema lift water fed the **Krishna delta** in the El Niño deficit; **Gandikota** reservoir on the **Pennar** serves Rayalaseema.
[30:4:11] ~~ Sources: NCERT XII India People & Economy ch.6 (OnlyIAS Human Geography 10 p.5); PMF Human & Economic Geography 02 p.45-46 (UPSC 2014 IWDP); Shankar Environment 02 (IWDP question); PIB / Drishti on Jal Shakti Abhiyan 2019; app notes 4:30 sub 1, 7
## SUB 5 | Forest Resources and Forest Movements
[30:5:0] - **Forests are renewable**; that they improve the environment is true but does not explain why they are renewable.
[30:5:1] - **Forest dieback:** a stand of trees losing health and dying **without an obvious cause**.
[30:5:2] - **FAO (Global Forest Resources Assessment 2010):** net forest loss fell from **8.3 million ha/yr (1990s)** to **5.2 million ha/yr (2000–2010)**.
[30:5:3] - Highest share of area under forest among China, India, Indonesia, Japan: **Japan** (about two-thirds).
[30:5:4] TABLE head: Movement | Facts
  [30:5:4.0] Chipko | Himalayas (Garhwal, 1973)
  [30:5:4.1] Appiko | Karnataka – Salkani forest, Sirsi, Uttara Kannada, 8 Sep 1983; modelled on Chipko; aims – save the forests of the Western Ghats, restore greenery to denuded areas, rational use of forest resources (NOT cleaning rivers)
[30:5:5] - **NFP 1988:** 33% of the country under forest, **two-thirds in hills**; formally introduced JFM (Centre's guidelines 1990; forerunner **Arabari, West Bengal, 1972**).
[30:5:6] - **Forest Rights Act 2006:** Gram Sabhas manage community forest resources. **National Agroforestry Policy 2014** – India's first.
[30:5:7] - Terms: silviculture (raising and tending trees), agroforestry (trees with crops or livestock), jhum (NE shifting cultivation; shorter fallow → degradation and erosion).
[30:5:8] - **ISFR 2023:** largest forest area – **Madhya Pradesh** (77,073 sq km).
[30:5:9] - World: **Amazon** – largest continuous rainforest (Congo second); **taiga** – largest terrestrial biome; Bhutan – Constitution keeps ≥ 60% under forest; Canada – largest softwood and pulp exporter; dense forests lie near the equator.
[30:5:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy P1 03 p.52 (Chipko, Appiko); PMF Environment 01 p.44 (dieback); FAO 2010 figures, Japan forest share and Appiko aims – general knowledge, not checked; app notes 4:30 sub 2

[30:6:0] TABLE head: Indicator | Figure
  [30:6:0.0] Rainfall water | About 3,880 bcm a year
  [30:6:0.1] Largest water user | Agriculture (irrigation)
  [30:6:0.2] Per-capita availability | Over 5,000 m³ at Independence → about 1,400 m³ (2026)
  [30:6:0.3] India's share | 4% of world renewable water, 2.4% of land, over 18% of people
  [30:6:0.4] Groundwater | India = world's largest user (about a quarter of world extraction)
  [30:6:0.5] PMKSY after 10 years | 24.61 million ha irrigation potential; about 27 million farmers (Jul 2026)
  [30:6:0.6] Basin (replenishable groundwater, km³/yr) | Ganga 171 > Godavari 40.7 > Brahmaputra 26.5 ≈ Indus 26.5 ≈ Krishna 26.4 > Mahanadi 16.5 > Cauvery 12.3 > Narmada 10.8
[30:6:1] - Among Narmada, Krishna, Godavari, Cauvery, the **Godavari** basin has the highest groundwater potential; the Cauvery has the highest **utilisation** (55%), not potential.
[30:6:2] - Groundwater depletion: excessive pumping, loss of forests, concrete cover – **afforestation recharges**, it does not deplete.
[30:6:3] - **CGWB categories:** safe, semi-critical, critical, over-exploited, saline. Worst over-exploitation: Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, Delhi.
[30:6:4] - **Tubewells and wells:** largest irrigated area – **Uttar Pradesh**.
[30:6:5] - **Tank irrigation:** Peninsular India; **AP first** (28–29%), **Tamil Nadu** over 23% (tanks = eris) – among Tamil Nadu, Odisha, West Bengal, Karnataka, **Tamil Nadu** leads.

## SUB 7 | Resources – Classification, Land Use and Land Degradation
[30:7:0] TABLE head: Basis | Types
  [30:7:0.0] Origin | Biotic (plants, animals, micro-organisms) vs abiotic (land, water, minerals)
  [30:7:0.1] Exhaustibility | Renewable (forests, water, wildlife) vs non-renewable (fossil fuels, minerals)
  [30:7:0.2] Development | Potential; developed; stock (technology lacking – hydrogen from water); reserve (usable now, part of stock)
[30:7:1] # Resource Depletion
[30:7:2] TABLE head: Resource | Cause of depletion (APPSC 2025)
  [30:7:2.0] Groundwater | Deep bore tubewells for irrigation
  [30:7:2.1] Topsoil | Brick production
  [30:7:2.2] Biodiversity habitats | Expansion of agriculture
  [30:7:2.3] Land for buildings | Urban construction on water bodies
[30:7:3] # Land Use
[30:7:4] - **Nine-fold classification:** forests; non-agricultural uses; barren and unculturable; permanent pastures; miscellaneous tree crops; culturable wasteland; current fallow; other fallow; net sown area ("seasonal plantation reserve" is not one).
[30:7:5] - Fallow ladder: current fallow ≤ 1 yr; other fallow 1–5 yrs; culturable wasteland > 5 yrs. Highest net-sown share: Punjab and Haryana.
[30:7:6] - **India's land use (approx.):** net sown area **~46%**, forests **~23%**, other areas ~31% (2022-23: 45.9 / 23.5 / 30.6).
[30:7:7] - **Trends (NCERT):** forest, non-agricultural use, current fallow and net sown area have **increased**; **barren and wasteland, pastures and tree crops**, culturable waste and other fallow have **declined**; non-agricultural use has risen fastest. Forest area has **not** declined.
[30:7:8] - AP (undivided, 2006-07): current fallow about **6.02 lakh ha** (printed key; figure not verified).
[30:7:9] - **Wasteland:** degraded land restorable with reasonable effort; mapped by satellite (IRS) National Wastelands Monitoring.
[30:7:10] - Land degradation: erosion, waterlogging, salinisation, nutrient loss, falling water tables; UNCCD (**1994**) – desertification in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas.
[30:7:11] - Milestones: Club of Rome (Apr 1968), Limits to Growth (1972), Brundtland "Our Common Future" (1987).
[30:7:12] ~~ Sources: NCERT XII India People & Economy ch.5 land use (general knowledge, not checked); Ministry of Agriculture land use 2022-23 (P) as quoted in the PYQ explanation; app notes 4:30 sub 0, 1
## SUB 8 | Mineral Policy – MMDR Act, DMF and Deep-sea Minerals
[30:8:0] TABLE head: Act / amendment | Provision
  [30:8:0.0] MMDR Act 1957 | Parent law of mining (Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, Act 67 of 1957); it replaced the 1948 Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act
  [30:8:0.1] 2015 | Auction mandatory; District Mineral Foundation (Sec 9B); NMET
  [30:8:0.2] 2023 | Centre auctions critical and strategic minerals (lithium); exploration licence
  [30:8:0.3] 2026 (14 Aug) | States may tax mineral rights / lands only within limits set by the Centre
[30:8:1] - **DMF:** non-profit trust in every mining district; purpose – **protect the interests and benefit of persons and areas affected by mining** (it neither promotes exploration nor issues licences); funded by miners (30% of royalty for old leases, 10% for auctioned leases), not the Consolidated Fund; runs PMKKKY.
[30:8:2] - **MADA v. SAIL (2024, nine judges):** royalty is not a tax; States tax mineral rights (Entry 50) and mineral land (Entry 49).
[30:8:3] - India: diamonds – Panna (MP); chromite – Sukinda (Odisha); gold – Jonnagiri (Kurnool, AP); Peninsular plateau = mineral heartland.
[30:8:4] - **Deep sea:** India first to sign an **ISA** contract for **polymetallic sulphides** on the **Carlsberg Ridge** (2025); sulphides – Cu, Zn, Pb, Fe, Ag, Au; nodules – Mn, Co, Ni, Cu. ISA – Jamaica; ITLOS – Hamburg.

=== NOTES 4:31 | World – Continents, Major Mountain Systems, Plateaus, Plains and Deserts
## SUB 0 | Countries – Area, Borders, Coastlines and Landlocked States
[31:0:0] # Largest Countries by Area
[31:0:1] - **Order:** 1. **Russia** 2. **Canada** 3. **USA** 4. China 5. Brazil 6. Australia 7. **India** (about **2.4%** of world land; first by population). So "Russia, Canada, USA, China" is the correct descending order.
[31:0:2] - **USA vs China:** by total area (land + water) the **USA is third**, China fourth – the answer most books and keys give; by land area alone China is slightly larger.
[31:0:3] - **France** (and Argentina) are smaller than India. Ascending: **Argentina (27.96 lakh sq km) < India (32.87 lakh) < Australia (76.9 lakh) < Brazil (85.1 lakh)**.
[31:0:4] - **Largest country without land borders:** **Australia**; among Japan, Philippines, New Zealand, Cuba it is **Japan**.
[31:0:5] # Borders
[31:0:6] - **Canada–USA:** **longest international border** (**8,891 km**, incl. Alaska–Canada); much of it follows the **49th Parallel**. Next: Russia–Kazakhstan (6,846 km), Chile–Argentina (5,308 km, along the Andes).
[31:0:7] - **Most land neighbours:** **Russia** and **China**, **14 each**; India 7, longest border with **Bangladesh**.
[31:0:8] - **Israel:** **Lebanon, Syria, Jordan, Egypt** (and the West Bank, Gaza).
[31:0:9] - **Myanmar** (besides India, China): **Bangladesh, Laos, Thailand** – not Vietnam, Cambodia or Malaysia.
[31:0:10] - **Afghanistan:** **Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan** in the north, China, Pakistan, Iran (and India's PoK claim) – **not Kyrgyzstan, Azerbaijan or Russia**.
[31:0:11] - **Ukraine:** Belarus, Russia, Moldova, **Romania, Hungary**, Slovakia, Poland – not Bulgaria, Czech Republic, Latvia, Lithuania.
[31:0:12] - **Lithuania:** Latvia, Belarus, Poland, Russia (Kaliningrad) – **not Ukraine**.
[31:0:13] - **Panama:** **Costa Rica, Colombia**, Caribbean Sea and **Pacific** – **not Venezuela**.
[31:0:14] - **Indonesia** land borders: **Malaysia** (Borneo), **Timor-Leste**, **Papua New Guinea** – **not Brunei** (Brunei touches only Malaysia).
[31:0:15] - **Zambia:** DR Congo, Tanzania, Malawi, Mozambique, Zimbabwe, Namibia, Angola and a **~150 m border with Botswana at Kazungula** (books treat Kazungula as a "quadripoint" and say Zambia does not border Botswana).
[31:0:16] - **Namibia** (capital Windhoek): Angola, Zambia, Botswana, South Africa and the Atlantic – not Zimbabwe.
[31:0:17] - **Luxembourg:** landlocked, the only sovereign Grand Duchy; borders **Belgium, Germany, France**.
[31:0:18] - **Germany–Poland boundary:** strictly the **Oder–Neisse Line** (1945; recognised 1990); GK books list it as the "**Hindenburg Line**" (really a WWI German defence line in France).
[31:0:19] # Coastlines
[31:0:20] - **Longest coastline:** **Canada** (~2,02,080 km, Arctic archipelago, three oceans), then Norway, Indonesia.
[31:0:21] - **Pacific coast in South America:** **Chile, Peru, Ecuador, Colombia** – **not Venezuela** (Caribbean side).
[31:0:22] # Landlocked Countries

  [31:0:23.0] South America | Bolivia, Paraguay | Peru, Suriname, Uruguay

## SUB 2 | Continents – Area, Order, Elevation and Antarctica
[31:2:0] # Continents by Area
[31:2:1] - Descending: **Asia > Africa > North America > South America > Antarctica > Europe > Australia**.
[31:2:2] TABLE head: Continent | Area (sq km) | Share of land | Countries
  [31:2:2.0] Asia | 44.57 million (~44 million; largest) | 29.8% | 48–49
  [31:2:2.1] Africa | 30.07 million | 20.3% | 54 (most)
  [31:2:2.2] North America | 24.47 million | 16.2% | 23
  [31:2:2.3] South America | 17.84 million | 11.8% | 12
  [31:2:2.4] Antarctica | ~14 million | 9.2% | –
  [31:2:2.5] Europe | 9.95 million | 6.8% | 49–51
  [31:2:2.6] Australia / Oceania | ~8.5 million | 5.9% | 14
[31:2:3] - Two smallest: **Australia** (smallest) and **Europe**; **Antarctica is bigger than both**. Among Europe, Africa, N. and S. America, **Africa** is the biggest.
[31:2:4] - **Asia:** largest and **most populous** continent. **Africa:** "**Cradle of Mankind**" (earliest human fossils); has the **largest number of people living in extreme poverty** (about 7 in 10 of the world's extreme poor, 2023).
[31:2:5] - **Australia:** maximum **per-capita land**. **Europe:** highest **percentage of plains**.
[31:2:6] - **South America:** "**Continent of Birds**"; nearest continent to **Antarctica** (across the Drake Passage).
[31:2:7] - **Oceania:** Australia, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea – Melanesia, Micronesia, Polynesia; **Indonesia is part of Asia**.
[31:2:8] - **Oceans:** Atlantic separates the Americas from **Europe and Africa** (not Asia); Indian Ocean – Asia, Africa, Australia; Southern Ocean encircles Antarctica.
[31:2:9] # Gondwana and Antarctica
[31:2:10] - **Gondwana:** South America, Africa, Madagascar, Antarctica, Australia, Arabia, **Peninsular India** – **not North America or Europe** (Laurasia).
[31:2:11] - **Antarctica:** **highest mean elevation** (~**2,300 m**, ice sheet over 98%); Asia 923 m, North America 760 m.
[31:2:12] - Canada's **RADARSAT-1** made the first detailed, complete map of Antarctica (**1997**).
[31:2:13] - **Taylor Valley** (Antarctica): discovered by **Robert Falcon Scott (1903)**, "Valley of the Dead".
[31:2:14] - **Indian stations:** **Dakshin Gangotri** (1983, first; abandoned 1990), **Maitri** (1989), **Bharati** (2012, the **third**), run by NCPOR Goa.
[31:2:15] > Order-of-area questions repeat (UPPCS ×4, IAS 2005 ×2); Antarctica mean elevation asked twice by UPSC 1995.

## SUB 5 | Plateaus
[31:5:0] TABLE head: Type | Nature | Examples
  [31:5:0.0] Intermontane | Enclosed by mountains | Tibetan, Pamir, Bolivian (Altiplano), Mongolian, Peru, Colombia
  [31:5:0.1] Piedmont | At the foot of mountains | Piedmont (USA), Patagonia
  [31:5:0.2] Continental | Broad uplifted surface | Peninsular India, African, Arabian, Australian
  [31:5:0.3] Volcanic / lava | Lava accumulation | Deccan (one of the oldest), Columbia (NW USA)
  [31:5:0.4] Fluvial | River deposition | Panna, Bhander, Rewa, Rohtas (Vindhyan region)
[31:5:1] - **Tibetan:** highest and largest plateau; average **4,500 m**; ~2.5 million sq km. **Pamir:** "**Roof of the World**".
[31:5:2] - **Meseta:** **Iberian Peninsula** (Spain). **Anatolian:** Turkiye, between the **Pontic and Taurus** ranges.
[31:5:3] - **Colorado:** USA, cut by the **Grand Canyon**. **Columbia** is in the USA, not Iberia.
[31:5:4] - **Patagonia:** "storehouse of minerals" of South America. **East African Plateau:** **Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda**. **Abyssinian** (Ethiopian) plateau is in **Africa**, not Arabia.
[31:5:5] - **Guiana Highlands:** **northern South America** (Venezuela, Guyana, Brazil), not Africa.
[31:5:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket General Geography p.35 (plateau types, Tibetan, Pamir, Meseta); PMF World Geography 03 p.28-29, 32 (Abyssinian, East African plateaus), 04 p.4 (Colorado Plateau), 04 p.26 (Guiana Highlands); app notes 4:31 sub 5
[31:5:7] - **Colorado Plateau** (~3.4 lakh sq km) is larger than the **Columbia** (~1.6 lakh); Coconino and Aquarius are small plateaus within the Colorado.
[31:5:8] - **Yukon Plateau:** upland of interior Alaska–Yukon between the **Brooks Range** and the **Alaska Range** – not the Great Basin (Nevada–Utah).
[31:5:9] - **Madrid** stands on the **Meseta** plateau (Spain).
[31:5:10] - **Tsaidam (Qaidam) Basin:** between the **Kunlun** and the **Altyn Tagh** (Qinghai, China); the Tarim Basin (Taklamakan) lies to their north.
## SUB 6 | Plains, Basins and Regional Names
[31:6:0] - **Great Plains:** **east of the Rockies** (USA, Canada). **West Siberian Plain:** between the **Urals** and the **Yenisei**.

[31:6:4] - **Okavango Basin:** Botswana (not Patagonia).

[31:7:5] - **Prairies:** interior plains of the **USA and Canada** (APPSC Group-II 2024).
